ואלה שמות בני ישראל, And these are the names of the children of Yisrael, etc. The reason that the Book of Shemot commences with the conjunctive letter ו is to teach that all these people were righteous, just like their parents. The word ואלה also is employed to show continuity with the people who had preceded them. In this instance the preceding people were Avraham, Yitzchak and Yaakov, all of whom were outstandingly righteous. The generation mentioned at the opening of the Book of Shemot too were righteous people.

Another reason for the letter ו in this instance is to remind us that the years of exile of the Jewish people were computed as having already begun during the time of Avraham, not merely after the arrival of Yaakov in Mitzrayim (compare Tanchuma Shemot 4).

Still another reason for the Torah writing that letter is to tell us that just as the earlier generations perceived that they were in exile and accepted their fate without resentment, so the generation of which we read here also accepted their destiny without complaint.

Perhaps this will help us understand why the Torah bothered to list the names of the tribes when we have been well aware of their names since the Book of Bereshit, and particularly since the list of the seventy people who descended to Mitzrayim with Yaakov. While Rashi claims that the Torah's repeating these names after their deaths is evidence of how fond G'd was of them, this is hardly more than a homiletical explanation. Besides, if Rashi were correct then the Torah should have recorded these names after verse six in which we heard that the members of that generation had all died. Verse seven should then have commenced with the words: ואלה שמות בני ישראל.

According to our approach the Torah informs us of the reason why the names appear once more, i.e. that they had all willingly accepted their destiny to endure exile as distinct from Esav who had decided to leave the land of Kenaan by moving to Mount Seir (Bereshit 36,8). Bereshit Rabbah 82,13, attributes Esav's move to the decree of G'd mentioned to Avraham in Bereshit 15,13 that Avraham's descendants would become strangers in a foreign land. Esav wanted to escape that obligation and that is why he moved away voluntarily at that time. הבאים מצרימה, who arrived in Mitzrayim; they came in order to endure exile; את יעקב, together with Yaakov; "with Yaakov," i.e. in the same spirit as Yaakov, to discharge their duty to become exiles. The Torah wants to prove that Bnei Yisrael did not move to Mitzrayim for other reasons and that is why it writes that they came איש וביתו, everyone with his respective family, i.e. they prepared for a lengthy stay; otherwise they would have left their families in the land of Kenaan.

באו, they had come. The Torah draws our attention to the difference between הבאים, and באו. We have explained already in Bereshit 46,7 that not all of Yaakov's family were of one mind about the timing of the descent to Mitzrayim. Some volunteered, others had to be more or less coerced. The Torah again alludes to this distinction when describing the descent of the people who accompanied Yaakov.

The division may also have been different. All those who are named came to Mitzrayim of their own initiative. They might even have come without Yaakov (if, for instance their father had died before the end of the famine). However, all those whom the Torah has not named again only came as part of the entourage of Yaakov; they would never have left ארץ ישראל unless their founding father had taken such an intitiative. This is why the Torah repeated: "they came with Yaakov, each one with his family."

There is yet another possibility. The word הבאים is to prove that those people were not forced to go to Mitzrayim with Yaakov. Proof: When they returned to the land of Kenaan with the funeral cortege of Yaakov, they all returned to Mitzrayim. Had their original descent been involuntary, why would they have chosen to remain in Mitzrayim 15 years after the end of the famine? The Torah therefore gives all these people credit for accepting Hashem's decree to be strangers in a foreign land though they could have resisted implementation of that decree at that time.

ויהי כל נפש…ויוסף היה במצרים. And the total number of persons…plus Yosef who was in Mitzrayim already." Why does the Torah introduce this paragraph with the word ויהי which always introduces a painful experience? If the Torah refers to the exile, this was not the place to mention this seeing that the negative aspects of the exile did not commence till over 90 years later. Furthermore, why does the Torah have to tell us again that Yosef was already in Mitzrayim?

Perhaps we have here an oblique reference to the comment in Sotah 36 that it had been planned originally that Yosef would become the founding father of twelve tribes and that it was only due to the attempts of Potifar's wife that he forfeited this opportunity as per Bereshit 49,24. We know already that but for that unfortunate circumstance Yosef himself would have founded twelve tribes. The Torah expresses regret over that missed opportunity and that as a result the number of Bnei Yisrael who descended to Mitzrayim were only 70. Had Yosef become the founding father by fathering twelve tribes in the land of Kenaan, many more Bnei Yisrael would have been the basis of what was to become the Jewish nation. The Torah streses ויוסף היה, "and Yosef was already in Mitzrayim," i.e. prematurely, before he could complete the task assigned to him as founder of the nation.

Perhaps the Torah wants to put Yosef and family on a par with the other members of Yaakov's family who descended to Mitzrayim at the invitation of Paroh and Yosef by phrasing it thus: כל נפש…ויוסף היה במצרים, "all the persons …including Yosef who happened to be in Mitzrayim already at that time." They were all righteous though some had been born in Mitzrayim, etc. The Torah uses the word נפש for persons in the singular to show that they all formed a single spiritual unit. This is a tremendous compliment for Yosef whose life-experience was so totally different from that of his brothers and who had been mistreated by them. The Torah testified that Yosef was in no way less of a Yisraeli or part of the common heritage than his brothers who had remained in the land of Kenaan all these years. If anything, Yosef was the prime example that given the proper strength of character, one could maintain one's spiritual integrity even after having lived in Mitzrayim for many years and having occupied a position of power and prominence in that society. I have already mentioned this aspect of Yosef when I explained why Yaakov was willing to die happy the moment he had made visual contact with Yosef in Bereshit 46,30.

-8. וימת יוסף…ובני ישראל פרו, And Yosef died…and Bnei Yisrael were fruitful, etc. Why did the Torah have to repeat again that Yosef died? We have heard this at the end of פרשת ויחי. Why do we have to be told that all the other brothers and that whole generation of Bnei Yisrael who had come to Mitzrayim died? What is the connection between the respective deaths of the brothers and that of the generation and the proliferation of the בני ישראל in the next verse? If this was only a description of the manner in which the Jewish population explosion in Mitzrayim occurred, the Torah should have written: ויפרו וישרצו בני ישראל, instead of ובני ישראל פרו וישרצו. The grammar is wrong here.

Actually, the two verses must be read in conjunction as describing the beginning of Jewish servitude and its causes. There were a total of four causes that brought about the enslavement of the Jewish people. The first cause was Yosef's death. Had Yosef lived on for some time the Mitzrim would never have ruled over his countrymen. The Torah therefore informs us that as long as Yosef was alive Bnei Yisrael lived a serene and comfortable life.

The second cause leading to enslavement of the Jewish people was the death of Yosef's brothers. As long as even a single one of these brothers remained alive the Mitzrim honoured them as our sages derive in Sotah 13 from Bereshit 50,14 which hints that after the Mitzrim had become aware of the honour paid by Kenaani kings to Yaakov's bier, they began to honour all of Yaakov's' sons, something they had not done previously.

The third cause leading to enslavement of the Jewish people was the death of the entire generation of Jewish immigrants, the sixty-six persons who had been born in the land of Kenaan. All of these people were regarded as invited guests by the Mitzrim, and there was no question of discriminating against them legally. This may also have been due to their being perceived as more intelligent than the local population so that they could outwit anyone planning to take advantage of them.

The fourth and final cause leading to the enslavement of the Jewish population was their unusual fertility. Any of the causes that had restrained the Mitzrim from planning some way of keeping the Jewish population increase at bay had now been removed. When we keep this in mind we understand why the Torah wrote: "and the children of Yisrael had already been fruitful, etc." The Torah did not want to inform us of this detail but to indicate that it now served as a cause of the process of enslavement.

A further cause, one that did not have to do with Yosef, the brothers, or the first generation of Jewish immigrants to Mitzrayim, was the fact that a new Paroh arose in Mitzrayim. Even according to the view expressed in Sotah 11 that the word "new" only referred to new legislation designed to subdue the Jewish population, the absence of the four causes already mentioned which had held up discrimination against the Yehudim also helped to shape Paroh's attitude now. The plain meaning of the verse is, of course, that it refers to a brand new Paroh, a person who had not known the Yosef who had interpreted the dream of Paroh at least 102 years earlier.

Our difficulty is that the Torah only needed to write that the whole generation had died out. Why did the Torah have to refer separately to the death of Yosef, the brothers, and that of the generation? If there had not been enslavement as long as a single one of that generation was alive, there most certainly had not been any enslavement as long as one of the brothers or Yosef himself had been alive!

Perhaps the Torah wanted to describe a gradual deterioration in the status of the Yehudim in Mitzrayim which commenced with Yosef's death. At that time the Yehudim who had up to then been considered the elite of Mitzri society were reduced to being no more than equals to the Mitzrim at large. Once Yosef's brothers died the social position of the Yehudim underwent a further deterioration, some Mitzrim beginning to detest them. However, they still had not lost their status of legal equality with the rest of the population. Once the last of the surviving Jewish immigrants died, the legal position of the Yehudim had become sufficiently shaky to enable a new king to legislate against them. The principal reason was that the proliferation of the Yehudim and the high degree of their visibility throughout the country frightened the local population and they feared that the Yehudim would eventually try to dominate them.

You may counter that according to the tradition of our sages the Yehudim did not suffer discrimination as long a single one of the tribal heads was alive, or according to our interpretation even as long as a Jewish immigrant survived. Our sages have not expressed themselves in such absolute terms. We find in chapter three of Seder Olam that 116 years elapsed between the death of Levi until the Exodus. The author adds that the actual enslavement did not last for more than 86 years, i.e. from the birth of Miriam. She was named מרים as a reminder of the מרירות the bitterness which characterised the life of the Jewish people at that time. You see from the above that at the time the last surviving brother of Yosef died, the Yehudim were still free. I conclude therefore that the enslavement did not commence until after the last of the immigrant Yehudim had died. The Torah compared these immigrants to the tribal heads because as long as they were alive their very lives protected the Yehudim against legal discrimination.

ויאמר אל עמו הנה עם בני ישראל, He said to his people: "here we have the nation of the children of Yisrael, etc." The expression הנה in this verse may be understood once we remember the interpretation of Bereshit 34,30 where Yaakov censured his sons saying עכרתם אותי, "you have made my image clouded" (as opposed to clearly transparent). Bereshit Rabbah 80,12 states that Yaakov and the Kenaani had a long standing tradition that the Yehudim would overpower the Kenaani. This was supposed to take place after the Yehudim numbered at least 600.000. Now that Shimon and Levi had jumped the gun by destroying the inhabitants of Shechem, Yaakov was afraid that such a premature action would backfire. Paroh, king of Mitzrayim referred to this ancient prediction that the Jewish people would display such military strength, when he observed how the Yehudim constantly gained in numbers and vigour. הנה, i.e. the time has arrived of which the prophecy foretold.

הבה נתחכמה לו פן ירבה, "let us outsmart them before they become more numerous, etc." If we do not put a stop to their population explosion they will do exactly what the prophecy had forecast, namely ועלה מן הארץ, "they will move back to the land of Kenaan and destroy our Kenaani brothers." Mitzrayim's first decree against such a possibility had been a ban on Yehudim leaving the country.

The word הנה may also be understood as follows: הנה עם, "this here nation," i.e. they are a people different from any other. Every other nation is an amalgamation of a number of different peoples. Not so the Jewish people. They are monolithic, like a single block. When Paroh added the words רב ועצום, he explained that the strength of the Jewish nation lay in its singlemindedness and unity of purpose. Because of this they represented a danger totally disproportionate to their actual numbers. Most military commanders are familiar with the phenomenon of a small, elite, but highly motivated force.

There is another aspect of the words רב ועצום. They are רב, i.e. they multiply at an unnatural rate; ועצום, although it is well known that multiple births usually result in the children being below average weight, physique, etc., in the case of the Jewish people this was not so. Not only did they multiply at a phenomenal rate, but they were all physically healthy specimens. In fact each individual Yehudi, though in most instances the product of a multiple birth, was ועצום ממנו, physically stronger than any of us Mitzrim. As a result, the only way to counter their physical predominance was to outsmart them. The word ממנו would then refer only to the word עצום, and not to the word רב.

Yet another way of understanding the sequence רב ועצום ממנו, is that the king stated that the fact that the Yehudim had developed as they did was by taking something that should have belonged to the Mitzrim, ממנו, "from us." He wanted to forestall any argument by his countrymen who would protest the injustice of suddenly declaring part of their citizenry as inferior, as slaves. To that end he told his people that the Yehudim were actually owned by the Mitzrim who had fed them during the years of famine and enabled them to not only survive but to thrive. Only 70 Yehudim immigrated. If they now were a numerous and strong people they owed it all to the Mitzrim. It was quite in order for the Mitzrim to legislate measures that would ensure their own supremacy. The way to do that was to outsmart them.

It is customary for the kings and leaders of highly developed countries to point with pride to the intelligentsia of their nation which alone is responsible for the prominence and the high regard in which their country is held. Wherever Yehudim were exiled, the host country developed out of all proportion due to the Jewish contribution to their host country (compare Eichah 1,5) "its oppressors developed into being the head." In the case of Mitzrayim, the elite were the Yehudim. Allowing the elite to depart was equivalent to what is called a "brain drain" in contemporary society. Paroh told his countrymen that unless they took measures to prevent such a brain drain, i.e. forbid the Yehudim to leave, they would eventually also lose their position in the world as a leading civilisation. The reason the Yehudim might decide to leave Mitzrayim was that they admired brainpower not military power. If Mitzrayim were to be involved in warfare, the Yehudim might prefer to migrate elsewhere.

וישימו עליו שרי מסים, They set taskmasters over them, etc. Where was the superior intelligence in applying brute force to the Jewish people? This was not an act of wisdom! Besides, why did the Yehudim appear to have accepted this procedure without protest? Why did the people who were famed for employing their brains suddenly become bricklayers? The sages in Sotah 11 describe the enslavement of the Jewish population as having occurred progressively; they were sweet-talked into volunteering their services for patritotic reasons until they suddenly found their labour not only as being taken for granted but they could not withdraw it from their superiors. This whole process must have started somewhow. We must assume therefore that before appointing taskmasters, the Mitzrim appealed to Bnei Yisrael to demonstrate patriotism in return for all the good the Mitzrim had done for them during the previous century.

The plain meaning of the verse, however, seems to be that force was used to make Bnei Yisrael become bricklayers. The words: "let us outsmart them" must therefore not be applied to the details of the enslavement but to the drowning of Yisraeli babies in the sea as discussed by the Midrash.

At first glance, the words "in order to oppress them" seem superfluous; the intent was clear without these words. We must also analyse why the Torah needed to add the word בסבלותם, "during their forced labour." What precisely is this word meant to exclude?

Perhaps the shrewdness of the Mitzrim can be understood thus: Paroh no doubt had a team of engineers and builders who were civil servants employed in the construction of towns, etc. Such engineers were known as Mass. The word occurs in that context in Kings I 5,27. The 30.000 people described there as מס were the ones appointed over the total work force of over 150.000 described as doing the preparatory work for building the Holy Temple. Paroh appointed such people to guide the inexperienced Bnei Yisrael in their labours. Bnei Yisrael were not able to object to this as the fact that they were being bossed by qualified engineers was not demeaning seeing they themselves were novices in that field. The Torah adds that the intention of the Mitzrim in appointing these engineers as taskmasters was not because of their superior skills as Bnei Yisrael assumed, but to assert progressively harsher pressures and discipline on the Yisraeli labourers. The Mitzrim withheld vital data from Bnei Yisrael without which the tasks allotted to the Yisraeli labourers could not be successfully completed. Bnei Yisrael therefore depended on the help of these engineers which gradually turned from help to oppression. This is what our sages had in mind when they spoke about the Mitzrim sweet-talking Bnei Yisrael into forced labour, i.e. פה דך turned in to פרך.

וכאשר יענו אותו כן ירבה, The more they oppressed them the more they increased. There is a beautiful explanation by the Zohar second volume page 95 on Kohelet 8,9. Shlomo says that "there is a time when one man rules over another to his detriment." The Zohar explains that when one has to endure persecution and troubles, the good [which may have been mixed with the evil. Ed.] is distilled from the evil joining other areas which are totally good; by the same token the evil of that mixture joins other areas of pure evil. These two details are hinted at when Shlomo speaks of לרע לו. Similarly, the Torah here tells us the same thing. The more persecution Bnei Yisrael suffered the more "good" was released from what had been only a mixture of good and evil previously. With the release of that "good", i.e. good qualities, the Yisraeli families merited having more and more children. Hence the Torah adds the words וכן יפרץ in the sense of ופרצת ימה וקדמה, "You will burst forth to the West and to the East, etc." Alternatively, the word may mean "it achieved a breaking forth" i.e. a separation from an environment in which the good had been forced to mix with the evil. The evil was now released and separated. This resulted in the famous "iron crucible" in which the character of the Yisraeli people was forged in Mitzrayim.

The plain meaning of the verse is that for every unjustified act of cruelty by the Mitzrim, Hashem compensated the Jewish people with a commensurate increase in the number of babies that were born to them. Additional hands enabled the parents to meet the work quota imposed upon them by the Mitzrim. The words כן ירבה, "so they would multiply," would then mean that the additional number of children made up for the reduced performance by their weakened parents in proportion to the emasculating effect of the hard labour. This became a vicious circle as the Mitzrim kept increasing the workload.

וימררו את חייהם, They made their lives bitter, etc. The Torah speaks of עבודה קשה, to describe work which was very difficult by its very nature without it being performed under intolerable conditions. What was the nature of this work? The making of clay bricks or working in the fields.

The Torah adds the words את כל עבודתם "with all their labours," meaning that you should not think that the Mitzrim at any time relaxed their demands on these Jewish labourers. On the contrary, they added new tasks to the existing daily quota of bricks that they demanded to be delivered. The Mitzrim's argument was that as long as the Yehudim had been inexperienced they had supplied them with the building materials. As the Yehudim became more experienced and faster they were no longer given the building materials but had to provide it themselves. This was all part of the Mitzrim's shrewdness to prevent an increase in the number of Yehudim. None of this helped them. This is why the king resorted to an order to kill all male Jewish babies.

ויאמר מלך מצרים למילדות, The king of Mitzrayim said to the midwives, etc. So far the Torah had described everything that happened in the plural, i.e. "they imposed taskmasters," "they enslaved them," etc. The king enjoyed a consensus of his people for his action (perhaps because the discrimination against the Yehudim had not yet been enshrined in law, but was "merely" a clever ruse to disenfranchise part of the population). Now, however, the king alone resorted to a measure which would not become public knowledge and would not run the risk of the Jewish mothers trying to hide the fact that they were pregnant so as to mislead the midwives. I will go into details later.

למילדות העבריות, to the Hebrew midwives, etc..It is interesting to surmise what exactly the king said to these midwives the first time. [remember that the Torah credits the king with a second אמירה in the next verse. Ed.] Perhaps the Torah has clued us in with the words: "the name of one was Shifrah, whereas the name of the other one was Puah." No doubt there had been numerous midwives who attended the Jewish women. The king did not bother to know any of them by name except those whom he entrusted with a specific task. The Torah tells us that the king spoke to them by name, thus selecting them to perform a Royal command. By calling them by name, the king elevated them to the status of "midwives -in-chief." He had to commence his instructions by saying: "when you deliver the Hebrew women, etc." meaning that the order he was giving applied not only to those two but to all the Hebrew midwives. He instructed them directly as a sign of promoting them over their colleagues.

We encounter the expression אמירה as one which describes appointing someone to a high position in Devarim 26, 17-18 where Yisrael and G'd each elevate the other to an exclusively superior status. Yisrael had appointed G'd as its only G'd, and in return G'd appointed Yisrael as His chosen people. Perhaps the fact that the midwives risked the displeasure of Paroh as well as being demoted or worse is reflected in the reward G'd gave them as reported by the Torah in verse 21.

ויאמר…וראיתן על האבנים, He said: "look at the birthstool, etc." Why did Paroh have to instruct the midwives to look at the birthstool? Was it not enough to instruct them to kill male babies? It is true that our sages in Sotah 11 say that Paroh gave the midwives a sign which would alert them to the approaching birth of a male baby i.e. if the head of the baby was facing downwards, whereas if the head faced upwards this was an indication that a baby girl was about to be born. I have never understood why the midwives would need to be told such a sign [After all they were supposed to be the experts, not Paroh. Ed.]. Another thing we have to know is why Paroh did not decree death on all Jewish babies. It is most unlikely that he was motivated by a desire to ensure that some Yehudim would survive. Why did he not command the midwives simply: "kill them," without suggesting that they do something first which would eventually result in the death of these boy babies? What is the precise meaning of "If it turns out to be a daughter, let her live?" If Paroh himself had only decreed death on the males, why would the midwives need to be told to let the girls live? Surely midwives would not murder voluntarily!

We must assume that Paroh wanted to ensure that his plan would succeed. Which expectant mother would expose her unborn child to be killed by inviting the midwife? Paroh therefore told the midwives to behave in a manner which could not arouse any suspicion. By having a look at the birthstool to determine if a girl or a boy was about to be born, they would be able to kill the baby prior to its being born and tell the mother that the baby had been stillborn. The midwives would announce this before the baby had left the mother's womb. How did the midwives know all this? This is where the sign mentioned in the Talmud comes in. Paroh told the midwives how to make sure beforehand. When he said והמתן אותו "and you shall kill it," the extra letter ו indicates that they should only kill after first having made sure that it was a male baby. The baby was to be killed before it could be heard at the moment of birth.

The words אם בת היא mean that Paroh was anxious to avoid having the mothers think that the midwives were implicated in murder; therefore as long as the mothers felt that some of their babies survived birth they would not grow suspicious of the midwives. Presumably the midwives were not even to reveal that the stillborn baby had been a boy. In this fashion suspicions could be long delayed.

Paroh displayed a double portion of shrewdness since it was also his objective to prevent the Yehudim from emigrating. As the proportion of females would increase they would be forced to look for Mitzri husbands due to the dearth of eligible Jewish males. Once the two peoples began to merge through intermarriage there was no longer any fear that they would try to emigrate. Moreover, from a mystical point of view, intermarriage results in holy souls becoming so intertwined with souls of impure origin that any eventual separation would become well nigh impossible. After all, our sages are on record in Vayikra Rabbah 32,5 that the Jewish people could not be redeemed from Mitzrayim until 4 conditions existed, one of which was careful abstention from all kinds of incest and sexual licentiousness. Kabbalists interpret the words גן נעול in Shir Hashirim 4,12 as "chaste as a garden locked," i.e. that if the Yehudim had intermarried in Mitzrayim they would never have been redeemed.

ותיראן המילדות את האלוקים, The midwives were Elokim-fearing, etc." Why did the Torah repeat that: 1) "they did not do what the king had told them to do," 2) "they kept the children alive?" According to Sotah 11 they supplied food and water for these boy babies. If so, why had they not been doing this before the king's decree came into effect? Perhaps all the Torah wanted to tell us is that they did not stop to provide these services at their own expense. The Torah therefore would describe the level of the midwives' fear of Elokim. They did what they could to keep these babies alive; they most certainly did not kill the babies.

It is also possible that as long as everything was normal they never even thought about providing food and water for the babies. Once Paroh had decreed that the boy babies should be killed, the midwives feared that if by chance one of those children should die they would be blamed for the death. They now began to provide food and water for these babies in order to deflect such suspicions. Perhaps this is the reason for the word את when the Torah describes the midwives as Elokim-fearing. They also wanted to be seen as Hashem-fearing in the eyes of man.

כאשר דבר, as he had said. The letter כ which precedes the word אשר is a Kaf hadimyon describing a comparison, a similarity. The Torah tells us that not only did the midwives not do what the king had ordered them to do, but that they did not even do anything similar to what the king had demanded of them. The Torah could also be telling us something about the general fate of Royal decrees. Normally, when a powerful king issues a decree it is observed by his subjects due to fear. As people notice that not every violation is followed by severe penalties, more and more people begin to ignore irksome decrees. In this instance the Torah tells us that the decree was not even observed when it was still new. The midwives לא עשו, never carried out, כאשר דבר, as soon as he had said it. The word כאשר may be understood as "as soon as," just as in Bereshit 27,30: "as soon as Yitzchak finished speaking."

מדוע לא עשיתם…זתחיינן את הילדים? "Why did you not do…and you kept these children alive?" What did the king refer to when he asked the midwives: "why did you do, etc?" Their crime was what they had not done! Not killing the babies surely is not described as an activity! The king should have asked: "why did you not do etc.?" Furthermore, what did the king mean when he accused the midwives of keeping the children alive? If he referred to the fact that they supplied food and water, how did the midwives' answer satisfy him? Their answer would be equivalent to rebellion against the king's command!

Perhaps Paroh was not really sure that they had been supplying food to these babies as they certainly would not do this while other Mitzrim were looking on. One could certainly not accuse any Bnei Yisrael as reporting such a thing to the king. Basing itself on Shemot 3,22 where Bnei Yisrael were told 12 months before the Exodus that at that time women would "borrow" silver trinkets from their neighbours, Vayikra Rabbah 32,5 points out that not a single Yisraeli revealed this information to Paroh or to any other Mitzri. Bnei Yisrael did not snitch on one another during that time. It must be assumed therefore that Mitzrim did observe the midwives bringing victuals to the houses of pregnant Yisraeli women. These Mitzrim also became aware that boy babies were being born and raised. Paroh therefore referred to the food the midwives were bringing to the pregnant mothers when he asked: "why did you do this?" Unless the midwives kept the boy babies alive, Paroh would have attributed their actions as designed to help the baby girls stay alive. Under the circumstances, i.e. the appearance of live baby boys, he had to assume that their existence was due to the midwives' action. Paroh simply used his powers of imagination. He had no proof of any sort that the midwives had contravened his orders.

כי לא כנשים המצריות העבריות, "the Hebrew women are unlike the Mitzri women, etc." Why did the midwives use such cumbersome language? All they had to say was לא כמצריות העבריות. Besides, how does their answer address Paroh's accusation that they supplied food to keep the babies alive? It appears that Paroh was satisfied with their answer! Another difficulty is the word וילדו; why did they not say ויולדות, "and they proceeded to give birth?"

The expression נשים מצריות mentioned by the midwives refers to the elite of the Mitzri women. The midwives explained to Paroh that the Hebrew women were superior even to the elite of the Mitzri women in that they either did not need the services of a midwife at all, or were חיות, knowledgeable in that art, and helped each other without reference to outside professionals.

Perhaps the midwives hinted that the Jewish women possessed a) the superior skills with which they were born, b) the skills possessed by the natural born Mitzri women which they had acquired during the years they had lived in Mitzrayim. They combined the best skills of both categories of women. If Paroh wanted to know why they had not assisted in the births as emissaries of the king, the Hebrew women had always given birth already before the midwife could arrive; the Hebrew women had misled them concerning when a birth would be due. All of this is part of the meaning of their being חיות. The word וילדו means the birth had already taken place by the time the midwives arrived. If they had visited these expectant women bringing with them food and water it was in order to win these women's confidence so that when the time to give birth arrived they would trust them and let them assist. However, all this had been in vain. If, after finding that these women had already had their babies, the midwives would have taken the food away they would only have aroused suspicion that the food had not been intended as a friendly gift at all. In this manner the midwives satisfied Paroh while admitting that what the Mitzri women had reported to him was absolutely true, but the conclusions they had drawn did not fit the facts.

וייטב אלוקים למילדות, G'd dealt well with the midwives, etc. We are entitled to know what precisely were the favours G'd did for the midwives. Perhaps the verse alludes to the houses that are described in the next verse. If that were so, however, there would have been no point in interrupting this sequence by stating that "the people increased and became very powerful." It appears rather that the verse explains the cause of the increase in the numbers of Bnei Yisrael. The very food and water which the midwives provided resulted in G'd dealing well with the midwives. G'd enabled the midwives to continue their economically expensive efforts to feed the many newly born babies. Had G'd not helped them economically, they would not have had the wherewithal to supply all that food which resulted in the increase of the numbers of Bnei Yisrael. The Torah reports the reward G'd provided for the midwives themselves only in the next verse where we are told that He built houses for them.

The Torah may also have hinted that when G'd realised the degree of piety demonstrated by the midwives, He decided to reward them by providing them with unlimited opportunities to continue their good work. The word וייטב is followed by וירב העם to show cause and effect. The "good" G'd did for the midwives was that they saw their efforts rewarded by an increase in the Yisraeli population. Who knows if leaders such as Moshe and Aharon were not provided by G'd for Yisrael as a direct reward for the selfless efforts of Yocheved and Miriam (the two midwives)? From a mystical dimension, Moshe is perceived as a soul embracing all of Yisrael, i.e. our souls are "branches" of Moshe's soul as per Yeshayahu 63,11 where Moshe is equated with G'd's people Yisrael.

According to Rashi who describes the "good" Hashem did for the midwives as the houses Hashem is reported to have provided for them as mentioned in the next verse, we could say that the Torah first had to mention that the people kept increasing as providing a caste of Priests as well as Royalty, would not make much sense unless there were a sufficient number of Bnei Yisrael to warrant all this.

ויצו פרעה לכל עמו, Paroh commanded his entire nation, etc. Whereas originally Paroh's command to the midwives to kill new born boy babies was a secret deal between him and the midwives, something the Hebrew women did not know about, now, in view of the failure of that plan, he resorted to a public announcement; he believed that in view of the continued expansion of the Yisraeli population he would have popular support for such a draconian measure. An additional factor forcing Paroh's hand to go public with the decree to drown all boy babies may have been that according to astrologers Paroh foresaw that the redeemer of Bnei Yisrael would be born and would end his career prematurely due to water (Sanhedrin 101). Paroh mobilised every Mitzri to participate in this decree in order to precipitate this event.

The Torah says לאמור, i.e. not every Mitzri should personally commit such a murder but that he should tell the Hebrew parent to drown his child seeing it was a Royal decree. Paroh's interpretation of what the astrologers had told him was that Moshe would find a premature death by water at the hand of a Yisraeli. This is why he insisted that Bnei Yisrael themselves kill the children. The fact that Yocheved herself exposed Moshe to a watery death is proof that the Mitzrim themselves did not drown the children.
It is also possible that the meaning of the word לאמור at this point is that only the neighbours of Bnei Yisrael were to be involved in this, not the entire population.

Some of our rabbis felt (Sotah 12) that Paroh commanded that all boy babies (Mitzri as well as Jewish) born on a certain day should be drowned as he believed that this was the day on which the Jewish redeemer was to be born. Such an exegesis is homiletics. The plain meaning is that the decree concerned only Jewish boy babies. Had it been in effect for only a single day, why did Yocheved feel she had to hide Moshe for three months? Surely the decree was in effect for an indefinite period during the time Moshe was born. The words לכל עמו simply mean that "his entire people be acquainted with this decree."

כי טוב הוא ותצפנהו, so she hid him. What precisely was the "goodness" that Yocheved observed when Moshe was born? Our sages (Sotah 12) say that Moshe was born without a foreskin and that the house was filled with light when he was born. Surely this is homiletics. Besides, what does Yocheved's hiding Moshe have to do with her observing that he was "good?" Assuming Moshe had not been "good," would she not have had motherly feelings of pity for his future?

We can determine the meaning of the verse from the comment of our sages in Sotah 12 that the Mitzrim calculated the length of her pregnancy from the day Yocheved remarried Amram. She gave birth to Moshe six months and a day after he was conceived. Normally, babies born after only six months of pregnancy do not have much of a chance to survive, whereas babies born after seven months have an excellent chance to develop normally. The average mother is unable to determine to the day how long her pregnancy has been in progress. When she gives birth to a baby after six months pregnancy the baby is considered as aborted. The Torah told us that when Yocheved looked at the fetus she realised that contrary to her expectations he was healthy and well. This was the "good" that she saw. This is also why she took extraordinary care to nurse this child through the difficult period until it would be out of danger. She endangered herself by hiding Moshe seeing that the Mitzrim used to carry out house to house searches for Jewish babies. Our sages base their exegesis on the Torah choosing the word טוב rather than any other word describing Moshe's state of health. They concluded that he must have been born without a foreskin. According to our tradition Adam was created without a foreskin. As a result of his sin his glans became covered with additional tissue, something that required removal if man wanted to regain a status the Torah describes as "perfect" when G'd instructed Avraham to circumcise himself (compare Sanhedrin 38).

ונערותיה הולכות, walking with her ladies-in-waiting, etc. Why is that detail pertinent to the story of Moshe's rescue? Perhaps the Torah felt that inasmuch as Batya (Paroh's daughter) had performed such a great deed in rescuing the life of a Jewish baby, she deserved that all the details be revealed for all to know. It is a well known fact that a Royal princess does not go down to the river to bathe without her attendants. Moreover, it is customary that amongst her attendants there should be one who is senior, in charge of all the other junior attendants. The Torah speaks about "her attendants who were walking, etc." Presumably, the Torah means that at the time when the princess was actually bathing in the water all the other attendants were walking some distance away, affording the princess a degree of privacy while she bathed. Only the senior attendant stayed close to the princess. The Torah referred to this senior attendant when it writes: "she sent out her maidservant who picked up the basket." It is possible that the princess sent her maidservant to save the baby whereas the maidservant merely picked up the basket without the baby. In either event, the princess deserves praise for displaying noble human feelings. Her soul was pure, indicating that sometimes something pure emerges from something impure (Iyov, 14,4). One of two things may have happened. 1) Although the princess was attended by only a single servant at the time, she sent even that servant away and she herself picked up the baby remaining alone and vulnerable at the time. 2) Although the princess had only one attendant close by at the time, having sent her other maids some distance away, she even took a chance by sending the one remaining servant to pick up the basket with the baby.

ותראהו את הילד והנה נער בכה, When she saw the child it turned out to be a crying boy. Why did the Torah write ותראהו, "she saw him," instead of simply "she saw, etc.?" Presumably she assumed that the basket would contain an abandoned baby and she planned to rescue the baby. The Torah therefore refers to the princess "seeing what she expected to see, i.e. an abandoned child." Had the Torah written ותרא את הילד, the Torah would have created the impression that the princess saw something she had not expected.

Our sages in Sotah 12 explain the pronoun הו at the end of ותרא as a reference to Batya seeing the שכינה together with the child. This is homiletics. We would have to assume that Batya had experience with the way the שכינה looked from her father and grandfather, something quite unlikely! Our sages may simply have meant that Batya saw that the baby was surrounded by a great halo; Hashem arranged for this in order to impress Batya that this baby was someone special. The Zohar section 2, page 12 writes something similar concerning the words "the boy was crying," namely that the cries were on behalf of the Jewish people's suffering in exile." Hashem opened her eyes in order for her to be able to "see" the great light surrounding Moshe.

Alternatively, Batya's experience with the שכינה may be explained in terms of Shemot Rabbah 1,23 according to which Batya suffered from Tzoraat, the dreaded skin disease. As soon as she touched the basket she felt that she had been healed. This was her encounter with the שכינה. The word נער may then have a double meaning. When the Syrian general Naamon was healed of his Tzoraat, the prophet described his flesh as again becoming like that of a teen-aged boy, נער, (Kings II 5,14).

ותחמול עליו. She pitied him. Seeing that she had already set out determined to save the child, the pity mentioned here may refer to her determination to nurse the child. This is why Moshe's sister immediately volunteered to call a Jewish wet nurse to nurse Moshe. According to Sotah 12 all this occurred after Moshe refused to accept milk from the breasts of non Jewish wet nurses.

ותאמר מילדי העברים זה. She said: "this one is one of the Jewish babies." This was quite obvious as the Yehudim would abandon their children near the river on account of Paroh's decree. On the other hand, if all this occurred on the one day when Paroh had ordered the Mitzrim to throw also their new-born boy babies into the Yeor, how did Batya know that Moshe was a Jewish baby? This may have forced our sages in Sotah to say that Moshe refused to drink the milk of non Jewish wet nurses. [I do not see this as a compelling explanation. The fact that the child had no foreskin clearly marked him as Jewish unless the Yehudim had abandoned the practice of circumcision already at that time as is evident eighty years later at the time of the Exodus. Ed.]

Accordingly, the Torah does tell us something that was not so obvious after all. Let us examine if the reason Batya saved the baby was because she thought it might be an abandoned Mitzri baby, or if she had made up her mind to save the baby even if it turned out to be a Jewish baby. If we were to assume the former, the words מילדי העברים זה express Batya's amazement at the fact that the child was Jewish. This would indicate that originally the thought of saving a Jewish child had not occurred to her. There would be nothing unusual about a Gentile displaying sympathy only for her own kind. Even though we observe that she held the child and hired a nursemaid for him after she found out that it was a Jewish child, this fact does not prove that she would have saved the child and have displayed pity for it if G'd had not first healed her from her affliction and provided a sign that the child was someone out of the ordinary. These incidents acquainted Batya with the wonderful ways of G'd.

If we are to assume that Batya already set out to rescue the baby although she was aware that it would turn out to be a Jewish baby, then the words מילדי העברים must be understood as the reason why the baby refused to suckle at the breasts of the Mitzri wet nurses. It was not because the baby had become weak through lying in the reeds of the river, or for any other biological reason, but because it was a Jewish baby. This is why his sister (Miriam) immediately volunteered the services of a Jewish wet nurse stressing the words: מן העבריות, "one of the Hebrew women," in order to prove that she knew the true reason why the baby refused to be nursed. This is also why the Torah had to report in verse nine that the child's mother took the child and was able to nurse him.

ותקרא שמו משה, she called him Moshe, etc. You will observe a difference between the way the Torah reported the naming of Yitzchak, Yaakov, and Yaakov's sons compared to the way Moshe was named. In the case of all the patriarchs the Torah first mentions the reason for the particular name (compare Bereshit 21,6, 25,25 25,26, and 29,33). In the examples mentioned the Torah first explained the reasons for the names before telling us what the names were. Here, on the other hand, the Torah first mentions the name given to Moshe by Batya before explaining its significance.

Perhaps all the matriarchs possessed a measure of the Holy Spirit which enabled them to appreciate the deeper meaning of these names. Batya did not possess Holy Spirit so that her naming Moshe did not reflect special insights on her part as to the deeper significance of that name. The Torah alludes to this by reversing the sequence in which it reports Moshe being named. It is very interesting to read what the Zohar section 3, page 276 in the Tikkunim 69 writes about the allusions contained in the name. Hashem inspired Batya to name Moshe as she did; she herself was totally unaware of the additional implications of the name Moshe. All she was aware of was that inasmuch as she had drawn him from the water that event should be reflected in his name.

It is also possible that Batya was very careful not to publicise the name Moshe and what had inspired it seeing she had flouted both her father's and her people's wishes that the Jewish boy babies be killed. She did call the child Moshe. The words: "for I have drawn him from the water," were revealed only by the Torah, not by her.

2,11 איש עברי מאח ;יו, a Hebrew man, one of his brethren. The Torah makes a point of adding "one of his brethren." This is the Torah's way of hinting that Moshe recognised that the individual in question was one of the righteous Bnei Yisrael. There were at that time both righteous and wicked Bnei Yisrael. It is worthwhile reading how the Mechilta 12,26 interprets the meaning of Shemot 13,18 that Bnei Yisrael marched out of Mitzrayim חמושים, reduced to one fifth of their original number. According to the Mechilta only one in every five Bnei Yisrael took part in the Exodus. The other 80% of Bnei Yisrael (the wicked ones) died during the plague of darkness so as not to publicise that fact and allow the Mitzrim to gloat. The two Yehudim who are described as Yehudim fighting amongst themselves in verse thirteen were not described as "Moshe's brethren;" this proves that they were wicked Yehudim; according to Shemot Rabbah 1,29 they were Datan and Aviram of whom we hear more in פרשת קרח.

?ויאמר לרשע למה חכה רעך He said to the wicked one: "why are you about to strike your companion?" Moshe addressed the one of the two who was clearly wicked. He referred to the victim as "your companion," because if the victim were as wicked as the attacker why would the attacker want to strike him, seeing they were birds of a feather. Alternatively, Moshe recognised that he dealt with one righteous and one wicked Yisraeli. This is why he challenged the attacker saying: "why are you about to strike a righteous person, someone who has not done you any harm?" He called the righteous person רעך, i.e. he relates to you like a friend. Although the Torah described the two as apparently on the same moral level when it says שני אנשים נצים, "two quarrelling people," it will be found that one of them started the fight because he was wicked, whereas the other continued the quarrel without compelling cause.

את הדבר הזה, this matter, etc. Moshe used the word הזה, to indicate that it was only after this aggressive Yehudi had said to Moshe: "are you going to kill me also, etc." that he realised with certainty that he had observed him killing the Mitzri.

ויבקש להרוג אותו. He tried to kill him. This means that Paroh tried to establish proof that Moshe had killed the Mitzri as a result of which he would be brought to trial and be executed. This is why Moshe fled from Paroh in case Paroh would obtain enough proof to make him stand trial. On the other hand, the words מפני פרעה may refer to Paroh's face. When Moshe looked at Paroh's angry face he realised that he was in danger and fled even though he did not know what Paroh knew and what he did not.

למה זה עזבתם את האיש, "Why did you leave the man?" Yitro meant "why did you abandon a man who had done you a favour?" Alternatively, he meant: "how long can you let a man who has done you such a favour wait outside? Bring him inside, etc.!" Still another meaning of Re-uel's (Yitro's) words may be that though ordinarily Yitro would not want his daughters to strike up an acquaintanceship with men to whom they had not been introduced, this situation was different. He stressed that this man had already proved himself by his deeds. The word זה indicates that Yitro meant that this situation was different. This was especially so in view of the opinion expressed in Shemot Rabbah 1,32 that the waters in the well rose of their own accord towards Moshe.

ויתן את צפורה בתו למשה. He gave his daughter Tziporah to Moshe. The reason the Torah repeats Moshe's name in this verse, when it could have simply written: "he gave her to him," is that Tziporah was the divinely appointed wife for Moshe, his בת זוג.

גר הייתי, "I was (used to be) a stranger, etc." The Torah deliberately phrases this in the past tense because the Torah reports events as of the time the Torah was written (at that time Moshe could speak of his being a stranger in the past tense, whereas at the time the baby was born he was still a stranger in Midyan). Alternatively, the words may be understood along the lines of Tehillim 119,19: גר אנכי בארץ, "I am only a stranger on earth." Righteous people in this world are merely strangers, they have no permanent abode. Moshe meant that ever since he was born he had merely been a stranger in a foreign land, seeing he had not been raised in his parents' home or shared his youth with his siblings.

מן העבודה, on account of the bondage. They did not appeal to Hashem to save them from their situation; they merely groaned, something which people who feel that their burdens are too great are wont to do out of a sense of helplessness. The Torah informs us that although this outcry was not a direct appeal to Hashem for help, it did reach the ears of Hashem because their situation was indeed intolerable; this is why the Torah adds that the reason Hashem responded was מן העבודה, their bondage was too intolerable. However, Hashem did not respond to a prayer but to a general groaning, i.e. נעקתם (verse 24).

The Torah may also teach us something that David referred to in Tehillim 118,5, where he speaks about מן המצר קראתי קה, "I have called upon Hashem out of distress, etc." One of the prayers to which Elokim responds is the one that is prompted by the distress a person finds himself in. We find that Yonah prayed from similar motivations (Yonah 2,3) when he said: "I called out because I am in distress." The Torah testifies that Elokim responded to the distress the people found themselves in. According to our analysis the word שעוה means prayer, as well as an outcry prompted by pain; this is hinted at by the Torah's use of the words מן העבודה ויזעקו; the Torah is quite correct therefore when it introduces Elokim's response as being in response to שועתם instead of זעקתם. The Torah wanted to point out that the outcry of the children of Yisrael consisted of two elements, i.e. both זעקה and שעוה.

The stress on the words מן העבודה may indicate that the prayer/outcry rose up to G'd without the help of any intermediary [such as the accompanying prayer of the patriarchs Ed.] because it was due to the intolerable burden of their workload and working conditions.

וירא אלוקים…וידע אלוקים. Hashem saw,….and Hashem knew. After the children of Yisrael had raised their voices in groanings and prayers and Hashem had heard those, He remembered His covenant with the patriarchs. This was the reason He turned His attention to the people. Whenever Hashem is described as viewing someone's pain this is sufficient to result in the removal of such pain from the person so afflicted, for His mercy extends to all His creatures. It follows that when Hashem is angry He must hide His face from the people otherwise He would have to act in accordance with the principle we have just described. This is why Hashem said in Devarim 31,18: "As far as I am concerned, I will surely have to hide My face, etc." The word וידע may refer also to information that had thus far been hidden even from Bnei Yisrael concerning evil the Mitzrim had perpetrated against that people.

ומשה היה רועה…וינהג את הצאן, And Moshe was a shepherd….and he led the sheep, etc. The Torah means that Hashem had His hand in this, i.e. He caused the sheep to move in that direction. Alternatively, it means that Moshe was in the habit of guiding his flocks as usual but the sheep walked to that mountain on that occasion for Elokim wanted to speak to him there.

ויאמר הנני, he said: "I am ready." This was different from the time G'd first called out to the prophet Shmuel (Shmuel I, 3,4) when Shmuel thought that the High Priest Eli had called him. Moshe knew right away that G'd was speaking to him. This was because Moshe was a prophet already from birth; this was merely his first vision. On the other hand, perhaps the words את המראה הגדול הזה "this great spectacle," merely indicates that compared to previous contacts between G'd and Moshe this one seemed infinitely more remarkable.

אל תקרב הלום, של נעליך, "Do not come closer; remove your shoes, etc." Hashem gave two instructions. 1) not to come closer. 2) to remove his shoes because even the site on which Moshe was standing at that moment was already holy ground. Why did Hashem not instruct Moshe to remove his shoes before he had accidentally stepped on holy ground wearing shoes? At that time Hashem could have warned Moshe not to step on holy ground (even without shoes).

We observe throughout the Torah that Hashem's principal concern is with the negative commandments, since failure to observe them is injurious to the soul of the person who violates them. This is what Shlomo referred to in Kohelet 12,7 when he spoke about the importance of the spirit Hashem has given man returning to Hashem after man dies. Shabbat 152 understand the word נתנה as if it it were written אשר נתנה לך, "which has been given to you," meaning that just as a pure soul was given to man so a pure soul has to be returned to Hashem. On the other hand, positive commandments are designed to enable man to achieve the "good" Hashem has made available to man. As a rule, failure to observe the positive commandments does not result in penalties with the exception of certain basic commandments such as Passover and circumcision [without which a Yehudi cannot demonstrate his Jewish identity, Ed.].

In this instance Hashem commanded Moshe both something negative, i.e. "do not come closer!" as well as something positive, i.e. "remove your shoes!" Our sages in Eyruvin 96 state that wherever the Torah uses the expression פן or אל such as here, what follows is a negative commandment. The words "remove your shoes," are a positive commandment, however. If Moshe were to cross the invisible dividing line by approaching closer to the burning bush (as he had intended to) he would be violating a negative commandment. Were he to fail to remove his shoes, however, this would imply a lack of respect for Hashem but it would not constitute transgression of a negative commandment because the commandment had been phrased positively, though it implied that no shoes were to be worn there. The Torah always speaks about שמירה, i.e. care not to violate a negative commandment, before demanding עשיה, performance of a related positive commandment (compare Devarim 4,6; 15,5, Bereshit 26,5 et al). This is why the sequence in which Hashem commanded Moshe at this point is no departure from the Torah's norm.

We still have to answer what Hashem had in mind when He did not call out to Moshe before the latter had a chance to stand on holy ground clad in shoes. Perhaps Moshe did not qualify for an address by Hashem unless He had been told not to come still closer. Perhaps the site on which Moshe stood at that time became sanctified only by reason of Hashem having revealed Himself to Moshe there. Perhaps the reason Hashem wanted to speak with Moshe at that site was in order to have an excuse to sanctify that spot. Perhaps this was the reason for the extra word הוא in the expression אדמת קודש הוא. That word was not really necessary.

ויאמר ה׳ ראה ראיתי את עני עמי, G'd said: "I have surely seen the plight of My people, etc." Why did G'd speak about two "sightings?" Why did He have to add the words "in Mitzrayim?" If Moshe had not been aware of the fact that the Yehudim were G'd's people how would the fact that G'd referred to them as being in Mitzrayim help Moshe identify them? There were very many different peoples in Mitzrayim! Perhaps no other people in Mitzrayim suffered persecution except the Jewish people. At any rate, Moshe must have known that Yisrael was G'd's people and His heritage on earth.

Hashem mentioned that He had observed two distinctly different things. 1) The time of redemption had not yet arrived; in spite of this, however, Hashem had taken into consideration the plight of His people and the misery they experienced in Mitzrayim. Shabbat 10 tells that the immediate cause of the descent of the Jewish people to exile in Mitzrayim was due only to the extra two shekalim Yaakov had spent on Yosef's striped coat which had aroused the brothers' envy. Tossaphot challenge this explanation saying that exile had long ago been decreed in the days of Avraham? They answer that the exile prophecy could have come true in some other country where Bnei Yisrael would not have been enslaved so cruelly. The words אשר במצרים are to indicate that the very fact that Bnei Yisrael experienced their exile in Mitzrayim instead of somewhere else was a reason for Hashem to to commence the process of liberation already at this time. Although the time had not come for redemption, the time certainly had come for relief from the oppressive measures the Mitzrim had introduced against the Jewish people.

Hashem may also have seen the pain the Yehudim were suffering. The Torah may have written ראיתי עני עמי in order to demonstrate Hashem's identification with the Yehudim. Inasmuch as they were His people, He was part of their suffering.

Another reason why G'd speaks of ראה ראיתי is that in addition to the suffering of the Yehudim which G'd had seen, He also saw that there were no more holy souls which had been taken captive by the forces of the קליפה and which were to be rescued by the Jewish people. Seeing that the exile had accomplished also this part of its function, the way was now clear for redemption. Pessachim 119 compares Mitzrayim at the time to a pond which had been drained of fish. There was therefore no point in continuing to angle (for souls) there. Continued residence of the Yehudim in Mitzrayim could only have counterproductive effects from that time on.

ואת צעקתם שמעתי, "and I have heard their outcry," etc. G'd added that in addition to factors already mentioned, He had also heard the outcry which was occasioned by the fact that the Mitzrim had been more cruel than warranted in their application of Paroh's decrees. All these statements were in order to justify the fact that G'd was appointing a redeemer already at this time. Bnei Yisrael, of course, had believed that the exile would last for 400 years. Besides, G'd revealed to Moshe that as soon as the Mitzrim would suffer the first of the plagues G'd had in store for them, the Jewish people would cease to perform slave labour for them. I shall explain this in detail when commenting on verse eight.

When the Torah added מפני נגשיו, "on account of its taskmasters," after having mentioned that Hashem had heard צעקתם "their outcry" (plural instead of singular) whereas the word נגשיו is in the singular this may describe that the Jewish people prayed to Hashem as a single body as we explained on the words ותעל שועתם. Had the Torah written: ואת צעקתם מפני נגשיו שמעתי, I would have thought that their outcry was merely a reflection of their forced labour without an element of prayer.

The reason that the word "their outcry" is in the plural whereas "its taskmasters" describes the people as a single unit is simply that no two people cry out with the same intensity. The more people cry out, the greater the divergence between the relative intensity of these various people. Since they all had the same taskmasters, however, the use of the singular with the word נגשיו is perfectly justified. These various factors contributed to the appointment of Moshe as the redeemer long before the time Bnei Yisrael expected their exile to end.

Another meaning of the additional words מפני נגשיו is in line with Yeshayahu 65,24 והיה טרם יקראו ואני אענה, "before they pray I will answer." In our situation G'd explains that He is sensitive to the abuse practised by even a single one of Yisrael's taskmasters. He does not wait until they all exceed their authority and abuse His people. G'd adds that the reason for this is that "I know their pains." The implication is that G'd is aware even before the people bring this to His attention through their prayer/outcry. All of this underscores G'd's strong love for His people, a love comparable to that of a father for his son.

According to our earlier explanation, the words כי ידעתי את מכאוביו would refer to the pains that are already way beyond what Yisrael could be expected to bear. The words refer both to the visible and to the invisible hardship inflicted on Yisrael.

Elokim conveyed to Moshe that He had not needed Yisrael's prayers in order to become aware of their problems. This awareness obligated Him to redeem Yisrael in accordance with His attributes. Elokim's attribute of Mercy received further impetus when He looked at the injustices suffered by His creatures so that He decided to apply special yardsticks known as לפנים משורת הדין in order to alleviate their suffering. Elokim told Moshe that He had decided to "descend" in order to save His people.

וארד להצילו… ולהעלותו מן הארץ ההיא, "I shall descend in order to save…and to bring them out of this land, etc." The reason Hashem speaks about His "descent" is that it is not really in keeping with the dignity of the supreme Hashem to convey His instructions to a vile human being such as the Paroh who now oppressed the Jewish people. This was all the more so seeing that Paroh had the effrontery to exclaim "who is Hashem that I should heed His words?" (5,2) Hashem explained that He waived some of the honour due to Him in order to expedite the redemption of Yisrael. It is worthwhile to study the comment in the introduction to Eycha Rabbah section 14 on Mishlei 29,9: איש חכם נשפט את איש אויל ורגז ושחק ואין נחת. "If a wise man goes to Court with a fool there is no peace whether the fool rages or laughs." It is remarkable that Shlomo uses the form נשפט instead of שפט. He means that getting involved in litigation with a known fool can only result in the so-called wise man becoming convicted. Hashem had to mention that He was going to "descend" to show that despite the fact that it was inappropriate for Him to deal with Paroh, He would do so for the sake of Yisrael. The meaning of להצילו refers to the near-term cessation from their slave labour, whereas the expression ולהעלותו refers to the longer term objective of Hashem's intervention.

Seeing the time for the redemption was not yet at hand, there had to be an interval of at least 12 months between the time Hashem spoke to Moshe and the actual Exodus. Shemot Rabbah 9,12 debates whether the plagues usually lasted one week with three weeks warning or vice versa. At any rate, our sages seem agreed that the plagues extended over a considerable period. Why would Hashem have deliberately delayed the redemption once He had embarked on the process? He could have given Paroh a single day's warning before each plague something that is certainly legal when a Yehudi is warned not to commit a transgression. In fact, Gentiles do not need to be warned specifically at all not to commit acts which they know to be criminal. We must assume, therefore, that Hashem waited for a certain date to be able to justify the Exodus although He wanted to relieve the burden of the Jewish people in the interval.

In view of our premise that the principal purpose of the exile in Mitzrayim was to salvage the souls which had been contaminated with the 50 levels of impurity at the time the forces of the קליפה "captured" some of the holy souls from Adam when the latter ate from the tree of knowledge (compare our comments on Bereshit 49,9), we can understand that if Hashem had redeemed Bnei Yisrael prematurely this would have aborted the plan to rescue all those lost souls. We have already explained that Moshe himself was equated with the Jewish people inasmuch as Moshe achieved the 49th level of בינה, intellectual insights, out of a possible total of 50 such levels. The reason that Moshe never reached the ultimate level of בינה was that the achievement must parallel the effort expended on achieving the goal in question. Had Bnei Yisrael descended to the 50th level of impurity the effort at gaining the 50th level of insights would have been possible. Since Yisrael was never quite at the bottom of the spiritual levels, the effort to reach the top was of necessity a little less than total. Moshe's achievements were directly related to the condition of the Jewish people whom he represented. We have been assured that in the future Hashem Himself will influence us by means of the Torah so that we will be able to achieve the fiftieth level of בינה. We will be indebted to the cumulative exile experiences for that eventual achievement. The most important individual factor will be our present and final exile.

One of the reasons the generation of the first exile was not able to attain that level of insight was that they had not yet had the benefit of Torah. Once we shall reach that level of insight we will be able to recapture any holy souls still under the control of the forces of the קליפה, i.e. Satan. At any rate, had Hashem led the Jewish people out of Mitzrayim even a single day sooner than He did, the number of souls which had not yet been rescued would have been commensurably greater.

ועתה הנה צעקת בני ישראל באה אלי, "And now, the outcry of the children of Yisrael has reached Me, etc." Why did G'd repeat here something that He had already told Moshe in verse seven? Besides, what did G'd mean by the word: "and now?" Why was there a need for the word הנה? The words באה אלי also seem superfluous. G'd again mentioned that He had seen the stress the Jewish people were under. Why the repetition?
It appears that Hashem told Moshe that while he was speaking with him the repeated outcry of the Jewish people had again come to His attention.

G'd said: באה אלי, because the prayers which come to the attention of G'd are not all of the same category. Some prayers are presented to G'd by one of His angels; others are of a calibre that do not need the intervention of any angel as the people who offer them are deserving. G'd now told Moshe that some of the prayers of the Jewish people had reached Him without the assistance of any of the angels.

G'd added: "I have also seen the stress that the Mitzrim subject the Jewish people to." In the Haggadah shel Pessach the author describes the word לחץ as meaning דחק. This is a detail which had not been mentioned before. This is why G'd had to tell Moshe all this. When G'd added the word וראיתי He meant to tell Moshe why the matter of commencing the process of redemption had suddenly assumed a degree of urgency. G'd continues in verse 10: ועתה לכה to indicate that the matter had now become urgent.

לכה ואשלחך, "Go please, and I will send you, etc." Why did G'd say: "I will send you," after He had already told Moshe to go? Besides, if anything had to be repeated the sequence should have been the reverse, i.e. "I will send you, go please!" Clearly then G'd wanted that Moshe should understand that the actual going to Mitzrayim was not the essence of the mission, only its preamble. Indeed we find later on, after Moshe had already gone to Mitzrayim, that G'd instructs him repeatedly to take the Jewish people out of Mitzrayim, i.e. that was the essence of his misssion.

G'd also used this form of instruction to hint to Moshe that one mission would not suffice to take the people out of Mitzrayim but that he would have to perform many errands on behalf of G'd and the people before the Exodus would finally take place. Paroh would not agree at once.

There is another element hinted at in the way G'd instructed Moshe. We are taught in Makkot 10 that "G'd leads people on the path they have chosen for themselves." Therefore He first said to Moshe: "Go, please!" He meant that if you Moshe are willing to perform this commandment, I will send you, i.e. I will fulfil your wish and make you My messenger. From this you learn that if Moshe would have refused the mission G'd would not have forced it upon him.

Perhaps this is the reason that Moshe argued with Hashem. He did not feel that Hashem had commanded him to accept the mission but had left it up to his own volition. Moshe felt that Hashem had given him leeway and would reply to any reservations he had about accepting such a mission. Hashem wanted that when Moshe would finally accept the mission he should do so because he wanted to and not because he had been forced to do so.

You may also take a look at what I have written in connection with Yaakov sending Yosef on his fateful mission. Hashem may also have assured Moshe that if he were concerned about any mishap, he would be a messenger of Hashem who had no reason to fear for his safety. In fact this fact saved him in the incident at the inn (Shemot 4,26).

מי אנכי כי אלך, "who am I that I should be qualified to go?" Moshe meant that even if he were anxious to accept such a mission he did not consider himself qualified to speak up in front of a king. Seeing that he lacked that self-confidence his mission was unlikely to succeed. We have other examples of prophets who lacked confidence that their mission would succeed because they were personally not confident; compare Shmuel I 16,2 or Amos who is reported in Kohelet Rabbah 1 as having suffered from a lack of self-confidence because his peers belittled him. Moshe added וכי אוציא את בני ישראל, "and that I should lead Bnei Yisrael out of Mitzrayim," in order to emphasize the enormity of the task G'd was about to place on his shoulders, i.e. to orchestrate the Exodus. He implied that in order for such an undertaking to succeed the messenger G'd chose would have to be an outstanding personality. He was afraid that if Yisrael would suffer some setback on the road to freedom he might be held responsible since he was not qualified to be that leader.

ויאמר כי אהיה עמך. He said: "For I shall be with you, etc." How was this answer going to put Moshe's mind at rest? Surely he had been aware that as Hashem's messenger he would enjoy Hashem's assistance! He had not argued that Hashem would not help him but that his own inadequacy might become the cause of his failure. Another difficulty in this verse are the words וזה לך האות, "and this will be a sign for you, etc." How could Hashem describe a sign as "this" when we have never heard about this sign? If the reference had been to the bush not having been consumed by the fire, as Rashi explains, did Moshe perhaps entertain any doubts about Hashem's ability to save the Jewish people? Another difficulty in this verse is Hashem saying: כי אנכי שלחתיך, which suggests that Moshe still entertained some doubt that it had been Hashem Who had addressed him in the first place and Who wanted to appoint him as His messenger. Moshe had not indicated the slightest doubt in this respect!

We need to view G'd as replying to Moshe's arguments one by one, in the order in which he presented them. G'd first answers Moshe's question: "who am I that I should go to Paroh?" G'd replies that He Himself will be with him during that interview. This would automatically raise Moshe's stature to one exceeding that of Paroh. Moshe was to regard Paroh as no more than an ordinary person.

G'd also contradicted Moshe who had said that he was not fit to lead the Jewish people out of Mitzrayim. He demonstrated to him that זה לך האות the sign that he was quite capable of achieving the task G'd alotted to him was that if He, G'd, did not consider Moshe as suitable, would He have appointed him to perform such a gigantic task? G'd added another dimension by telling Moshe that when he would lead the Jewish people out of Mitzrayim, they (including Moshe) would serve Him at the very spot Moshe was standing on at that moment. This promise should convince Moshe that he would indeed complete his mission successfully.

By saying: זה לך האות, G'd may also have indicated to Moshe that the very fact that he did not consider himself as adequate for the task was the factor which had made G'd choose him. G'd needed a humble person, not an arrogant one. The reference to that mountain which was not a high mountain was to confirm that G'd preferred the humble and the modest to the high and mighty, and therefore arrogant. G'd could have chosen Mount Chermon as the site for the revelation; instead He chose Mount Sinai.

הנה אנכי בא אל בני ישראל, "When I come to the children of Yisrael, etc." At this point Moshe had agreed in principle to accept the mission, conceding that the arguments he had voiced previously had now become irrelevant. However, he needed accreditation as a prophet in order to make Bnei Yisrael accept him as such. As soon as he would come to them they would ask him to identify himself by revealing the name of the G'd Who he claimed had spoken to him. We find that whenever G'd began to speak to the patriarchs He identified Himself by stating His name (compare Bereshit 15,7; 17,1; 28,13). Moshe wanted to know which of G'd's names he was to mention when he would come to Bnei Yisrael. Moshe had been wondering that seeing G'd had identified Himself to him as "the G'd of your father Avraham, the G'd of Yitzchak, and the G'd of Yaakov" without adding any other attribute as part of His identification, whether he should similarly identify G'd to the children of Yisrael when they would ask him who had communicated with him and had appointed him as their redeemer. Did G'd really think that this would suffice as an identification for the people to accept Moshe as their leader?

Moshe implied that inasmuch as both he and Bnei Yisrael were already familiar with that aspect of Hashem, in what way was Moshe better or more intimate with Hashem that they should believe he was a prophet sent on such a great mission? On the other hand, if Moshe were to claim that the name of the Hashem in whose name he had come was one that was unfamiliar to them, why would such a name carry any weight with them at all? I have seen many different commentaries on this verse, but I do believe that any person with an ounce of common sense will appreciate the way I have presented the problem Moshe poses here. At this stage Moshe most certainly did not ask Hashem to provide him with a miracle he would be entitled to perform in order to prove that his claim was not spurious. You will note that Hashem told Moshe to tell Bnei Yisrael that He had identified Himself as אהיה. It is true that this was an attribute that Hashem had never employed in His communications with the patriarchs. Moshe realised now that as a true messenger he would never presume to interpret something Hashem had said without first making certain that he had understood Hashem correctly. No doubt Moshe had been familar already with more than one attribute of Hashem. However, he did not dare to convey to the people something he himself thought Hashem had meant without checking. It is also possible that this verse merely reflects Moshe's curiosity to learn more about the attribute Hashem presently employed when speaking with him.

ויאמר…אהיה אשר אהיה, Hashem said: Ehyeh asher Ehyeh. Hashem revealed the attribute He was using while speaking with Moshe. This attribute is closely related to the attribute of Mercy, an attribute employed in leading someone from slavery to freedom. It is interesting to study what is written in the Sefer Tikkunim section 50 about the mystical dimension of why the Torah mentions the Exodus from Mitzrayim a total of 50 times.
