This is also the mystical dimension of why Hashem smote the Mitzrim with 50 plagues at the sea as mentioned in Shemot Rabbah 23,9. Actually, Hashem had already alluded to this name when He had said to Moshe וזה לך האות כי אנכי שלחתיך, when the meaning of אנכי is the attribute that Hashem would employ during that entire mission. The same name occurs again at the revelation when Hashem commences the decalogue by referring to אנכי ה׳ אלוקיך אשר הוצאתיך. At the present juncture Moshe had simply not yet understood the connection between אנכי and אהיה. Hashem had been aware from the beginning that Moshe would question Him as to how to identify the Hashem Who had spoken with him.

Perhaps Moshe was aware of these meanings and only asked if he were to reveal these meanings to the people when they would ask him. Hashem responded אשר אהיה, i.e. that the reason He employed this attribute was because it was appropriate when He would share the pain of Bnei Yisrael whenever they would endure suffering. The Talmud Chagigah 12 has already explained this. Hashem identified Himself sometimes as שדי to indicate that it was He who put a stop to ongoing proliferation of the universe (Chagigah 16). He employs the attribute צבאות when He acts as the Commander-in Chief of His hosts. The attribute הויה reflects that He is an eternal Presence, was, is, and will be (Zohar third volume page 297). Hashem revealed the mystical dimension of His great name to Moshe at this point, namely that He would always be at the side of His people whenever they would find themselves in distress. There is also an allusion in that attribute to the three "crowns" [Torah-Priesthood-Royalty, Ed.]. Students of the Kabbalah will get my meaning.

ויאמר כה תאמר לבני ישראל, He said: "Thus you shall say to the children of Yisrael, etc." Although Hashem revealed to his servant Moshe the mystical dimension of His attribute, i.e. אשר אהיה, He repeated that all this was only contained in the "name," i.e. אהיה. As far as Moshe was concerned he was to tell Bnei Yisrael only that the One who calls Himself אהיה had sent him. As to the aspect of that name which referred to the future, i.e. אשר אהיה, that Hashem would also demonstrate that attribute of His when the Jewish people would face problems in the future, this was something Moshe was not to mention.

Our sages in Berachot 9 have already stated די לצרה בשעתה, it suffices to deal with one problem at the time it is topical. They claim that Moshe suggested to Hashem not to draw attention to the אשר אהיה aspect of this attribute. I have made a careful search of the text and found that the sages in the Talmud who attributed this reply to Moshe were absolutely correct. If there had been no new dimension added at the end of the verse which had not been present at the beginning, why would the Torah have inserted the word ויאמר once more within the same verse? Our sages therefore concluded that Hashem had originally meant to conclude His answer with the words אהיה אשר אהיה. He added the new version, i.e. אהיה שלחני as a result of Moshe's question "why speak about future troubles already now?"

You will no doubt ask how it is that G'd was not sensitive to that consideration even before Moshe raised it? When you examine G'd's words closely you will observe that G'd had already indicated His awareness of that aspect. When G'd instructed Moshe to speak to the children of Yisrael, His instructions should have commenced with the words: כה תאמר לבני ישראל, as this would have been the appropriate answer to Moshe's question: "when they say to me what is His name what shall I say to them?" However, since G'd already knew that Moshe would query that answer G'd immediately pre-empted his question by explaining that he should identify G'd first as the One who is known as אהיה. If G'd first spoke about אהיה אשר אהיה, this was privileged information for Moshe only at this time that just as G'd could be relied upon in this crisis so He could also be relied on in any future crises; however, Moshe was to keep the latter part of the promise to himself at this stage. In the future, after the Torah would be revealed and the generation reading this had already experienced G'd's salvation, they would realise that the same G'd who appeared to Moshe out of the burning bush would also be at their side in any future troubles. If G'd would have answered Moshe by saying immediately: "The G'd of your fathers has sent me to you, etc.," then the words אהיה שלחני would have lost their impact since the principal message had already been delivered. It is also possible that seeing that Moshe was exraordinarily perceptive he only wanted to hear G'd spell out in detail what he had already surmised to be the meaning of אהיה.

ויאמר עוד אלוקים, Hashem continued to say, etc. The reason the 4-lettered name of Hashem is repeated here once more when Hashem could have been content with having the 4-lettered name אהיה is that the latter 4-lettered name of Hashem comprises all the holy aspects that are unique to Hashem. To begin with, Hashem had revealed only a single one of these attributes which Hashem ascribes to Himself when intervening at a time when the Jewish people are in difficulties. The attribute אהיה was used to address itself to Yisrael's current problem.

Another reason why G'd repeated the words כה תאמר "Thus you shall say, etc.," is that G'd realised that Moshe had misinterpreted His reluctance to have invoked the 4 lettered name י־ה־ו־ה to mean that He would also not invoke the fact that He was the G'd of the patriarchs at this stage and would content Himself with the Identification: אהיה שלחני אליכם. G'd therefore added mention of His 4-lettered name י־ה־ו־ה- in association with identifying Himself as the G'd of the patriarchs. I believe that by doing so G'd alluded to the fact that His name אהיה which has a numerical value of 21 was also the numerical value of the respective first letters in the names of the patriarchs, א=אברהם, י=יצחק, and י=יעקב, a total of 21.

Verse 15 has yet another message. It is that the G'd now identifying Himself as אהיה is none other than the One who had promised the patriarchs there would be redemption even though this name of His had not appeared in that connection previously. G'd had to introduce this name also because in the future He would reveal legislation attesting to the holiness of His name. The name אהיה was alluded to when G'd said: אנכי, whereas the 4-lettered name י־ה־ו־ה was spelled out directly in order to justify what Moshe told the people, i.e. that when G'd would speak to them (at Mount Sinai) He would use the words אנכי י־ה־ו־ה. These considerations suffice to explain the sequence of these verses.

לך ואספת את זקני ישראל, "Go and gather the elders of lsrael,etc." The reason that Hashem repeats here again what Moshe is to say maybe that when Moshe would arrive in Mitzrayim he was to tell the entire people that he had come as messenger from Hashem. After that he would assemble the elders and tell them the nature of his mission, namely that Hashem had remembered His people and was about to redeem them.

The reason that Moshe was to announce the fact that he came as Hashem's messenger to the whole people first, was to make them assemble around him. Who would bother to gather around him unless he had first made an announcement that would make Bnei Yisrael take notice of him? In His wisdom Hashem had instructed Moshe what to say to Bnei Yisrael and what to say to the assembly of elders. He was to address the elders separately out of respect for them as we know from Vayikra Rabbah 11,8 that in the future Hashem will allocate a special place where the elders will be seated.

פקוד פקדתי, "I have surely remembered, etc." G'd speaks of two separate remembrances, 1) the final stage of the redemption, 2) the end of their suffering. When G'd says: אתכם He referred to the final stage of the redemption, when He said: ואת העשוי לכם He referred to the torture Bnei Yisrael were experiencing while performing slave labour. G'd also hinted to Bnei Yisrael that He would punish the Mitzrim for what they had done to Bnei Yisrael already.

ושמעו לקולך, "they will listen to your voice, etc." Hashem added the apparently superfluous word לקולך when the word לדבריך would have sufficed, in order to convince Moshe that the people would believe him even if he did not reveal to them an additional name of Hashem. The word קול implies something that is effective only for those who actually hear it. דברים are effective even if not heard directly. Hashem wanted Moshe to know that anyone who would hear Moshe's voice, i.e. the good tidings he would convey, would believe him as there was no impediment such as a lack of faith standing in the people's way. Moshe would not even have to perform miracles in order to gain the confidence of the Jewish people.

ה׳ אלוקי העברים נקרה עלינו, "Elokim, Hashem of the Hebrews has manifested Himself to us, etc." Elokim revealed here that although He did not want that His four-lettered name be associated except with the Hebrews, and that this was the reason He had not revealed it except to the Hebrews, He wanted the Mitzrim to know about this name so that when Moshe would appear to Paroh citing that attribute of Elokim, the latter could not claim that he had never heard of such a Elokim. He was not familiar with that name because he had not qualified for familiarity with such an exalted name of Elokim seeing he was a contemptible person.

נקרה עלינו. "manifested Himself to us." G'd did not want Paroh to think that Moshe was in regular communication with G'd day by day. It is also possible that the choice of the word נקרה, i.e. a chance encounter, was to forestall Paroh demanding to see that Moshe and Aharon would receive communications from G'd on a regular basis.

ועתה נלכה נא, "and now let us go, etc." Moshe used the word "now" to indicate that this request was an urgent one, requiring immediate action; Elokim had not said that these sacrifices were to be offered on a specific date. It is also possible that Moshe wanted to indicate to Paroh that as far as he was aware this march into the desert for three days in order to offer sacrifices there was a one time affair.

שלושת ימים. "Three days." Moshe had to make it appear that Bnei Yisrael meant to go for only three days because Hashem told him in verse 22 to tell Bnei Yisrael to borrow silver trinkets from the Mitzrim. Unless the Mitzrim would believe that the Yehudim planned to return they would not lend them the silver trinkets.

This explains also why Hashem announced the matter of borrowing the silver trinkets already now, 12 months before Bnei Yisrael would actually "borrow" these trinkets. Had that instruction been issued only on the night of the Exodus (when the Torah mentions it as being carried out) it would have been difficult to carry out. We might have assumed that mentioning it at this juncture was merely to make Bnei Yisrael believe that the Exodus was really at hand. This is not correct, however. We believe that the reason we have proposed, i.e. that in order to make the eventual request for these trinkets plausible, the Mitzrim first had to be under the impression that all the Jewish people really wanted was a three day religious holiday in the desert, away from Mitzri urban areas.

We still have to account for the fact that Hashem instructed Moshe to deceive Paroh by asking for a three day religious pilgrimage when in fact he did not mean for the people to return to Mitzrayim at all? Hashem appears to have tricked the Mitzrim both regarding the nature of Bnei Yisrael's departure and regarding the nature of the "borrowings." Actually, everything Hashem told Moshe to say was perfectly just and fair. Firstly, inasmuch as Bnei Yisrael had performed many decades of slave labour for which the Mitzrim had not paid any wages, they were entitled to recompense themselves, if only partially. Sanhedrin 91 records a disputation in front of Alexander the Great on that subject when the Mitzrim demanded the return of these borrowed trinkets. The representative of the Yehudim at that time, a certain Gevihah ben Pesisah, succeeded in making the Mitzrim withdraw their claim seeing that what the Yehudim had taken was so much less than what had been owed them at the time of the Exodus. Still, why did Hashem have to resort to trickery? Surely Hashem was capable of executing all His designs without having to resort to some form of deception!

We must assume therefore that the reason Hashem deceived the Mitzrim (on both counts) was in order to orchestrate the pursuit of the Yehudim by the Mitzri army and the crossing of the sea as well as the drowning of the Mitzri cavalry. Had the Mitzrim not felt themselves deceived by Bnei Yisrael they would never have undertaken a chase. Compare what we have written on Shemot 14,5 that Paroh had a change of heart.

You will find a sign that we are on the right track when you read Shemot Rabbah 14,3 that during the plague of darkness the Yehudim who were not affected by this discovered the secret hiding places of the Mitzrim so that at the time of the Exodus they could prove that the Mitzrim lied when they claimed not to possess the items the Yehudim wanted to borrow. The question is, of course, why, if Hashem already enabled the Yehudim to discover these trinkets, why did He not allow them to help themselves at once? It was only a few days prior to the Exodus! No doubt Hashem wanted that the Mitzrim should remain under the impression that the Yehudim were only borrowing these trinkets so that once they realised they had been deceived they would feel morally entitled to pursue the Yehudim and to retrieve these items.

Now let us look at the legality of the matter. If the Yehudim had helped themselves to what they discovered in the homes of the Mitzrim during the days of darkness they would have been perfectly in order. When a person is forcibly deprived of his possessions there is no law which prevents him to take back what was his. Yaakov used subterfuge to compensate himself for what Lavan had tricked him out of. The Talmud tells of an occurrence involving three great sages in Yuma 83. When two of them were swindled out of money they had deposited with the innkeeper, they resorted to deception in order to retrieve what was rightfully theirs. Not only did their action not involve a forbidden practice but they did what David refers to in Tehillim 18,27 as a practice employed by G'd Who engages in being wily with those who have been devious themselves.

In our situation the matter is even more clear-cut. If you examine the text, you will find that Moshe (at G'd's behest) did not utter a single lie. He never mentioned a word about Bnei Yisrael ever returning to Mitzrayim. Furthermore, Moshe was careful that the deceptive words could not be attributed to G'd himself but only to Bnei Yisrael, if at all. The words starting with: "and now we want to go," were to be spoken by Moshe, Aharon and the elders. They were not part of what G'd had said. If the Torah had not inserted the word ועתה, we would indeed have assumed that they said, quoting G'd: "Now let us go three days travel into the desert, etc." In chapter 5, verse 1 we do indeed find that Moshe quoted G'd saying: "send My people off so that they can celebrate for Me in the desert." He did not mention any time frame at that time. It was only Bnei Yisrael who added (in 5,3) "let us go for three days into the desert, etc." While it is true that at that point Bnei Yisrael did not say ועתה, they simply assumed that the word ועתה Moshe had mentioned in 3,18, was sufficiently clear. The fact that even the Yehudim had not lied to the Mitzrim is proven by history. The Yehudim who left Mitzrayim celebrated only in the desert seeing that the whole generation died before they came to the land of Kenaan. While it is true that many of the children of that generation entered the Holy Land and celebrated there also, it was not the minors who had negotiated with Paroh about their release from bondage. People under twenty years of age were under no obligation to offer sacrifices to G'd. Bnei Yisrael also did not lie when they asked for the silver trinkets as the Torah says: "they asked for, etc." Initially, they borrowed these trinkets. When the Mitzrim did not pay them the wages owed, they kept the trinkets as partial payment. They planned to present the Mitzrim wih a bill for the balance at a future date.

One problem has bothered me for a long time; why did Hashem not simply drown the Mitzrim who deserved drowning by letting the river Yeor spill over? This would have been the appropriate punishment for the people who had drowned the Jewish babies in the Yeor. Why did Hashem wait till the Mitzrim had pursued the Jewish people and He had to perform a major miracle by splitting the sea and allowing the Yehudim to cross on dry land? Also, why the devious method of the Yehudim borrowing the silver instead of their helping themselves to it during the days of darkness? After all, according to the interpretation of the Midrash the meaning of Shemot 11,23 that the Yehudim "had light in their dwellings" is that they had light "even in the Mitzrim's dwellings?" Perhaps Hashem was motivated by two considerations. 1) The splitting of the sea and everything connected with it aggrandised His name amongst mankind in a way that could not have been achieved by any other means. 2) Hashem applies the yardstick of "measure for measure." Sotah 11 states that the Mitzrim had cleverly inveigled Bnei Yisrael into slave labour by sweet-talking them into such patriotic service, whereas gradually they became more and more cruel and demanding. Hashem orchestrated the steps leading to redemption in a similar fashion. First He had Moshe speak about a three day religious holiday for Paroh's labourers as well as borrowings of the Mitzrim's silver and of their fancy garments. Hashem gradually upped the ante, just as the Mitzrim had done in their treatment of the Yehudim. At the same time Hashem was still careful so that even the Yehudim themselves did not utter a lie. The prophet Micha was quite correct (Micha 7,20) when he characterised one of the greatest Jewish virtues with the words: "You give truth to Yaakov."

לא תלכו ריקם, "You will not leave empty-handed." At this point the Torah already foreshadowed the legislation applicable when a Jewish servant is to be released by his master. The Torah commands in Devarim 15,13-15 that you must not set him free empty-handed but that you have to provide him with a stake so that he can establish an economic base for himself. Presumably, this is also measure for measure. What Hashem did for you, you in turn are to do for the servant you set free.

ונצלתם את מצרים, "you will empty Mitzrayim." Here the Torah alludes to the fact that a person may rescue his possessions from someone who robbed him by force. Alternatively, our verse may be a preview of what caused the Mitzrim to drown in the sea, i.e. the combination of Bnei Yisrael's demand to borrow their silver trinkets and their declared intention to travel a distance of three days into the desert. The two demands eventually prompted the Mitzrim to pursue the Yehudim believing their leader Moshe had overstepped his authority. As a result G'd drowned them in the sea.

ויען משה ויאמר והן לא יאמינו לי, Moshe replied saying: "But they will not believe me, etc." What could have prompted Moshe to claim that the Jewish people would not believe him when Hashem Himself had told him "they will listen to your voice?" Furthermore, why did Moshe even add the almost unbelievable: "and they will not listen to my voice?" One might be tempted to say that inasmuch as a person is free to do what he wants to do and to believe what he wants to believe in, Hashem's assurance on that score could not be absolute seeing He is not in control of our feelings. This is why Moshe did not believe in the righteousness of their faith. He said: "and they will not listen to my voice," as if to say "they will not even want to listen to my voice." However, such an explanation would not do justice to Moshe who certainly did not want to question Hashem's attributes, nor to slander Yisrael by uttering such a gross suspicion. Besides, we must consider that Moshe did not even say "suppose they will not believe me," but he made a flat statement והן לא יאמינו לי, "they will definitely not believe me."

The correct answer to our problem is that outlined by Maimonides in chapter seven of his treatise Yesodey Ha-Torah where he writes that the gift of prophecy is given only to people of outstanding intellectual capacity, people who are whole in body and spirit. The author of כסף משנה, a major commentator on Maimonides' works, comments as follows: "We must analyse why Maimonides did not add some more qualifications such as that the prophet has to be wealthy, humble, of physical prowess, etc." He concludes that Maimonides certainly feels that the prophet must possess these attributes as well. However, inasmuch as someone who practices prophecy on a regular basis must possess these attributes as a matter of course, Maimonides did not bother to mention this in that paragraph. In the chapter mentioned, Maimonides was concerned only with people who prophesy only on occasion. Even if we were to consider Moshe as someone who practiced prophecy only on occasion-something we cannot accept,- he argued what he did as a result of his extreme humility, out of a conviction that he personally lacked the qualities needed for someone to be accepted as such by Bnei Yisrael. When Moshe said והן לא יאמינו לי, he meant that "as the result of my many shortcomings they will have no reason to believe me, etc." This was all the more true, Moshe said, since I have not been accredited as a regular prophet, but am only making an occasional appearance as a prophet. When a person who has not yet established his credentials as a prophet appears and claims to be a prophet he has to be able to demonstrate all the attributes the people expect of a prophet; these attributes include wealth, physical prowess, a body without blemish, etc. If the people needed proof that Moshe lacked the attribute of personal wealth, all they had to find out was that he Moshe, had been a mere shepherd in the employ of his father-in-law Yitro. (He had attained personal wealth only by being allowed to pocket the splinters of the tablets of the Covennant as per a comment in Nedarim 38). In view of all this, as soon as Bnei Yisrael would consult with their elders if Moshe was believable, the elders would tell the people, quite correctly, that Moshe had failed to legitimise himself adequately.

When Moshe had added ולא ישמעו בקולי he alluded to yet another argument, namely his stutter. His voice would give him away as someone who was not fit to be a prophet. Later on he indeed spelled out his concern on that score. At any rate, the absence of a speech impediment is an absolute necessity even for prophets who appear as such only on occasion. If someone suffered from such an impediment it is equivalent to a physical blemish. When Moshe said Bnei Yisrael would argue that Hashem had never communicated with him, they would be quite justified in their assumption as they would base their rejection of his claim on his physical blemish, saying Hashem would not appear to such a person even on a temporary basis. The reason Moshe had not advanced this argument at once but had asked Hashem what he should say when Bnei Yisrael would ask him in what capacity Hashem had appeared to him- something which appears to show that he was not concerned about the people rejecting him personally- was because Hashem had interrupted him by saying: "this is My name, etc."

It is also possible that Moshe wanted Hashem to reveal more of the mystical aspects of His name, and that in order for Hashem to do so he made what sounded like a provocative statement. Moshe hoped, that if successful, Hashem would equip him with all the visible and invisible attributes that he felt he lacked in order to qualify as a regular prophet. We find this concept in Tehillim 91,14 אשגבהו כי ידע שמי, "I will raise it (the Jewish people) high since it has become aware of My name." Moreover, if they would appreciate the qualities Hashem had equipped Moshe with their regard for Hashem Himself would be appreciably enhanced.

Still another reason why Moshe was not perturbed at saying what he did, i.e. that the Jewish people would not believe him, was that Hashem Himself had told him after He had said that the Jewish people would hearken to his voice (3,18) that He knew that Paroh would not respond to Moshe's entreaties and would not let Bnei Yisrael depart (3,19). Moshe reasoned that if Paroh would not take his mission seriously then Bnei Yisrael would surely lose faith in his leadership in short order. If Moshe would have repeated audiences with Paroh all of which did not produce results, the people would eventually even stop listening to him altogether. They would claim that the reason he failed was that לא נראה אליך השם, "Hashem never appeared to you in the first place." They would argue that if indeed Moshe's mission had been authorised by Hashem, who would have the effrontery to refuse to carry out Hashem's orders? Do we not know from Kings I 14,10 that if someone contravenes Hashem's commands deliberately he will be utterly destroyed by Hashem?

?זיאמר ה׳ מזה בידך "Hashem said: "what is this in your hand?" This question cannot be compared to when Hashem asked Bilam (Bamidbar 22,9) "who are these men?" Our sages in Bamidbar Rabbah 19 state that Bilam should have answered Hashem that He was well aware of even a chamber-pot Bilam had in his bedroom, how much more so would He be aware of who the messengers were who had come to him that evening? However, the two situations cannot be compared. When Hashem asked Bilam who the men were who had come to him, Bilam had some excuse to assume that Hashem really was not aware of their identity; When He asked Moshe what the latter held in his hand, it was daylight and Hashem had obviously seen it. The question therefore could only be a rhetorical one. Hashem only wanted Moshe to confirm what it was he held in his hand. Moshe complied and said "it is a staff."

ויהי לנחש, it had turned into a snake. G'd hinted to Moshe that the forces of the קליפה are characterised by the symbol snake. We know from the original serpent that it represents סם, i.e. something potentially poisonous. G'd wanted to teach Moshe that his hands possessed the power to neutralise the power of that serpent and to turn it into a harmless piece of wood. If, however, Moshe would not keep firm control and allow it to escape from his hands, he would unleash all the latent powers of evil which are controlled by the serpent. This would become so threatening that Moshe would flee from it [although he stood on consecrated ground, Ed.]. When G'd asked Moshe: "what is this in your hand?" He wanted Moshe to understand that the staff was biologically analogous to a certain kind of desert-mouse. If Moshe were to even loosen his grip on his staff it was liable to develop into a serpent just as earth can turn into a certain species of mouse. [In Talmudic times there was a widespread belief that this specimen of mouse was half flesh and half earth, and developed out of the earth. This belief has halachic implications regarding the laws of ritual impurity, compare Chulin 9,6, Ed.] Moshe replied to G'd's question that he was certain that what he held in his hand was a staff, i.e. one hundred per cent wood, without potential to develop into a living organism. When G'd made him throw the staff down to earth, He demonstrated that not only did the staff contain the potential to develop into a living creature, but it did not do so only very gradually, such as the desert-mouse, but it did so in a single moment.

The reason G'd had said: "throw it to the ground," was that in the eyes of the serpent the earth assumes great significance since it derives all its needs for survival from the earth, and earth (dust) is its exclusive habitat (Bereshit 3,14). G'd taught Moshe many lessons by means of this small demonstration. Amongst other things Moshe was to demonstrate this very miracle before the eyes of Bnei Yisrael.

When G'd instructed Moshe: "stretch out your hand," He wanted Moshe to realise that though he thought that he had already lost control over what had been his staff, he still possessed the power to master what had become a serpent and to turn it into a harmless piece of wood again.

Hashem instructed Moshe ואחוז בזנבו, instead of ואחוז בו. This was to teach him an additional lesson. Normally, people are afraid of the poisonous head of the snake and when they try to grab it they try to get hold of its head and crush it in order to neutralise its poisonous bite. Hashem told Moshe that it would suffice to grasp the tail of the snake and he would not have anything to fear. When the Torah nevertheless describes Moshe as ויחזק בו "he took hold of it," and not as ויחזק בזנבו, "he took hold of its tail," this does not mean that Moshe did not obey Hashem's instructions but that he took hold of the nearest part of the snake without fear. When the Torah goes on to describe that ויהי למטה בכפו, "it turned into a staff in his palm," this means that it ceased being a living organism as soon as Moshe's palm touched it i.e. ויהי, "it remained as a staff only."

למען יאמינו כי נראה אליך השם. "So that they will believe that Elokim has appeared to you." The reason that Elokim kept repeating "the Elokim of their fathers," may have been to hint to the people present that unless one believed in the Elokim who had been the Elokim of the patriarchs one could not hope to achieve control over the serpent, i.e. the forces of evil in this universe. A demonstration of such control would therefore imply that one was on intimate terms with Elokim.

והיה אם לא יאמינו גם לשני האותות, "In the event that they will not believe even both these two signs, etc.," This sounds strange. Does G'd then entertain any doubts so that He has to phrase this verse in such a way? Besides, G'd had already told Moshe that the people would listen to his voice! Perhaps the thrust of the message is addressed to Moshe's concerns, and G'd is saying to him: "In the event you are afraid that even these two miracles will not be sufficient to convince Bnei Yisrael of your authenticity and the authenticity of the message of the imminent redemption, I will let you perform another miracle which will be the clincher and as a result of which they will certainly believe you."

G'd may also have wanted to tell Moshe not to worry about aspects of the people's faith which could not be discerned on their faces. In the event that Moshe worried that though externally the people would appear to believe both in him and in the success of his mission, they might harbour reservations which Moshe could not detect. G'd reassured him on that score and told him that as a result of all three miracles they would believe him without reservations.

והיו המים….לדם ביבשת. "The waters…will turn into blood on the ground." Rashi has enlightened us by remarking that the repeated use of the word והיו in this verse indicates that the waters will not turn into blood until they touch the dry land. I only wish to add one more comment concerning the statement of our sages in Shemot Rabbah 9,10 that Hashem eventually commanded Aharon and not Moshe to perform this miracle in front of Paroh because the Yeor had saved Moshe's life at the time his mother placed him amongst the reeds and it would have been gross ingratitude to strike at the part of nature which had saved his life. In this case where Hashem commanded Moshe to strike the waters personally, He did so with the proviso that the waters would become blood only after they had already ceased to perform their life-giving and life-preserving function, i.e. after they had been spilled on the ground.

ויאמר משה בי א־ד־ו־נ־י לא איש דברים אנכי, Moshe said: "Please my Hashem, I am not a man of words, etc." After Moshe's previous arguments had been silenced, Moshe now appealed to the attribute of Mercy. This is why the Torah emphasises the name of Elokim Moshe used here. Moshe had not used that name of Elokim previously. The word בי is a word of entreaty.

Alternatively, we can understand the word בי as a pronoun in which case Moshe would have answered Hashem that he considered his own unsuitability for the mission as due to בי, his own shortcomings. As soon as the people would become aware of him stammering they would realise that even after he pronounced the words he had no command of language. They would reject him. Moshe added the words גם מתמול גם משלשום, to point out that despite his repeated conversations with Hashem, Hashem had not cured him of his deformity. It appeared therefore that he was meant to suffer from this deformity also in the future. If so, the people would surely reject him because they would think that if Hashem had spoken to him He would first have cured him of that blemish. (He left the last part of the sentence unspoken).

ויאמר ה׳ אליו מי שם פה, Hashem said to him: "Who has given man a mouth, etc." Hashem criticised Moshe. He should have relied on the fact that the One who provides others with the ability to speak without impediment could also do the same for him. If Hashem had failed to do so thus far, surely He must have had an adequate reason. If and when the need arose, Hashem would surely remedy Moshe's deformity. Hashem responds with the words (verse 12) "and now go and I will be with you." He does not, however, assure Moshe that He will cure him of his deformity. It is also possible that Hashem only hinted to Moshe that he should express repentance at his lack of trust that Hashem would cure him.

On the other hand, one may read meaning into what Hashem did not say, i.e. that He did not instruct Moshe how he could ensure that Hashem would provide him with a healthy mouth, i.e. the equipment to impress people with his eloquence. Hashem did not even hint that He is in the habit of rectifying defects such as speech defects that did not originate at birth. He declared that He provides the initial equipment, i.e. a sense of hearing, a sense of sight, etc. Hashem did not refer to His taking remedial action in that regard. We are therefore at a loss as to what precisely Hashem wanted to convey with His reply in verse 12.

We must assume that in verse eleven Hashem asserted His sovereignty inasmuch as He is the supreme intelligence having provided man with the organs necessary including a mouth, etc. Considering all this Moshe should understand that if he was plagued by a deformity this was not accidental or an oversight but was part of an overall design by Hashem who knows best. It is precisely because Hashem had not seen fit to remedy Moshe's deformity that the latter should have given Him credit for knowing what He was doing. Most of you are familiar with the aggadah reported in Shemot Rabbah 1,25 according to which the young Moshe playfully removed Paroh's crown and placed it on his own head. Some of Paroh's advisers were alarmed at this and saw in it an omen of the future. They decided to test the child by placing two bowls in front of him. One contained glowing coals, the other glittering jewels. If Moshe were to try and grab for the jewels he would be considered as potentially dangerous to Paroh and would be executed; if he grabbed for the glowing coals this would be seen as proof that his having removed Paroh's crown had only been a youthful prank by a child with average or below average intelligence. According to the aggadah, Moshe was about to grab for the jewels when an angel guided his hands to the coals and he burned his mouth. As a result he was afflicted with a stammer. Hashem hinted to Moshe that unless He had seen some positive value in Moshe's burning his mouth at that time He would not have allowed this to happen. Hashem either allows something like this to happen because of something that will happen in the future, or it is retribution for some sin committed, something that could not apply in Moshe's case. Rabbi Ami said in Shabbat 55 that no one is saddled with afflictions unless he has become guilty of some sin. If someone suffers from a stutter such as Moshe, this too is considered an affliction. If so, it would have been incumbent for Moshe to know the reason for his affliction and to remove its cause and then to pray to Hashem concerning removal of his affliction. The fact that he did not do so indicates that his affliction had nothing to do with any sin of his. This is why Hashem said to him: ועתה. This is to be understood as contradicting previously held convictions. In other words, there was no need for Moshe to blame himself for his stutter and to take remedial action.
As to his concern that Yisrael would not believe in his leadership because of his stammer, G'd told Him that He would assist him and teach him what to say.

The words: לך ואנכי אהיה עם פיך "go and I shall be with your mouth," was an ironclad answer valid as long as Moshe had not actually commenced his mission. As long as he had not yet become G'd's instrument there was no reason to cure his stammer. This is why G'd urged Moshe by saying: "Go!" He implied that if Moshe were to accept this mission he would notice that as soon as he began speaking his stammer would have disappeared. G'd said: והוריתיך אשר תדבר; there is a subtle difference between this and את אשר תדבר, which is what we would have expected. G'd did not tell Moshe that He would teach him what to say, but He told Moshe that He would demonstrate to him that he had developed fluency in speaking, etc. The reason G'd used the word: "I will teach you" instead of "I will show you," is that Moshe was to notice that his cure was not something temporary, only for the benefit of fulfilling his mission, but that it would remain the norm from then on.

בי אדני שלח נא ביד תשלח. "Please my Lord, send the one whom You usually send on missions." Moshe meant that he did not hold G'd responsible for his stammer; he was well aware that G'd could cure it. If He had not done so it was clear to him that the fault must be his; therefore he recommended that G'd send someone better qualified than himself on that mission.

ויתר אף ה׳ במשה, Hashem became angry at Moshe, etc. I believe that as a result of Hashem's anger Moshe did indeed remain afflicted with his stammer even after he undertook the mission in the end. The Torah says that Hashem became angry במשה, at Moshe; I understand that to be a reference to his body, i.e. it had an effect on his deformity. Our sages in Zevachim 102 who suggested that Moshe referred to his older brother Aharon when he made the comment Hashem found objectionable, believed that Moshe who had been meant to also fulfil the function of High Priest was deprived of this function as a result of Hashem's anger. The Talmud's comment is perfectly compatible with my own, as the words ויחר אף hinted at two things.

כי דבר ידבר, "for he will certainly speak," etc. The reason that G'd repeated the word דבר is that G'd indicated that though Aharon was able to speak fluently now, i.e. דבר, he would also speak in the future, ידבר, though he would also become afflicted with a handicap similar to that of Moshe. On the other hand, in line with our explanation of the consequences of G'd's anger (which had not been spelled out in detail as yet), the word דבר may refer to G'd's instruction to Moshe, whereas the words ידבר הוא have to be read together and tell us that Aharon would do what Moshe had refused to do. The emphasis on הוא implies also that whereas he, Aharon would display fluency of speech, Moshe would not be cured.

וגם הנה הוא יוצא לקראתך, "and he is also on the way to meet you, etc." If this is a continuation of G'd's praise of Aharon that he would be willing to speak although he too would stammer, this is additional praise for Aharon; the word וגם, "and also," is in place then. G'd is saying then that Aharon not only does not mind his handicap but he is glad to be able to perform a task G'd assigns to him. [I believe the reason the author says that Aharon suffered from a speech handicap is that he reads the words דבר־־ידבר as graphically describing the stutter. Ed.]

The word וגם may also be understood in conjunction with Shabbat 139 where we are told that Aharon was granted the position of High Priest in recognition of his being happy that his younger brother had been appointed as the redeemer. When we consider that G'd had decided not to cure Moshe of his speech defect because he had declined the request by G'd to assume leadership of the people, the word וגם would refer to the additional result of that refusal by Moshe.

The Torah may also have wanted to underline the virtues of Aharon and his humility. Normally, one could have expected him to be slighted for being appointed to be merely his younger brother's mouthpiece, but the Torah testified that far from feeling slighted, Aharon actually rejoiced over Moshe's promotion. One of the lessons to be learned from this is that humility should not be carried to the point where one endeavours to escape fulfilling the will of the king (G'd). G'd had to tell Moshe that Aharon would rejoice as the latter was not displaying this joy openly. The Torah could also have wanted to tell us that Aharon did display this joy on his face, but that G'd wanted Moshe to know in addition that Aharon was equally joyful about Moshe's appointment in his heart.

ואת המטה הזה תקח בידך, "and take this staff in your hand, etc." According to the Zohar section 3 page 28 there were two staffs. The Torah then spoke about "this one" to tell Moshe that he should not take the other staff.

The expression "take in your hand" means "permanently;" The reason was that this staff should be a mark of distinction, something not unlike present-day rulers who carry a mace with them as a sign of their constitutional right to legislate. Moshe took the "staff of Elokim" with him as mentioned in verse 20 as a memento of this conversation and as a sign of his authority. Hashem had said: "take it in your hand" so that we should not interpret that Moshe took his staff like ordinary people take a walking-cane.

אשר תעשה בו את האותות, "the one with which you will perform the miracles." This may be a reference to the staff with which Aharon performed such miracles as turning it into a snake (7,10). According to the Zohar we have just quoted that staff became known as "the staff of Aharon;" G'd had commanded Aharon also to have his staff ready at all times. According to Targum Yonathan 2,21 the staff was made of sapphire and no one was able to even move it except Moshe. Accordingly, the very fact that Moshe could "take" it was a miracle in itself. The words וזה לך האות therefore meant that no one but Moshe would be able to handle the staff.

אלכה נא, "I wish to go, etc." According to the agreement between Moshe and Yitro reported in Shemot Rabbah 1,29, Yitro had made Moshe swear an oath not to take Tzipporah away. Moshe now had to ask Yitro to release him from that oath.

ואראה העודם חיים, "and I want to see if they are still alive, etc." He did not tell Yitro a word about the mission Hashem had asked him to undertake, seeing that Hashem had not used the word לאמור when He had appointed Moshe. We have repeatedly quoted Yuma 4 to the effect that one must not reveal information received privately unless authorised to do so.

לך לשלום, "go and be well!" Yitro forgave him his oath. We learn from this that no formal annulment is necessary if the second party to the oath himself expresses his agreement that it be invalidated.

אל משה במדין, to Moshe in Midyan. The reason that the Torah stresses that this communication from Hashem to Moshe took place in Midyan is to praise Moshe who was not afraid of his adversaries in Mitzrayim at the time he argued against acceptance of the mission. All that concerned him was his own inadequacy for the gigantic task Hashem wanted to charge him with. The Torah had to mention where the conversation took place as otherwise we would have assumed that the argument which swayed Moshe was Hashem's assurance that all the people who had tried to kill him had already died. Moshe had already asked Yitro to release him from his oath before Hashem mentioned that his pursuers were dead.

כה אמד ה׳ בני בכורי ישראל. Thus said Hashem: "Yisrael is My firstborn son." Why is this prophecy- i.e. that the Jewish firstborn would not be killed- recorded out of context, i.e. a long time before Moshe would announce it to Paroh? We need to know also why, apparently, Moshe was not to mention this to Paroh on their first encounter?

It appears that Hashem in His wisdom provided Moshe with some information which would temper his disappointment at the long drawn-out process of the often broken promises by Paroh. There was a danger that when Moshe observed that Paroh remained obstinate month after month despite the plagues Hashem inflicted upon him and his people, he would become fed up with his mission. Hashem therefore informed him of something that would not happen until the end of the process. As long as the plague of killing the firstborn Mitzrim had not occurred, Moshe had no reason to believe that Hashem's timetable had been upset. The synopsis of the prophecy was: "be aware that I will make Paroh's heart obstinate; he will suffer many plagues without collapsing; in the end you will announce to him that Hashem will kill all the firstborn Mitzrim, etc."

Hashem was also clever in announcing to Moshe in this fashion that it would be the plague of killing the firstborn which would prompt Paroh to dismiss the people. Moshe would eventually realise that the redemption was close at hand when Hashem did not mention to him anymore that He would harden the heart of Paroh. When Paroh told him in 10,28: "do not come to see me anymore," Moshe realised that the time to fulfil the instruction given in our verse had arrived. This is why he announced that plague the moment Paroh told him not to come and see him again. While it is true that the Torah reports many additional instructions Hashem gave to Moshe at that time, Hashem may have mentioned them already at this time while recording them at an appropriate moment. When we look at matters in that light we do not need all the Midrashim which try to determine when precisely Hashem had made this announcement. Hashem did not worry that Moshe would misunderstand and reveal this prophecy too soon. He knew that Moshe would report back to Him any response from Paroh. As soon as Hashem would then instruct Moshe to bring on another plague, Moshe would know that the time had not yet arrived for that final plague. Once Paroh told Moshe not to come and see him again, Moshe realised he did not have time to consult with Hashem outside the limits of the city as he was in the habit of doing. This is why he himself announced the plague of the killing of the firstborn without awaiting specific instructions from Hashem. Perhaps Moshe simply used the words "I will make Paroh's heart hard" as his guidelines. He did not know beforehand how long this process of hardening Paroh's heart would continue; when he noticed that Hashem did not mention this anymore after the plague of darkness, he took his cue from that and warned Paroh of the final plague.

It is also possible that Hashem indicated that Paroh had three choices. If he were to release Bnei Yisrael he would be spared any plagues. If he were to deny Bnei Yisrael their freedom without at the same time insulting Hashem, Hashem would bring on the plague of the killing of the firstborn immediately; this would bring about the Exodus. If, however, Paroh were to deny Bnei Yisrael their freedom and at the same time insult the honour of Hashem, he would have to endure the entire range of plagues, as did in fact happen. Hashem told him through Moshe in 9,16 that He had decided to let Paroh experience the full extent of His power.

ויבקש המיתו, He tried to kill him. The reason that the Torah describes G'd as only "trying" to kill Moshe may be that the fact that Moshe was on the way to carry out a commandment by G'd. This acted as partial protection based on Pessachim 8 that "people engaged in the process of carrying out a מצוה do not suffer harm either on their way to or from carrying out that מצוה." The מצוה which Moshe was occupied with at that time acquired one heavenly advocate for him; this advocate was his companion at the time and prevented the destructive forces poised against him from approaching him too closely. Perhaps the Torah's description of all this happening בדרך במלון is to inform us that at the time Moshe was not so much involved with his primary mission but with private matters; this is what provoked the destructive forces to attack him. Nonetheless he still enjoyed some protection seeing that he had not abandoned his mission. While the positive and negative forces were confronting each other, Tziporah removed the impediment to saving Moshe's life by circumcising her son.

לך לקראת משה, "go towards Moshe, etc!" Although we have heard Hashem say to Moshe already in 4,14 that his brother Aharon was on his way to meet him, the actual instruction to Aharon came from Hashem while Aharon was still in Mitzrayim. There is no question that the prophecy in this verse was adressed directly to Aharon even though we learned in Torat Kohanim 1 that wherever the Torah writes: "Hashem spoke to Moshe and Aharon," that the directive was spoken to Moshe only and he in turn was to convey it to Aharon, this does not apply here. Even according to the view of Rabbi Yossi Haglili who excludes Aharon from receiving a communication from Hashem directly even while both were in Mitzrayim, he referred only to communications which concerned an independent mission to outsiders. There is no reason to believe that Hashem did not speak to Aharon directly concerning what Aharon himself was to do. Our verse proves that Aharon was a prophet in his own right.

ואחר באו משה ואהרון ויאמרו אל פרעה, afterwards Moshe and Aharon came to Paroh and said, etc. The word "afterwards" means after the people had believed that Hashem had despatched Moshe to them as their redeemer. The verse refers to fulfilment of what Hashem had told Moshe in 3,18. We now appreciate the dividing tone sign etnachta under the word לקולך in 3,18; we would have expected the words "and you will proceed to Paroh" to be part of the same sequence. Inasmuch as some considerable time passed between what was mentioned in the first half of that verse and the completion of what it was meant to lead to, the Torah repeats here that now the second part of verse 18 in chapter 3 was being played out.

אשר אשמע בקולו, "that I should listen to His voice." Paroh challenged Moshe regarding his G'd's great power. Surely the Jewish G'd was not so powerful that He could demand such obedience in a matter of such overriding importance! He added gratuitously: "to dismiss the Jewish people," meaning that however great His power it would surely not suffice to liberate the Jewish people. Paroh did not mean to concede that he did know of the Jewish G'd after all, but that the latter was not great enough to make such a demand; rather he said: 1) "I do not know of Him;" 2) even if I would be told that He does indeed exist this would not mean that He could demand the freeing of the Jewish people." The word גם refers to a hypothetical situation.

ויאמרו אלוקי העברים ..פן יפגענו "The G'd of Yisrael…. lest He punish us." The last words were spoken by Bnei Yisrael. Even though our sages in Shemot Rabbah 5,14 told us that the elders melted away on the way to the first confrontation with Paroh, Bnei Yisrael expressed fear of being punished by G'd. The elders were punished for not accompanying Moshe and Aharon. Perhaps the entire nation went to see Paroh and told him it would be in Paroh's own interest to excuse the Jewish people from work for three days and to take the chance that they would return; otherwise, if they would be punished by their G'd, Paroh would lose their labour altogether if they were to die of a pestilence. Perhaps they even implied that such a pestilence would also pose a problem for Paroh himself who might become infected. They used the well known method of describing such a plague as afflicting them rather than Paroh, as they did not want to threaten Paroh outright.

ויאמר..למה משה ואהרון תפריעו את העם, He said: "Why Moshe and Aharon to you deter the people, etc.?" After Paroh had first faced both the elders and Moshe and Aharon and they had told him about the demands of the Hebrew Elokim, Paroh now turned to Moshe and Aharon telling them that he had no complaint against the elders who were obviously motivated by their fear of pestilence. His complaint was directed against Moshe and Aharon on two counts. 1) Seeing that Moshe and Aharon had brought a message from their Elokim, it appeared that the decision was up to him. They had therefore not been entitled to threaten the people with punishment by their Elokim for something that was not up to them but up to him! 2) If Moshe and Aharon had told the people that they could simply leave Mitzrayim without being granted permission, why had they come to ask his permission at all? Perhaps this is what our sages had in mind in our Midrash when they said: "why does the Torah write אתם and why the word למה? This may mean that Paroh asked why they came at all, and why they told the people in the name of Elokim that they could leave. Paroh then turned towards Bnei Yisrael and told them: לכו לסבלותיכם, "go and do your work!"

ויאמר פרעה הן רבים עתה עם הארץ, Paroh said: "now the people in the land are very numerous, etc." Paroh meant that in view of the large numbers of people involved it was impossible to convince all of them that they did not face a danger if they did not march to the desert to offer sacrifices to their G'd. This was why he held Moshe and Aharon responsible for the work stoppage if it would occur. He directed this accusation exclusively at Moshe and Aharon. Paroh meant that even a brief work stoppage was a major economic disaster considering the number of people involved.

ויצו פרעה ביום ההוא, On that day Paroh issued orders, etc. This directive was to be effective only on that particular day. He hoped that by forcing the people to concentrate on their immediate and overwhelming problem they would forget about their fear of what might happen if they failed to offer sacrifices to their G'd in the desert. Any intelligent person understands that an immediate and pressing problem is apt to push other problems that are not so immediate into the background. Paroh hoped that a single day of the new decree would suffice to accomplish this objective.

On the other hand, the Torah could have indicated with the words ביום ההוא that there was only a single day left on which Bnei Yisrael performed slave labour, seeing that on the morrow Moshe and Aharon would turn the life-giving river Yeor into blood. According to our tradition no more slave labour was performed from the day the plague of blood occurred. Not only that, but the Mitzrim would pay Bnei Yisrael good money to obtain some drinking water from them seeing that water did not turn into blood once Bnei Yisrael held it in their hands (compare Shemot Rabbah 9,10). The expression כתמול שלשום, poses no problem as Bnei Yisrael did not complete their quota on the day prior to Moshe's interview because it was a public holiday.

כי נרפים הם, "for they are lazy!" Who had ever suggested that the idea to sacrifice to their G'd originated in the relatively light burden of work that Paroh had imposed on Bnei Yisrael up until then? Perhaps what Paroh meant was that Bnei Yisrael felt that now that Moshe had arrived their lot would become easier and that therefore they wanted to thank their G'd for that by offering up thanksgiving sacrifices so that He would cancel out the servitude altogether. Paroh countered this euphoria by making the workload heavier so that they would not even entertain any idea of their servitude being near an end, i.e. those lies that Moshe had fed them.

Paroh also reacted to Bnei Yisrael having said: נלכה נזבחה, "let us go slaughter, etc." He understood this as an implied promise that Bnei Yisrael planned to make up the time lost by working extra hard after their return. He reasoned that if they could really do this it was proof they had not been working hard enough thus far. This is why he withdrew the supply of straw which had been provided up until then and referred to them as lazy. Eventually, their holiday would backfire and the would cry out, i.e. צועקים that they had to work too hard. Paroh wanted to head off all these complications by ordering now that the straw would be withdrawn so that the people would stop dreaming about all kinds of improvements in their lives.

The expression ואל ישעו reflects weakness. Paroh interpreted the people's weakness as stemming from the "illusions" (in his view) which Moshe had come to feed them. As a result they had expressed fear of punishment by their G'd if they did not offer the sacrifices their G'd demanded. When people live in fear they are weak and it undermines their ability to perform good work. Paroh wanted to stop this process at the source, hence his decree to suspend the deliveries of straw.

כי אין נגרע מעבודתכם, "for your workload will not be diminished." Why did the taskmasters say: כי אין נגרע "for it will not be reduced" instead of ואין נגרע? "and it will not be reduced?" When the taskmasters had first said: "go and get your own straw," Bnei Yisrael had thought of this as a welcome diversion. They considered collecting straw as less demanding than either building, or forming bricks. The taskmasters "dropped the second shoe" by adding that it was not as Bnei Yisrael thought that collecting straw was instead of their other work; rather it was in addition to their regular work. They explained that the reason for the decree was precisely so as not to diminish Bnei Yisrael's workload.

וישב משה אל השם, Moshe returned to G'd, etc. The verse must be understood in this order: "Why did You G'd not tell me at the time when You told me that You would harden Paroh's heart that this would involve additional hardship for the people? If You were to answer that the appointed time for relieving the burden of their servitude has not arrived yet, why did You send me already at this time? Moshe implied that G'd should have waited with sending him on this mission until the actual slave labour of Bnei Yisrael had come to an end.

We have a reaction by Moshe to what Hashem had told him previously, namely that the end of the redemption process was not yet at hand but that He, Hashem, would advance the time for rescuing the Jewish people by saving them from their oppression. At the end of twelve months the Exodus itself would take place. Moshe now asked: "why did You bring harm upon this people?" He meant that if Hashem were to tell him that this suffering would advance the redemption, "why did You send me already now? You Yourself have told me that the only reason to commence the mission now was to relieve the people of having to perform slave labour. If as it now appeared, my mission was to be effective only at the time of the Exodus, why did You send me ?" The word זה (numerical value 12) in Moshe's question was an allusion to the 12 months the people still had to wait for the redemption. Moshe was clearly afraid that Paroh's most recent decree would be in effect for the 12 months until the redemption.

Perhaps Moshe also referred to the fact that amongst Bnei Yisrael there were those who had to perform slave labour, and others, such as the the tribe of Levi, who were free from that burden. Concerning the former group Moshe asked: "why have You brought harm upon them?" Concerning the latter group he asked: "why did You send me on this mission?"

Moshe may also simply have asked: "why did You cause harm to Your people?" G'd's answer would have to be that the harm was the result of Moshe's mission. To this Moshe retorted: "Why is this (זה) that You have sent me on this mission?" Moshe's adding of the word זה was his way of saying that this was why he had been unwilling to undertake the mission in the first place.

לדבר בשמך…והצל לא הצלת את עמך. "to speak in Your name…but You have not saved Your people." Moshe added another argument to his previous ones. He wanted to know how it was possible that since he had spoken to this wicked king in the name of Hashem, not only had He not responded but He had actually made things worse for the people whom Moshe represented. He emphasised the word מאז to point out that Paroh's obstinacy appeared to have been a direct consequece of Hashem's intervention through Moshe. Clearly what Paroh did was motivated by his hatred for Hashem. He was unparalleled in his rebellious behaviour against the king of the universe. Moshe was amazed at Hashem's apparent lack of jealousy of His reputation. Surely Hashem now had an additional reason to redeem Yisrael immediately. Even if Yisrael did not merit redemption at this time due to its own merit, it had to be redeemed as a gesture against the blaspheming Paroh! The words והצל לא הצלת should be read as a question expressing Moshe's amazement that Hashem had not yet saved His people. Moshe spoke of two "salvations," i.e. the one due to Yisrael's merit and the one due to Paroh's excesses.

עתה תראה אשר אעשה לפרעה, "Now you are about to see what I shall do to Paroh, etc." The word עתה was G'd's answer to Moshe's ומאז באתי, that G'd had made things worse for Yisrael than prior to Moshe's appointment. G'd told Moshe that not only would the additional hardships cease forthwith but also the hardships endured by the people up until then would come to an end immediately. We have already mentioned that slave labour ceased from the time the river Yeor was struck and turned into blood. G'd made it plain to Moshe that not only had he been wrong in assuming that the most recent decree of Paroh would last for twelve months, but even his previous decrees would become inoperative at once.

Hashem also answered Moshe concerning what Moshe had perceived as Hashem's failure to respond to the way Paroh had slighted Him. This is why He told Moshe that He would smite him until Paroh would dismiss Bnei Yisrael because he had experienced Hashem's strong hand. We explained already that Hashem delayed the final plague in order to punish Paroh for his blasphemy.

וביד חזקה, "and with a mighty hand, etc." This second reference to G'd's mighty hand was a preview of the consternation G'd would cause at the time of the killing of the firstborn when the Torah reports that there was not a single house in Mitzrayim in which not at least one person died at that time (compare Yalkut Shimoni on Shemot 12,30 where it is explained that if there was no actual firstborn in a specific house at the time, the oldest would be killed). As a result of all this the Mitzrim would not only dismiss Bnei Yisrael but would actually יגרשם, "expel them," as each Mitzri feared for his own life every minute (compare Shemot 12,33). G'd answered Moshe's other argument as to why He had allowed things to get worse in the next פרשה.

וידבר אלוקים אל משה, G'd spoke sternly to Moshe, etc. Why did the Torah not tell us what G'd said? Besides, why did G'd refer to Himself as י־ה־ו־ה after He had already told Moshe who He was in 3,15? At that time He had added: "this is My name forever!" Why then did He have to tell Moshe at this juncture אני ה׳?

Inasmuch as Moshe had spoken in an unseemly manner in the presence of the Almighty, something that he never would have dared to do if G'd had not previously shown him His smiling face as represented by the attribute י־ה־ו־ה, G'd had to show him a different attribute i.e. אלוקים before answering him in detail. The Torah introduces this chapter (from verse 2) by letting us know that G'd spoke in His capacity as the attribute of Justice, i.e. אלוקים.

When Hashem appears to make a turnabout at the end of our verse and refers to Himself as the attribute of Mercy this is in line with the principle expressed in Berachot 30 that "wherever there is גלה, joy in one's relationship with Hashem, there must be רעדה, fear or dread, simultaneously." Although Elokim had previously displayed His attribute of Mercy this did not mean that man should not display an appropriate degree of trepidation when facing Him.

Our verse may also be understood thus: וידבר אלוקים, Elokim spoke to Moshe on matters of justice. Since Hashem wanted Moshe to know that his argument had been heard and considered, He added: אני השם. The use of this attribute at this juncture is equivalent to Hashem asking Moshe: "how could you attribute to Me a negative virtue such as being the originator of harm befalling My people? My outstanding characteristic is the sttribute of חסד, love, mercy, etc." Even the prophet Yirmiyahu has already made it plain that evil never originates with Hashem (compare Eichah 3,38: "Evil does not originate from Hashem (but only Good)." The letter ו in front of the word והטוב in the verse in Lamentations refers to the fact that Hashem does not interfere if a person wants to be good or evil. These decisions are up to each individual. It is up to man to choose good rather than evil. When you study the Bible you will find that whenever Hashem mentions that the wicked are being remembered when they receive their deserts, the Bible underlines that the evil they are being punished for is of their own making. Compare in this respect Shmuel I 24,13: "Wicked deeds come from wicked men." Yirmiyahu 2,19: "Your evil deeds will cause you to be disciplined." Yeshayahu 64,6: "You have made us melt because of our iniquities." There are many more similar quotations in the Bible. In view of this what gave Moshe the right to assume that Bnei Yisrael's additional hardships were not due to something they had done themselves? It is also possible that Bnei Yisrael had not yet been adequately punished for whatever they had been guilty of prior to Moshe's appointment. Perhaps some of the people had even become guilty of lack of faith after Moshe had accredited himself as their prophet and leader. Your best proof that this was possible is the fact that the elders who set out to face Paroh together with Moshe and Aharon dropped out on the way. Perhaps Hashem would not have allowed Paroh to make the decree of withholding straw if the elders had not abandoned Moshe on the way? At any rate Moshe had been too quick to describe what happened to the people as being Hashem's fault.

Perhaps G'd simply responded to the two questions Moshe had raised in their proper order. G'd responded harshly to the question: "Why have You let evil happen to the people? Moshe's question/accusation had been inappropriate. The Torah was so concerned about Moshe's honour that it did not spell out the fact that he had spoken in an inadmissible fashion. G'd responded kindly to Moshe's question: "Why have You sent me?" G'd may even have hinted that in due course Moshe would have to answer for his question and this is why the details are not spelled out here. When G'd reverted to "I am the merciful G'd," this was the answer to "Why have You sent me?" G'd meant that He had sent Moshe because He could not longer sit idly by when His people were being tortured, and this is why He had decided to advance the date when they would cease to suffer by sending Moshe now so that he could orchestrate a string of plagues with which G'd would hit the Mitzrim. Moshe would begin to see immediately how at least the slave labour would come to an end.

Perhaps we can understand G'd manifesting Himself simultaneously as the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy through reference to Bamidbar Rabbah 3,6 where we find a discussion about what merit led to the Exodus of the Jewish people from Mitzrayim. One of the sages quotes Tehillim 68,7 מוציא אסירים בכושרות to mean that the word כושרות is a combined form of בכי, weeping, and שיר song. Accordingly, two attributes of G'd were at work during the Exodus. G'd applied His attribute of Justice to the Mitzrim, hence weeping, whereas He applied His attribute of Mercy to Bnei Yisrael, hence song. In our verse we find a parallel to that when G'd is introduced as אלוקים i.e. His attitude to the Mitzrim, and immediately afterwards as י־ה־ו־ה i.e. as His attitude to the Yehudim. We have a principle that once G'd allows the destructive forces free reign, those forces do not distinguish between the guilty and the innocent. This principle is especially apparent when the innocent and the guity dwell in close proximity to one another, something that was certainly the case with Yehudim and Mitzrim at that time. Moshe would have assumed that when G'd would bring the plagues on the Mitzrim there would be a negative fallout also on Bnei Yisrael. This is why G'd hinted already at this time that whereas He would act as אלוקים against the Mitzrim, He would at one and the same time act as השם towards the Yehudim so that they would not suffer from any of these plagues. All of this is spelled out later in greater detail such as that even in the midst of such a plague as darkness no darkness engulfed a single Yehudi (compare Shemot 10,23). The same occurred in 9,6 during the plague of pestilence when not a single one of the animals owned by Yehudim died.

We have a tradition expressed in Bereshit Rabbah 73,3 that "wicked people can cause the attribute of Mercy to be converted into the attribute of Justice." Our verse may refer to such an instance. It commences with the attribute of Justice, and continues by mentioning the attribute of Mercy. This is a way of the Torah telling us that the attribute of Mercy agreed with what the attribute of Justice was about to do to Paroh and the Mitzrim.

In the same Midrash where we are told that the wicked may cause the attribute of Mercy to co-operate with the attribute of Justice, we are also told "hail to the righteous who are able to convert even the attribute of Justice to co-operate with the attribute of Mercy." Accordingly, the Torah i.e. וידבר אלוקים ויאמר may tell us that the reason the verse commences with Elokim as His attribute of Justice and then appearing as the attribute of Mercy is, that even the attribute of Mercy had agreed to the proposal of the attribute of Justice that the Yehudim should cease to perform slave labour and that the means to bring this about was the infliction of the plagues on the Mitzrim.

We may also see in this verse G'd's response to Moshe's amazement why He had not reacted to the insult Paroh had committed when he denied His existence. The words וידבר אלוקים are directed at Paroh who was about to experience proof of G'd's existence by being subjected to a string of retributory plagues. G'd could have eliminated Paroh in a single plague if He had employed only the attribute of Justice. The reason He chose not to do so was that He wanted to acquaint Paroh with one of His other attributes, i.e. His long patience, ארך אפים. G'd is in no hurry to conclude His dealings with the recalcitrant sinners, giving them a chance to repent. This is why we have input by the attribute of Mercy even in His dealings with Paroh.

On the other hand, G'd may have demonstrated that His harshness, i.e. וידבר אלוקים was reserved for the messenger, i.e. Moshe. The Jewish people, i.e. the ones under the messenger's care, were not to suffer from the mistake their leader had made. This is why G'd continued: ויאמר השם.

G'd may also have told Moshe here that although He ought to employ the attribute of Justice against him at this stage, He did not do so because He kept in mind that that attribute was reserved for people who had committed a sin consciously (compare Rosh Hashanah 17 defining עובר על פשע). It is well known that Moshe was extremely humble; as a result, G'd employed His own attribute of being נושא עון, demonstrating a forgiving nature, when reacting to Moshe's error in this instance. He alluded to this when He told him אני השם.

Finally, G'd may have revealed a mystical dimension of His to Moshe when He explained that He could combine the attribute of Justice and the attribute of Mercy within Himself; this was a new aspect of G'd's unity which Moshe had not been aware of.

וארא אל אברהם, I used to appear to Avraham, etc. The reason Hashem did not lump the three patriarchs together but referred to each one by name is, that Hashem's relationship with each one of the patriarchs was based on something unique to the patriarch in question. Avraham was unique in that he recognised his Creator without having had guidance from another human being. If someone had foreknowledge of the existence of Hashem and His power, he does not deserve special credit for conducting himself in line with such knowledge. Every intelligent being would choose good over evil once he possessed such knowledge. Avraham did not possess any of these advantages which would have acquainted him with Hashem's attributes. We have explained in connection with Yeshayahu 41,9 that the reason Hashem called Avraham "the one who loves Me" was because his faith and morality was the result of his being a "self-starter." He cleaved to his faith in Hashem in spite of the most demanding tests Hashem subjected him to.

Yitzchak possessed another unique characteristic; he had submitted without question to his father's request made in the name of G'd to give his life for that G'd. He did not even ask for an explanation of why he had to give his life.
Yaakov was unique in not wasting a single drop of semen by producing offspring which was not worthy of him. All his children remained loyal to his teachings.

Hashem explained to Moshe that He had not revealed His attribute of the four-lettered name י־ה־ו־ה which He had revealed to Moshe to any of these three patrirachs, but had revealed to them only His attribute שדי. Hashem now told Moshe that in view of the revelations He had already made to him, he had displayed ingratitude by speaking to Him in an inappropriate, critical manner.

While it is true that in the Torah's report of Hashem's communications with Avraham (Bereshit 18,1) we find such an expression as וירא ה׳ אל אברהם, which seems to suggest that Hashem revealed this aspect (the tetragram) of His attributes to Avraham, this is misleading. Hashem may have dealt with him on that basis, but He had not confided that fact to Avraham, i.e. Avraham remained unaware of the difference between Hashem in His capacity as אל שדי and Hashem in His capacity as י־ה־ו־ה. This is what Hashem meant when He said ושמי ה׳ לא נודעתי להם, "they were not informed of My name י־ה־ו־ה.

G'd also meant that the patriarchs were not aware of the unique simultaneous effectiveness of both of G'd's attributes, as we mentioned in connection with verse two. The mystical dimension of this is recorded in Kings I 18,39 when the assembled people realised this after Eliyahu's demonstration on Mount Karmel. The prophet Zachariah also makes reference to this phenomenon in Zachariah 14,9 when he describes that in the futre והיה ה׳ אחד ושמו אחד, people will realise that in spite of G'd's many attributes these are all part of the same Essence. G'd's name and G'd's Essence will be perceived as an indivisible unit, unlike all creatures whose names do not necessarily reflect anything about their essence. It was inappropriate for G'd to say לא הודעתי, "I have not made known," since it was G'd's "name" who was speaking. This is why the Torah had to write: לא נודעתי "I have not become known."

Hashem may also have answered Moshe's question why He had sent him on this mission before the time designated for the redemption. He explained that Hashem's timetable is not absolute. When He had spoken to Avraham about a period of 400 years after which Bnei Yisrael would leave their exile and bondage with great wealth (Bereshit 15,14), that timetable had been based on Hashem having revealed His attribute אל שדי to Avraham. That attribute is one which is inflexible. It reflects the fact that Hashem has set absolute limits to certain developments. However, that attribute is part of the overall attribute אלוקים, an attribute which governs Hashem's manifestations in nature. Hashem had not taught Avraham that by appealing to His attribute of רחמים, Mercy, the limitations which are part of the אל שדי syndrome can become more flexible. Since the prayers of the whole Jewish nation had reached His attribute of Mercy this is why He decided to respond before the time which had originally been designated for the redemption. Hashem began by saying that he was י־ה־ו־ה in order to teach Moshe that when one "knocks on the door of Mercy," such knocks are apt to evoke a response on the other side of that door.

There may be yet another nuance in Hashem's saying "I have appeared to Avraham." The implied message is Hashem's rhetorical question: "How could I turn a deaf ear to a nation who are the offspring of My most beloved Patriarchs, to each of whom I made a point of revealing Myself separately at the appropriate time. The Torah made a point of not writing אברהם,יצחק,יעקב, but of interposing the word אל each time. This underlines that each one of the patriarchs merited a revelation in his own right. In spite of all this, Hashem continues, I still did not reveal the aspect of the attribute of Mercy to these patriarchs. One of the reasons I could not do this was because I had not yet demonstrated how this Mercy is expressed in practice, such as now when I am about to change My timetable for the redemption.

וגם הקימותי את בריתי, "And I also maintain My covenant, etc." G'd may have added here (according to our previous commentary) that even if He had already fulfilled His covenant with the patriarchs, they still would not have become privy to the degree of revelation that Moshe had already now become privy to.

Put simply, Hashem explains to Moshe in our verse that He owed the patriarchs something over and beyond His having revealed Himself to the patriarchs as the אל שדי. That something was the fulfilment of His promise/oath that the people of Yisrael would be redeemed from bondage. The time had now arrived for that promise to be kept; Hashem also explained to Moshe why he had to wait for the redemption somewhat longer, i.e. that Hashem now invoked His מדת הרחמים. Hashem was afraid that Moshe would not have the emotional fortitude to pursue his mission with all the necessary vigour when he saw Paroh's obstinacy, or when he would face the pursuing Mitzri cavalry behind him and the sea in front; Hashem therefore explained to Moshe that the purpose of the redemption was not only the Exodus but also the conquest of the Holy Land.

את ארץ מגוריהם, "the land in which they (the patriarchs) used to sojourn." Why did the Torah not content itself with describing the land the patriarchs had lived in as "the land of Kenaan?" Why did the words את ארץ מגוריהם have to be added? Perhaps the Torah wanted to make us aware that the status of being aliens (which was part of the period of 400 years G'd had spoken to Avraham about) had already commenced during the lifetime of the patriarchs. This would have a great bearing on the timing of the Exodus. Still, this would leave open why the Torah had to use the word את twice when referring to that land.
