Use of that word creates the impression that the land of Kenaan and the land in which the patriarchs sojourned were two different countries. Perhaps the Torah wanted to include the land of the Plishtim [the coastal strip including Azah, seeing that the Plishtim were not of Canaanitic descent Ed.]. I have already explained this on Bereshit 26,3.

וגם אני שמעתי את נאקת בני ישראל, "I have also heard the groaning of the children of Yisrael, etc." The word וגם, "and also," refers to something over and beyond the prayers of Bnei Yisrael to the attribute of Mercy. In addition to the prayers of Bnei Yisrael and G'd's love for the patriarchs, there was a third consideration which had a bearing on G'd's timetable for the redemption, namely the outcry of Bnei Yisrael due to the torture they were experiencing. This third element is referred to by G'd in our verse by the words: וגם אני, "also I." G'd reveals His name of אני as an aspect of the attribute of Mercy. Previously, this name had only appeared in conjunction with the tetragram. G'd revealed that there are occasions when people's groanings even when not accompanied by verbalised prayer reach the attribute of Mercy and evoke a response. This is why He added אשר מצרים מעבידים אותם, "the manner in which the Mitzrim have enslaved them." I refer the reader to my comments on Shemot 2,23 in this respect.

ואזכר את בריתי, "I have remembered My covenant." G'd means that He remembered both parts of the covenant, i.e. to redeem the people and to bring them to the Holy Land. [This had been a covenant with the patriarchs. What is new is that the present generation of Bnei Yisrael would be the ones who would experience realisation of that covenant.] In this instance G'd spoke about a covenant which had not yet been spelled out but which follows immediately in the next four verses. G'd repeats the covenant only as an explanation of why He has advanced the date it is to become effective. The commentators who understand this covenant as a promise to punish the Mitzrim are wrong; none of this has been mentioned in the verse following this declaration.

לכן אמור לבני ישראל אני ה׳. "Therefore, say to Bnei Yisrael: 'I am י־ה־ו־ה.'" Moshe was to tell Bnei Yisrael in the name of Hashem that He was the attribute of Mercy and that He had decided to invoke this attribute on their behalf. As a result, He would lead them out of Mitzrayim and perform the other stages which would complete the process of redemption.

The word לכן is a form of an oath as we know from Yechezkel 20,30-42. In that instance the prophet refers to our verse as something concerning which Hashem had said: "I have raised My hand," i.e. a clear form of an oath.

Elokim enumerates the steps of the redemption. 1) First "I will take you out from beneath the hard labour of Mitzrayim;" this is the removal of the slave labour performed for the Mitzrim. It would commence immediately with the plague of blood. Although this resulted in the dispersal of the taskmasters, Bnei Yisrael continued to perform light duty tasks. 2) "I will save you from their bondage;" this referred to the remaining kind of labour Bnei Yisrael performed for the Mitzrim. 3) "I will liberate you;" this refers to the actual departure of Bnei Yisrael from the country. This also includes the splitting of the sea as the departure would have been meaningless without that final stage. The word וגאלתי must refer to a liberation which is not followed by pursuit. Following that stage the Jewish people would experience ולקחתי אתכם לי לעם," I will take you to be My people" which is a reference to the revelation at Mount Sinai when Elokim gave us the Torah. At that point Elokim would be able to say that: "I have truly become your Elokim."

These latter words may also refer to Moshe's prayer in Shemot 33,16 which Berachot 7 interprets to mean that Hashem should not reveal Himself to any other nation nor give them prophets. The operative word in והייתי לכם לאלוקים then would be לכם, "for you exclusively."

One could also understand this verse as speaking of four separate redemptions as does Shemot Rabbah 6,4. This may be alluded to in G'd first again repeating His attribute as the tetragram. Accordingly, the four activities of which G'd speaks here would each be a redemption from a different decree of Paroh. The words "I shall be your G'd" would then refer to G'd having proved that He kept His promise. The name אלוקים often occurs as symbolic of truth and honesty. The knowledge of G'd as the attribute of Mercy will become widespread amongst the people as a result of these four redemptions.

וידעתם כי אני ה׳ אלוקיכם, "you will know that I י־ה־ו־ה am Hashem your Elokim." Elokim means that Bnei Yisrael will now receive clear evidence which attribute of Elokim it is that will set in motion the various steps of the redemption. They will also realise in retrospect that the attribute of Mercy had been predominant in all of Elokim's actions.

והבאתי אתכם אל הארץ, "And I shall bring you to the land, etc." It is difficult to reconcile this promise with our tradition that Hashem speaks the unvarnished truth when we know it to be a fact that the generation Hashem was addressing at that time did not get to the Holy Land. Only the children of that generation actually crossed the Yarden and took possession of the land of Kenaan. Every one of the people who left Mitzrayim at an age of twenty or over died on the way. Our problem is even more serious in view of the statement of our sages (Shemot Rabbah 6:4) that the word לכן in 6,6, is a form of an oath.

I believe that Hashem Himself was already aware of this problem and that is why He prefaced the statement "I will bring you to the land, etc," with the words: "you will know that I am the merciful Hashem who is about to take you out from under the slave labour of Mitzrayim." The two statements are to be considered as conditions. What Hashem meant was simply this. "Provided that you will have realised that I am the One who takes you out of Mitzrayim and that I have demonstrated to be the merciful Hashem,-then you will also experience that I shall bring you to the land which I have sworn to your forefathers and will give it to you as an inheritance." Hashem was very careful to insert this condition in the very midst of the promise He made and not only as an afterthought. In the event that Bnei Yisrael would not fulfil the conditions laid down history would have to take its course in accordance with their conduct.

מקצר רות ומעבודה קשה, for impatience of spirit and cruel bondage. Perhaps the people did not respond positively to this assurance because they had not yet received the Torah. Since Torah broadens a person's mind, the Torah may hint at that by describing Bnei Yisrael's state of mind as "narrow minded, limited."

ומעבודה קשה, and because of the cruel bondage. The reason that the Torah writes: "and because of the cruel bondage," is that they suffered from קצר רוח, impatience, quite independently of the effects of the bondage on their state of mind. They had become impatient at their fate when they pondered the additional workload Paroh had imposed upon them. A person who is in that frame of mind cannot even perform the labour he is normally capable of performing. This is why the Torah adds the words ומעבודה קשה.

The people had good reason for becoming impatient at their fate because when Moshe had come he had given them hope that their liberation was close at hand. This had given them a new and broader perspective on life. Now, when Paroh had decreed additional hardships their minds could concentrate only on how to cope with the immediate and even worse situation. The word מעבודה may therefore be understood as something comparative, i.e. the even greater bondage than had been their lot prior to Moshe's coming.

ויאמר…. בא דבר אל פרעה, He said:" come and speak sternly with Paroh, etc." Moshe was to tell Paroh that G'd had instructed him to speak to Paroh and to demand that he should let the Jewish people depart from his land. The letter ו at the beginning of the word וישלח is significant because it does not make sense as a conjunctive letter; nothing else had been demanded prior to that in the conversation described. It must therefore refer to Moshe telling Paroh that his first instruction had been to tell him that he spoke at the behest of G'd. It was quite an event that an ordinary individual should present himself at court without invitation and make demands on the Monarch. The manner in which these demands were to be made was even more astounding.
Moreover, it appears that Moshe was to demand not only that Paroh should not object if Bnei Yisrael would leave of their own accord, but he was to demand that Paroh actually give them a "send-off."

לפני ה׳ לאמור הן בני ישראל לא שמעו אלי, in Hashem's presence, saying: "here Bnei Yisrael do not listen to me, etc." What is the meaning of the word לאמור in this context? Who was Hashem to communicate Moshe's comments to? Perhaps we should not understand this verse as Moshe's contemplating to refuse this mission but as a comment addressed to himself, bemoaning his failure thus far. The word לאמור could be a rhetorical comment Moshe made that instead of results, all his attempts of speaking to Paroh would remain just that, words.

Moshe may also have alluded to his inability to speak effectively due to his stammer which had made even Bnei Yisrael unwilling to respond to him. He implied that Hashem should heal his disability in order to make him a more effective spokesman.

הן בני ישראל לא שמעו, "even the children of Yisrael have not listened, etc." The logic expressed by Moshe in this verse seems untenable if Moshe accepted the Torah's statement in verse nine that the reason Bnei Yisrael did not respond to Moshe was their קצר רוח, their understandable impatience. How could Moshe compare Paroh's potentially negative response to that of Bnei Yisrael? What comparable pressure had Paroh been under?

Perhaps Moshe's logic is valid when we consider some other aspects. While it is true that Bnei Yisrael suffered from an impatient state of mind, there were other reasons why they should have listened to Moshe. The most important such reason was their faith in Hashem. Secondly, this inherent faith should have been reinforced by the good news Moshe had brought them. When contrasted with these two factors which certainly did not influence Paroh who had blasphemed "who is Hashem?", the fact that Bnei Yisrael did not listen to him made it seem totally unjustified to expect that Paroh should take Moshe's demands seriously. Moshe suggested that the קצר רוח displayed by Bnei Yisrael was minor compared to the קצר רוח which Paroh would display once he heard Moshe's demands.

The reason Moshe added at this juncture that he had a stammer was because he felt this would reinforce Paroh's rejection of anything he had to say. Paroh would reason- at least to himself- that if the powerful Elokim that Moshe spoke about had not even cured his spokesman of a simple speech defect, it was laughable to think that He could impose His will on the mightiest ruler in the world. In fact, if this kind of reasoning were to be conveyed to Bnei Yisrael, it might further undermine their faith in Elokim.

There was another reason for Moshe's argument at this point. Whereas in Shemot 4,16 Hashem had countered Moshe's argument about his stammer by appointing Aharon as his mouthpiece, this was only in order to convey Hashem's message to Moshe to the Jewish people. We find confirmation of this in 4,30. However, already in 5,1 we find that Moshe himself spoke in his mission to Paroh (at least also). If we look for confirmation of this thought in the text we may find it in the way Moshe describes Bnei Yisrael's attitude to him and the attitude he expects from Paroh. Concerning Yisrael he said: "they did not listen to me" seeing Yisrael only heard the voice of Aharon. When describing Paroh's anticipated reaction Moshe says ישמעני "he will hear me," meaning he will hear Moshe's defective speech. It is important to remember this little detail in order to facilitate understanding of what is still to come.

וידבר ה׳ אל משה ואל אהרון, Hashem spoke to Moshe and to Aharon, etc. First of all we need to know what Hashem said to them, secondly what did the Torah mean when it added :"He commanded them to the children of Yisrael and to Paroh, etc." According to Shemot Rabbah 7,3 Hashem informed Moshe and Aharon about how intractable the people could be and how they were apt to heap abuse on their leaders. Moshe and Aharon should therefore lead them בנחת, in an easy-going manner. Hashem also told Moshe and Aharon not to be disrespectul to Royalty, i.e. to the person of Paroh. These comments are purely homiletical. Furthermore, where is Hashem's response to Moshe who had questioned the point of this whole mission? The very least Hashem could have told Moshe was that his logic was faulty! Whereas it is possible to construe Hashem's silence as disapproval of Moshe's reasoning, we cannot do so in this instance. Let us look for a moment at the verse that follows. Assuming that Moshe had not been concerned about what Hashem would answer him in response to his question "how can Paroh listen to me if even Bnei Yisrael do not listen to me?" Why wouldn't Hashem have continued immediately with what He had to say in verse 29? What is the whole point of the Torah repeating Moshe's question again in 6,29-30 unless Moshe had not received an answer from Hashem to his קל וחומר, his logical argument?

In view of the above I believe the correct explanation is that Hashem did reply to Moshe's argument that Bnei Yisrael had not listened to him, and even to his second argument, that Paroh would most certainly not listen to him either as long as he was still afflicted with his speech defect. We need to understand Hashem's reply thus: וידבר ה׳ אל משה ואהרון, Hashem equated Moshe with Aharon in their mission so that Aharon would speak to Paroh (just as he had spoken to Bnei Yisrael as Moshe's mouthpiece) Seeing that thus far Bnei Yisrael had not listened to either Aharon or Moshe ויצום, He commanded them, He appointed them as "kings" over Bnei Yisrael so that the people would accept their authority forthwith. We find something similar in Shmuel I 13,14 where Shmuel told King Shaul that he would be supplanted and that Hashem had looked for someone else (David) whom "Hashem appointed as leader for His people" i.e. ויצווהו ה לנגיד על עמו.

When Hashem added the words להוציא את בני ישראל, He meant that the reason Moshe and Aharon would have to wield the kind of authority only a king can have was in order that He should be able to take the children of Yisrael out of Mitzrayim. Moshe would have the authority to deal with anyone who refused to leave Mitzrayim, for instance. At the same time Moshe's and Aharon's authority would also ensure that Paroh could not refuse them. It is even possible that when Moshe referred to Bnei Yisrael who had not listened to him, he referred to his lack of legal authority to force them to leave Mitzrayim when the time came, and that he was already aware that there would be such Yehudim. When we consider all this, Hashem did indeed answer Moshe's claim that Bnei Yisrael did not listen to him by saying that as of now they would be under orders to listen to him. At the same time, Hashem instructed Moshe not to address Paroh as someone who appeals to him but as someone who ordered Paroh to carry out his instructions.

אלה ראשי בית אבותם, These are the heads of the various families, etc. The reason the family background of Moshe is listed here is in accordance with the principle that only people whose genealogy can be traced back directly to Yaakov are fit to be appointed as kings over Yisrael. This is the reason the Torah did not state the יחוס of Moshe and Aharon until they had been given Royal authority. This is all still part of the answer of Hashem to Moshe's comment that Bnei Yisrael did not and would not listen to him.
הוא אהרון ומשה, they are the same Aharon and Moshe, etc. The ones whose genealogy has been traced in our paragraph are the ones whom Hashem gave the authority to orchestrate the Exodus, etc.

הם המדברים אל פרעה מלך מצרים, they were the ones who talked tough to Paroh the king of Mitzrayim. They spoke to him as does a king who issues decrees. The Torah also wanted to remind us that though Hashem had instructed Moshe to speak, Aharon spoke also, as I shall explain in greater detail on verse 28.

הוא משה ואהרון, they are the same Moshe and Aharon, etc. The Torah wants to convey that Moshe and Aharon enjoyed equal status; this is why sometimes Aharon is mentioned first whereas other times Moshe is mentioned first. The Torah makes this point doubly clear by referring to both of them in the singular i.e. הוא, as opposed to הם. The Torah uses the plural also i.e. הם המדברים. This is because Moshe and Aharon did not speak simultaneously but they alternated when speaking to Paroh.

ויהי ביום דבר ה׳ אל משה, It was on the day that Hashem spoke to Moshe. The Torah here wants to correct any mistaken impression that the equality of Moshe and Aharon had already existed on the day Hashem told Moshe while still in Midyan (Shemot 4,14) that his brother Aharon was on the way to met him. This is why the Torah adds here: "On the day Hashem spoke to Moshe in the land of Mitzrayim," as if to say: "on that day Moshe and Aharon were of equal stature."

The Torah therefore had good reason to repeat that Hashem told Moshe: "I am the Hashem י־ה־ו־ה, speak sternly to Paroh." The repetition was meant to reassure Moshe that he could rely on what Hashem had told him. He was to go and speak to Paroh personally. In other words, nothing had changed since the first time Hashem had identified Himself to Moshe as the tetragram at the beginning of our portion. I explained that at that point Hashem had not yet appointed Aharon to be Moshe's mouthpiece except when Moshe wanted to say something to Bnei Yisrael. What happened in the meantime was that Moshe repeated his argument that he had a speech defect and was not suited to speak in public after Hashem had told him to speak to Paroh. Hence Hashem authorised Aharon to speak to Paroh also in 7,1. As a result Aharon had become Moshe's equal concerning what they had to tell Paroh. Inasmuch as Moshe had not previously complained about his not being fit to speak to Paroh there had been no need for Hashem to appoint Aharon as His spokesman.

All the above shows Hashem's concern to employ Moshe as His exclusive messenger. He had co-opted Aharon only when Moshe had raised repeated objections. Perhaps the reason that our verse employs the word ויהי, which always reflects something regrettable, is to let us know how much Hashem regretted the necessity of having Aharon share what was originally meant to be Moshe's exclusive mission. The word ויהי may therefore suggest that if Moshe had indeed remained Hashem's sole messenger the quality of the redemption might have been different; some of the side-effects of the incomplete redemption which led to such disasters as the golden calf episode might never have occurred, for instance.

Perhaps the reason that the editor of this paragraph in the Torah saw fit to write our verse as a paragraph by itself and not as the beginning of chapter seven or even before verse eight in chapter seven was, that he wanted us to know that G'd was saddened by the fact that He had to appoint someone to share Moshe's mission with him. Had Moshe been the only one, he himself might have entered the Holy Land as leader of the people as had been G'd's original intention. He might have lived to participate in the building of the Holy Temple which Shlomo built over 400 years after Moshe's death. That Temple might then have endured forever.

It is also possible that the Torah made a special paragraph out of this single verse in order to tell us that Aharon's status was equal to Moshe as of that day in Mitzrayim, and that even previously when Hashem had announced to Moshe that he would be Moshe's spokesman, this did not imply equal status. When Aharon would speak alone Hashem describes his position as "he will be your prophet," or similarly when the Torah states: "he will speak to Paroh."

ולא ישמע אליכם פרעה, "and Paroh will not listen to you." Why did the Torah have to say that Paroh would not listen to Moshe and Aharon after G'd had already said in verse three that He would harden the heart of Paroh? We also need to understand what G'd meant when He spoke about placing His hand on Mitzrayim, which appears to mean something over and beyond the plagues with which G'd will strike Paroh and the Mitzrim.

I believe that we must understand the verse thus: First of all, Hashem announces that He would harden Paroh's heart as a result of which He would bring many plagues upon him. The plagues would prove counterproductive (initally) and make Paroh even more obstinate, adding still more sins to his already considerable culpability. Eventually, he would not even want to listen to what Moshe and Aharon had been instructed to tell him. This is in fact what happened in 10,28 when Paroh bans Moshe and Aharon from appearing again in His presence. Hashem announces to Moshe already at this point that when that stage will be reached it would be the limit of obstinacy that Paroh is allowed. Immediately after that ban Hashem brought the final plague of the dying of the Mitzri firstborns upon him, as a result of which he would not only release Bnei Yisrael but expel them.

We find confirmation of this meaning of the word "My hand," when we read in Chronicles I 21,16 that David observed the angel of death with drawn sword in "his hand." In our instance, Hashem refers to the fact that He personally would bring this plague upon Paroh by describing His activity as ידי, "My hand." This is why the Mechilta on Shemot 11,4 states that He Himself would be active as distinct from any of His agents. Elokim also alluded to the destruction He would bring upon the various Mitzri deities at that time.

When we keep all this in mind we can understand Moshe's comment that "I will not continue to see your face," which appears as somewhat high-handed at first. Whence did Moshe know that G'd would not send him to speak to Paroh again in spite of Paroh's threat? The answer is that Moshe had been told already in our verse exactly how things would develop. Instead of questioning Moshe's statement we should congratulate him on recognising that Paroh had reached the end of his rope when he forbade Moshe and Aharon to appear before him and threatened to have them executed in the event they would come to him again. Up until then Paroh had only refused to listen to G'd's instructions. The moment he even refused to grant an interview to G'd's messengers he had forfeited all further consideration. Actually, this was already the second allusion to the eventual slaying of the firstborn, the first time being when G'd referred to "My firstborn, Yisrael," as I have demonstrated in my commentary on 4,22.

והוצאתי את צבאותי את עמי, "I will take out My hosts, My people, etc." Who exactly are the ones Hashem describes as צבאותי, "My hosts?" If the reference is to Bnei Yisrael, the Torah should have written: את צבאות עמי, "the hosts who are My people." Perhaps Hashem wanted to illustrate the superior stature of Bnei Yisrael, i.e. that of all of Hashem's hosts none could compare to His people Yisrael. Had the Torah used the words: את צבאות עמי, the impression would have been created that Hashem has many hosts, Bnei Yisrael being merely one of many. By saying צבאותי, further identification became unnecessary as only one people qualified for such a description. Subsequently the Torah does identify Hashem's people by mentioning Yisrael by name. The whole verse can be understood according to the classic principle of כלל ופרט. Whenever that rule is applied the פרט, i.e. the details are automatically closely related to what is stated in the כלל, the subject in the general statement, i.e. only Bnei Yisrael could have been meant in the description צבאותי. The Torah therefore wanted the world to know that as of that moment whenever mention is made of Hashem's hosts only Bnei Yisrael are meant.

ויעש משה ואהרון…כן עשו, Moshe and Aharon did (as Hashem had commanded)..so they did. Why does this verse mention twice that Moshe and Aharon did what Hashem had commanded them to do? The Torah may be telling us that Moshe and Aharon carried out their mission on two levels. 1) The carried out all those instructions of Hashem that made sense to them. 2) They tried to understand Hashem's purpose in every detail of the instructions they received. By not deviating in a single detail from the instructions they had received, Moshe and Aharon proved that their only concern was to carry out Hashem's intention to the letter.

The Torah may also testify here that Moshe and Aharon had no ulterior motives in carrying out any details of Hashem's instructions. We find a parallel to this in Devarim 6,25 where the Torah states that carrying out Hashem's laws will be considered צדקה, righteousness for us, if we perform them כאשר צונו, "as He has commanded us." It is not enough to merely carry out Hashem's instructions, but in order to qualify for praise one must carry them out precisely as He commanded us. In our verse the Torah testifies that this is what Moshe and Aharon did.

Another point that our verse wanted to mention is that both Moshe and Aharon did not miss any opportunity to mention Hashem every time they did anything. The Torah underlines the word עשו to show that Moshe and Aharon carried out Hashem's instructions immediately after they had received them.
בדברם אל פרעה, when they spoke to Paroh. The word בדברם refers to the first day Moshe and Aharon spoke to Paroh. They were certainly somewhat older as time went on.

-9. לאמור…כי ידגר אלכם פרעה, to say: "when Paroh will say to you, etc." The reason the Torah adds the word לאמור is to inform us that they had been allowed to inform Paroh that they would perform the miracles in Hashem's name. Unless such permission had been granted explicitly, they would have been forbidden to reveal this even in response to a question by Paroh. We have learned in Yuma 4 that under normal circumstances one is not to reveal the source of one's information unless specifically authorised to do so. The first time the Torah writes לאמור here it is to give Moshe and Aharon permission to reveal this information. The Torah repeats the word לאמור once more in order to show that Hashem ordered Moshe and Aharon to reveal this information.

Another piece of information contained in this verse (according to Torat Kohanim is 1) is that wherever the Torah writes: "to Moshe and Aharon," the meaning is that Moshe should tell Aharon to carry out G'd's instructions. This piece of exegesis is derived from the very word לאמור here. It means that unlike your impression that G'd spoke to both Moshe and Aharon simultaneously, the truth is that G'd spoke to Moshe to relay the information to Aharon. The reason that the Torah makes it appear as if G'd had spoken to both of them simultaneously is only to tell us that the commandment performed by Aharon in relaying the information to Paroh was equal in importance to Moshe having performed his part of the commandment.

פרעה לאמור, תנו לכם מופת, Paroh saying: "perform a miracle for your accreditation," the reason the Torah inserts the word לאמור in addition to already having quoted Paroh as כי ידבר, was to tell Moshe not to volunteer a miracle until Paroh actually asked for it. At that point they were to perform the miracle described in our verse. Alternatively, if Paroh challenged Moshe and Aharon about the authenticity of their mission Moshe would also be entitled to tell Aharon to demonstrate the miracle described here.

ויעשו כן כאשר צוה, They did as Hashem had commanded, etc. The reason the Torah writes the words כן כאשר, i.e. repeating basically the same word is, because it tells us that Moshe and Aharon a) did what Hashem had told them to, b) did not do so until Paroh had requested the miracle from them.

The Torah also wanted us to know that though anyone who performs miracles immediately raises his own image in the eyes of the onlookers, Moshe and Aharon had no such considerations. They did what they did only at the behest of Hashem. It is the mark of the truly righteous not to perform their own will but to perform what they perceive to be Hashem's will.

ויאמר ה׳ אל משה כבד לב פרעה, Hashem said to Moshe: "Paroh's heart is stubborn, etc." What did Elokim tell Moshe here that he did not already know? Perhaps Paroh had not refused the request to let Bnei Yisrael go in so many words, but had merely remained silent after watching Aharon's demonstration. Hashem informed Moshe that the meaning of this silence was that Paroh refused to release Bnei Yisrael and did not even think it necessary to say so.

ואמרת אליו ה׳..שלחני אליך, "Say to him: Hashem.. has sent me to you, etc." This entire verse appears to be superfluous. Verse 17 would have been quite adequate. Paroh did not need to be told that Hashem had sent Moshe! Perhaps the Torah wanted to tell us that Paroh had objected to being met by Moshe at a time when he performed his morning ritual. Moshe was to explain that he had not intended to invade Paroh's privacy but had been commanded by Hashem to do so. Moshe was to imply that instructions from the Supreme Hashem must be carried out immediately.

G'd may have intended another lesson for Paroh, one which is alluded to in Shemot Rabbah 8,1 based on Yechezkel 29,3 where Paroh is described as claiming that he had made the river Yeor and that he owned it. Since Paroh had thus elevated himself to the level of a deity, he had to leave the palace every morning and answer a call of nature where he would not be seen in order that he could maintain the myth of being a god. G'd exploded this myth by sending Moshe to him at the time and place Paroh had reserved for his very human needs. Moshe first told Paroh that the G'd of the Hebrews was well aware of his whereabouts and wanted him to know this and embarass him with this knowledge. Paroh was now under threat that his myth might be shattered if Moshe were to tell his servants of their master's weakness. When G'd added that so far Paroh had not listened to him, He wanted Paroh to know that though the latter had not specifically refused Moshe's latest demand, G'd could read his thoughts.

The words "the G'd of the Hebrews has sent me to you," may also be a way of telling Paroh that the demand to release Bnei Yisrael need not be repeated before Moshe would strike the river Yeor and turn it into blood. The word כה was quite enough to show us that the plague that follows was the result of the demand to let Bnei Yisrael go which Paroh had thus far ignored. After all, Moshe had previously identified himself and Paroh had ignored the demand to dismiss Bnei Yisrael. If Paroh thought that the fact that he had not yet been smitten for his refusal was a sign that G'd's threats were not to be taken seriously, he would find out immediately how wrong he had been.

בזאת תדע כי אני ה׳, "In this you shall know that I am י־ה־ו־ה." The reason G'd used the plague of blood to prove to Paroh that He was who He said He was, is understandable when we consider Shemot Rabbah 9,9 according to which the Mitzrim looked upon the Yeor as a benevolent deity. By striking this deity first and turning it into a source of curse instead of a source of life, G'd demonstrated that He owned the Yeor. According to the Zohar volume 3 page 297 the tetragram implies the eternity of G'd. He had preceded the river Yeor just as He had preceded every other phenomenon in the world.

G'd also hinted at His attribute of Mercy when He smote the river. He wanted to give Paroh a chance to repent when the latter realised His awesome power as manifested by His turning the river into blood. If not for the attribute of Mercy as represented by the tetragram, G'd would have already killed Paroh outright at this stage. The words בזאת תדע therefore refer to G'd's attribute of Mercy.

ויעשו כן משה ואהרן, Moshe and Aharon did so precisely, etc. This means that when Moshe and Aharon smote the river the result was that Hashem's will was done and the result was the same as if Hashem Himself had struck the river. Please read what I have already written on verse six concerning such expressions in the Torah, as well as what I shall be writing on the verse following.

לעיני פרעה ולעיני עבדיו, before the eyes of Paroh and the eyes of his servants. Although Moshe issued the warning to Paroh when the latter was unaccompanied because he hid his need to answer calls of nature, the Torah tells us that G'd delayed implementing the plague until it could be done publicly in the presence of Paroh's servants. While it is true that the text does not mention this, it is most likely that G'd had mentioned this to Moshe for reasons of maximum effect. It is even possible that the words כן כאשר צוה, "exactly as He commanded," refer to words G'd had told Moshe but which were not spelled out in our text.

והדגה…מתה, and the fish…died; the Torah reports this detail to show that the Mitzrim realised that the plague was not just a sleight of hand, i.e. make-believe. The blood would kill the people who drank it (in quantities). The fact that the river stank proved that the plague was for real. When the Torah adds ויהי הדם בכל ארץ מצרים, "the blood persisted throughout the land of Mitzrayim," the reference is to bath-houses, bathtubs, etc. Perhaps the Torah wanted to tell us that the Mitzrim took the "blood" from one location to another. If the "blood" had been the result of witch-craft it would have reverted to water as soon as it had been removed from the sphere of the sorcerer who had performed the trick (compare Zohar volume 2 page 192). The Torah tells us that the Mitzrim realised that this phenomenon was something over and above the kind they were used to see their own sorcerers perform.

ויעשו כן חרטומי מצרים, The Mitzri sorcerers did likewise, etc. If we follow the sages in Shemot Rabbah 9,11 according to whom all the waters in Mitzrayim were struck, where did the Mitzri sorcerers practice their art and convert water into blood? Perhaps only visible sources of water had been turned into blood, whereas subterranean water had remained in its original state. This would explain why the Torah described the Mitzrim as digging for water in verse 24.

It is also possible that the sorcerers used the water which Bnei Yisrael had sold to the Mitzrim according to Shemot Rabbah 9,10. Although we have explained that the average Mitzri had already realised that the miracle performed by Moshe and Aharon was real, Paroh's attitude remained obstinate and he refused to see a qualitative difference between the magic of his own magicians and that of Moshe and Aharon. This is why he did not examine if what his magicians had done was more than make-believe.

ויפן ..ולא שת לבו, He turned…and did not take due notice of this, etc. The Torah is careful not to write that Paroh expressly refused to let Bnei Yisrael depart; Paroh was very anxious not to expose himself to additional retribution. We will explain on 8,4, why Paroh had not asked Moshe and Aharon in this case to pray on his behalf and to remove the plague.

וימלא שבעת ימים, Seven days went by, etc. The word וימלא, "became full," refers to the pre-arranged length Hashem had ordained for the plague. After that period had elapsed, Hashem told Moshe to go and see Paroh again (verse 26). The Torah tells us this detail to show us the obstinacy of Paroh who could let an entire week go by without making an effort to somehow have this plague terminated. All of this is in accordance with an opinion expressed in Shemot Rabbah 9,12 that Moshe spent 24 days warning Paroh of the impending plague whereas once the plague materialised it remained in effect for seven days. According to the opinion that it was the other way around, i.e. that Moshe warned Paroh of the impending plague for seven days running, whereas once the plague materialised it lasted for 24 days, the seven days mentioned here refer to the period of warning. The plague then would have remained in effect for the remainder of the month. The problem with this explanation is the plague of darkness which is described as being intense for three days (10,22). Perhaps both the plague of darkness and the plague of blood were exceptions and the author of the opinion that the plagues remained in effect for 24 days agrees that the water in the river did not remain blood for 24 days on end. This would account for the fact that the Torah mentions a time frame only in the case of those two plagues. I believe that even though Hashem had set a time-limit for each plague, Moshe's prayer would have sufficed to terminate the plague sooner.
ואם מאן אתה, "if you should refuse, etc." We learn from here that for a warning to be legally valid it must be delivered immediately preceding the sin.

העתירו אל ה׳, "Implore Hashem, etc." Why did Paroh not simply go to his home as he had done during the first plague? After all, his magicians had demonstrated in both instances that they were able to duplicate Moshe's and Aharon's magic? Actually, we should interpret Paroh's beliefs as reflected by his reactions. He would not have called in Moshe and Aharon to pray for him unless he had been afraid of the deathly effect of the plague in question.

The plague of blood did not represent a threat to life as people could still their thirst by either digging for water in the vicinity of the river or buying same from Bnei Yisrael. As a result, Paroh did not become overly agitated at that plague.

The plague of frogs contained two elements. 1) It was accompanied by an overpowering noise orchestrated by all those frogs; 2) the frogs invaded people's entrails as we know from 7,29 "and the frogs shall come upon you, etc." This plague was very frightening, no one being certain of his survival. These considerations are what prompted Paroh to implore Moshe to remove this plague accompanied by a promise that he would release Bnei Yisrael to offer sacrifices to their G'd. When he said: ממני, he referred to his entrails, which was the most frightening aspect of the plague.

Paroh did not ask Moshe for removal of the third plague, the insects, even though he had watched his magicians' impotence and admission that this plague was indeed a "finger of Elokim;" his heart remained obstinate as the plague, painful though it was, did not constitute a danger to life.

The fourth plague, that of wild animals invading Mitzrayim's urban areas was truly fear-inspiring and resulted in Paroh instructing Moshe and Aharon to go and take Bnei Yisrael to sacrifice to their Hashem within the country. For the first time, Paroh was prepared to negotiate where this could take place. At any rate, he pleaded with Moshe to pray on his behalf.

The plague of pestilence did not move Paroh particularly as its main effect was on the animals, though none of the livestock owned by Bnei Yisrael died. Paroh remained obstinate, did not release Bnei Yisrael and did not ask Moshe to pray to stop the plague.
The sixth plague, painful boils on the skin, also did not move Paroh to prayer as it was not a life-threatening situation although for the first time even his magicians did not remain immune.

The plague of hail was a major spectacle not only ruining the crops but killing people who had not heeded Hashem's warning. For the first time Paroh reacted by admitting that he and his people had sinned against Hashem. He pleaded with Moshe to pray and not only promised to release Bnei Yisrael but did so without attaching conditions.

During the eighth plague, the locusts, the Torah quotes Paroh's alarm when, for the first time, his servants move him to negotiate Bnei Yisrael's release before the onset of the plague. Negotiations having broken down, the plague does occur and Paroh pleads for G'd "to remove this death."

We do not find that Paroh asked Moshe to pray on his behalf during the plague of darkness; perhaps this was due to his attempt during the first three days of that plague to counter it by lighting all kinds of lanterns, etc. During the following three days when no one could even rise from his seat, Paroh was incommunicado and could not send a messenger to call Moshe to intercede on his behalf. After the seven days of darkness were complete, Paroh immediately sent for Moshe to tell him that he and his people could leave and that they only had to leave their livestock behind as insurance that they would return. Moshe immediately refused the condition. Seeing that the plague of darkness was already over, there was no point in asking Moshe to pray for its removal.

התפאר עלי, "have this glory over me, etc." What exactly did Moshe mean by the expression התפאר עלי? If what he meant was that even if Paroh would ask for an immediate removal of the frogs this would constitute his glory, the result of Paroh asking that the frogs be removed only on the morrow would indicate that he was not interested in besting Moshe; Moshe's confirmation: "as you have said," would make little sense in that scenario. We also need to analyse why Moshe did not say מתי אעתיר לך which we would have expected, but said למתי וגו׳?

I believe Moshe wanted to demonstrate that Hashem tries to oblige those who are dear to Him so that it was beyond his imagination that Hashem would forsake him (not do what he promised). He did this by contrasting the relationship between man and Hashem with that of slave and master. When a slave asks a favour from his master he will be happy if his master grants the favour at all and it would not occur to him to attach conditions as to the time when such a favour has to be granted. He will be even less likely to ask for the date of such a favour to be advanced or delayed, but will await the time when he judges his master to be in a favourable frame of mind to grant his request. He will be most happy if his request is granted at the time it pleases his master. Not so the relationship between Moshe and Hashem. Moshe was anxious to demonstrate to Paroh that a) he could offer a prayer at any time; b) his prayer would not only be granted but that he could attach conditions as to the "when" of Hashem's response. This is why he asked Paroh what time or day he wanted him to pray that the frogs should disappear. Paroh was to prove himself superior in that he could determine when Moshe should pray.

It is difficult to understand why Paroh wanted the frogs to be removed only on the following day. Although we know from Mishlei 21,10 that wicked people harbour a death wish (unconsciously), this applies only in the abstract. No wicked person deliberately opts for continued flagellation when given a chance to escape the pain involved. Why then did Paroh ask Moshe to make his prayer effective only on the following day? At first glance one may be tempted to conclude that Paroh misinterpreted Moshe's offer as proof of his awareness that the plague was about to come to an end, and that he wanted to take the credit for this by appearing to pray for the removal of the frogs at once. Paroh therefore wanted to show up Moshe as a fraud. He interpreted Moshe's use of the word התפאר as a trick designed to induce him to ask for the immediate removal of the frogs. This is why he decided to suffer a little longer if only he could expose Moshe as a fraud.

What is wrong with this theory is that if Paroh wanted to unmask Moshe as a fraud he did not really have to extend the period of his suffering at all by asking Moshe not to pray until the following day. Besides, Paroh had never heard of a prayer that is offered up at one time and is not to be effective until the following day. This is why he wanted Moshe to demonstrate that though he prayed now and his prayer would be accepted, the removal of the frogs would not be implemented until the morrow. This was the challenge Paroh presented to Moshe when he said: למחר. He wanted proof that Moshe prayed immediately though the frogs would not disappear until the morrow. When Moshe told Paroh: כדברך, "as you said," he meant that he had accepted Paroh's challenge. Moshe did not leave the city to offer his prayer (as he did on other occasions) but prayed inside the city in order for everyone to be aware precisely when he had prayed. This is why the Torah writes: "Moshe and Aharon left the presence of Paroh and Moshe cried out to G'd concerning the frogs G'd had brought on Paroh, etc." Moshe prayed concerning two matters. 1) Removal of the frogs. 2) Not to remove the frogs until the following day. This is why the Torah states על דבר הצפרדעים, "concerning the matter of the frogs," instead of להסיר הצפרדעים, "to remove the frogs."
אשר שם לפרעה, which He had brought on Paroh. We learn from this that one must be articulate and precise when offering a request in prayer.

ותהי הכנם באדם, the insects remained on man, etc. We would have expected the Torah to say: כל עפר הארץ היה כנים, ותהי הכנים באדם "the whole dust of the earth turned into insects, and the insects remained on man, etc." Why did the Torah reverse this sequence by telling us first that the insects remained on man? We may understand this with the help of an argument between Rabbi Yoseph from Orleans and Rabbenu Tam cited on Shabbat 12 concerning the meaning of the word כנה. Some rabbis hold that what is meant is a black flea, an insect which originated in the dust and which is able to jump very high. Other rabbis hold that these "insects" were white parasites which originated on the clothes people wore. These rabbis prove their point by basing themselves on a statement in Berachot 51 according to which vermin is generated from rags. In order to prevent the reader from making the error that the כנה described here is the so-called כנה לבנה, the parasite, the Torah makes the point that it originated from the dust of the earth. Had the Torah used the version commencing with the words: כל עפר הארץ היה כנים, there could have been no question about the insects originating in the earth. The Torah therefore displayed wisdom by writing ותהי הכנם באדם, to tell us that the insects which were normally generated in dirty clothes now became a plague of intolerable dimensions so that both man and animal suffered from an excessive amount of fleas, etc., each of the variety they were familiar with.

It is also possible that the Torah speaks about both variants of insects. The first category is alluded to in the words: ותהי הכנם באדם ובבהמה, meaning the varieties of parasites man and beast experience on their skin from time to time. This was in addition to the insects which originate in the earth and which are called כנים as distinct from the first variety which is called כנם. If this is correct, our verse does not serve as support for the opinion of Rabbi Yoseph from Orleans, and we would have to accept the view of Rabbenu Tam who proved in the Talmud that the insect known as the white one is a parasite, whereas the other one known as the black one, which is distinguished by its great jumps, is incorrectly referred to as כנה but is in reality a פרעוש. (This is also the ruling of the halachah compare Tur Shulchan Aruch, Or Hachayim ruling 315).

ומלאו בתי מצרים את הערוב, the houses of Mitzrayim will be filled with wild beasts, etc. The reason the Torah repeats the word הערוב, "the wild beasts," is that the houses will be filled with the wild beasts; if the Torah had merely written once: "the wild beasts will fill the houses of Mitzrayim," we would have thought that the purpose of the plague was simply to fill the Mitzrim's houses with wild beasts; this was not so, however, as the Torah had already stated: "I will send the wild beasts against you, your servants, your people as well as against your houses;" the obvious meaning is that the beasts were to cause damage and destruction. As it is, the additional message is that the houses would literally be filled with wild beasts.

Another meaning of the words את הערוב the second time could be that had the Torah not repeated these words we would have assumed that the plague would have exhausted its purpose as soon as the houses of the Mitzrim had become full of wild beasts; however, this was not the full extent of the plague. There were so many wild beasts that they could not be accomodated even after they had already filled all the houses of the Mitzrim. This is why the Torah added: "and also the ground whereon they are."

ושמתי פדות, "I shall set apart, etc." Hashem meant that not only would the wild beasts respect the boundary of the province of Goshen and not invade that province, they would not even approach those Bnei Yisrael that happened to be outside the province of Goshen at the time. The Torah made this clear by the nuance "between My people and between your people." This means that whenever members of both people were found next to one another, only the Mitzrim would be bothered by the wild beasts. The beasts would not bite a Yehudi.
תשחת הארץ, the land was ruined. This means that the beasts would destroy everything except the human beings.

לא תרחיקו לכת. "Do not go very far." Paroh meant: "not as far as the three days you have requested." His argument was that if Moshe was afraid the Mitzrim would stone Bnei Yisrael if they slaughtered animals the Mitzrim regarded as sacred, there was no reason to travel a distance of three days to escape that particular danger. Apparently, Moshe did not make an issue of this at this time; he reasoned that Bnei Yisrael's major purpose was to get out of the urban areas, no matter how far. If Paroh would pursue them, Moshe was certain that G'd would deal with him. At that point Moshe wanted only to ensure that Paroh would not have a reason to renege on his promise; this is why he warned Paroh not to deal deceitfully with him and the Jewish people. He emphasized this by use of the word רק. Moshe meant that though they would travel for a distance of less than three days the important thing for them was to get out of town for a while.

בא אל פרעה, "Go to Paroh, etc." You may consider it a rule that whenever Hashem told Moshe to go to Paroh, He meant that Moshe should enter Paroh's palace without waiting for permission to do so. No doubt Paroh had the usual complement of bodyguards at the entrance to his palace. Nonetheless Moshe was commanded by Hashem to ignore the presence of those guards. We have reason to believe that Moshe acted in accordance with these instructions since Yalkut Shimoni item 175 describes that Paroh not only had armed guards but also trained lions at his palace gate but that Moshe walked in without being challenged. I have found conclusive proof for the opinion expressed in the Yalkut in 10,28 where Paroh for the first time warns Moshe not to attempt to enter the palace again. Why would Paroh have had to warn Moshe about entering the palace unless Moshe had been in the habit of doing so unchallenged up until then? Clearly, even the trained lions had respected Moshe and not challenged his entry, a great miracle indeed. If Hashem had to command Moshe to enter Paroh's palace i.e. בא אל instead לך אל, "go to," the reason was that he assured Moshe he would not be challenged by either the palace guards or the lions. On the other hand, whenever Hashem told Moshe to meet Paroh near the river Yeor, He used the expression לך אל פרעה as there were no guards near the river Yeor where Paroh desired privacy. The only reason Hashem told Moshe to go to Paroh there was that Moshe would not have done so on his own initiative seeing Paroh went there to answer calls of nature, as already explained elsewhere.
אשר בשדה, which are in the field, etc. This is to be taken literally; they all died because the Mitzrim left them in the fields as mentioned in 9,6.

וישם ה׳ מועד לאמור, Hashem appointed a set time, etc. He informed the Mitzrim of when the plague would strike to enable them to bring their livestock indoors as we also find when the plague of hail struck (9,19). In that instance Hashem told the Mitzrim outright to bring their animals indoors to protect them, whereas here He only hinted at this. The hint is expressed in the Torah by the word לאמור. This meant that Moshe and Aharon were to inform both Paroh and the Mitzrim of the timing of that plague.
.כל מקנה מצרים, all the cattle of Mitzrayim. This refers to the cattle the Mitzrim had not brought indoors, this is why the words "in the field" are missing here.

וממקנה בני ישראל, and of the cattle of Bnei Yisrael none died. They owned cattle going back to the time Yaakov had come to Mitzrayim. On the other hand, they may have acquired cattle from the money they received from the Mitzrim when they sold them water during the plague of blood. It is even possible that some smart Mitzrim "sold" their cattle to the Yehudim before the onset of the plague [much as we sell chametz to the Gentiles before Passover Ed.] so as to escape the plague and not interfere with their cattle's grazing outdoors. The Torah then would tell us that such "sales" did not protect such cattle; only the cattle which were truly Jewish-owned survived the plague without having been indoors. We ought to understand what the verse tells us: 1) "All the cattle of the Mitzrim as well as some of the cattle "owned" by the Yehudim died;" the Torah added the extra letter מ in the line וממקנה בני ישראל to tell us about these so-called Jewish-owned cattle which died. The letter מ applied only to part of the cattle and not to part of the sheep and goats. To sum up: animals owned outright by Yehudim did not die; animals owned by Yehudim in name only, died.

השכם בבוקר, "rise up early in the morning, etc!" Moshe was given three separate instructions here. 1) To go to see Paroh early in the morning. 2) To adopt an erect posture when facing Paroh, not to bow down as was customary. G'd needed to command Moshe to do this as his natural habit was to appear deferential before Paroh. Moshe was not do discard his natural humble stance except in the presence of Paroh. 3) He was to communicate G'd's message to Paroh.

כי בפעם הזאת…את כל מגפותי, "for this time… all My plagues." G'd informed Paroh of the powerful impact of the impending plague of hail. This is why the warning was as severe as the death that would follow if it were not observed. This was in accordance with the rule that if someone guilty of a sin carrying the death penalty by stoning was warned of a lesser death penalty such as strangulation, the court would not be able to convict.

כל מגפותי, "all My plagues, etc." The obvious question here is that we observe that this was not the last plague but was followed by three more plagues; what did G'd mean then when He described hail as "all My plagues?" One would have been tempted to say that the severity of that plague made it qualify for the description "all My plagues," were it not for Rashi who said that the plague of the dying of the firstborn was equal in severity to all the other plagues combined. Perhaps we have to understand this plague as being equal in severity "to all the preceding plagues together." If we accept such an interpretation the plague of the dying of the firstborn would then be equivalent to 14 plagues, something that does not seem to make too much sense.

I therefore feel that G'd meant to tell Paroh that the impact of this particular plague would change his attitude to all the plagues G'd had brought upon him thus far. Up until now Paroh had not really attributed the plagues to G'd's superior power, but had seen in them a display of powerful magic, the work of ghosts and demons. One of his reasons was that his own magicians appeared able to duplicate those plagues. Although his magicians had told him that they could not duplicate (or remove) the plague of כנם, insects, and this was a "finger of G'd," Paroh chose to interpret this as an admission that they felt outclassed by Moshe and Aharon in their craft. Paroh was still convinced that somewhere there were magicians who could do what Moshe and Aharon had demonstrated. G'd wanted to disabuse Paroh of such ideas and that is why He said "this time," etc., meaning that even Paroh would be forced to admit that no human being was capable of producing the kind of hail he was about to experience. G'd added that He would bring this to the attention of Paroh's heart, לבך. Up until that moment Paroh may have reacted only with his eyes or with his mind. G'd stressed the word מגפותי, "My plagues," to emphasise that these phenomena emanated directly from G'd. No demon or sorcerer could possibly wield such power.

בעבור תדע..ולמען תספר שמי בכל הארץ….בעבור הראותך את כתי. "In order that you should know….in order to show you My power…and in order that you will proclaim My name in the whole land, etc." You who have said: "who is Hashem?" will now be the first one to proclaim My name all over the earth. Obviously, Paroh did not have the kind of communications media which are at our disposal today. The Torah means that as a result of what would happen to Paroh he would be the instrument through which the whole of mankind would become aware of what Hashem does to those who refuse to accept His orders. Even nowadays kings have been heard to say that if the Jewish Messiah arrives and performs a miracle they would not repeat Paroh's mistakes.

ועתה שלח העז את מקנך, "And now, send, and bring in your cattle, etc." You may well ask that if the Mitzrim heeded Moshe's warning, what effect would the forthcoming plague have? Remember, Hashem's purpose in bringing plagues upon the Mitzrim was not to inflict pain and suffering on them. The pain was only one way of demonstrating Hashem's power. If this could be achieved by making the Mitzrim obey, so much the better. At any rate, the crops would be destroyed by the hail even if there would be no deaths amongst the livestock. The Torah states specifically that both the grass and the trees were destroyed by the hail (9,24).

We still have to understand why Elokim said: ועתה, "now," when He issued the warning. If the meaning was "immediately," then it is difficult to understand as the hail was not meant to occur until the following day at about the same time. Perhaps the warning had to emphasise that immediate action be taken as most of the cattle were grazing far from home and would not be able to find shelter at once.

We also need to understand to whom Hashem addressed the advice to let the animals and people take shelter. Those who feared the word of Hashem would do so immediately after they heard that there would be hail on the morrow. They did not need advice on that matter. The advice therefore was directed only at those Mitzrim who did not yet fear Hashem. We therefore may interpret the call ועתה as a call to repentance. In fact Midrash Tehillim 100,2 claims that this expression always denotes repentance. Hashem gave these people a chance to repent. When they failed to do so in spite of having been warned, Hashem punished them.

ואשר לא שם לבו…ויעזב, and whoever paid no heed…left his cattle outdoors, etc. The extra letter ו in ויעזב, is to draw to our attention that those people who had up to now refused to heed Hashem's warning added to their previous sin by continuing in their ways, deliberately exposing their livestock and servants to death by hail despite Hashem's warning. Their obstinacy was such that though they could have saved their property by the simple expedient of bringing it indoors for a while, they defied Hashem and did not do so. It is clear from the Torah's report that what motivated the Mitzrim was not so much their economic need of the cheap labour that Bnei Yisrael represented and which made them refuse to liberate them, but their defiance of the Jewish Hashem. Even those who doubted Hashem's ability to orchestrate a plague of hail such as Moshe had predicted preferred to demonstrate their defiance by risking their property. Perhaps the reason they took such a chance was that the previous six plagues had not been severe enough so that they did not believe that Hashem could suddenly bring such a terrible plague.

ויהי ברד ואש, there was hail and fire simultaneously, etc. The word מתלקחת is used to inform us that though water and fires are opposites, one of which is bound to prevail over the other in any encounter, in this instance they demonstrated the ability to co-exist. This was possible since both were performing Hashem's will by so doing.

והברד לא יהיה עוד, "and the hail will cease to be, etc." No new hail will fall, whereas the hail which had descended already will cease to be. Moshe's promise was essentially what is described in verse 33, i.e. that the hail and rain stopped in mid-air. According to an aggadah in Berachot 54 the function of that hail which was arrested in mid-air was completed in the days of Yehoshua when the latter was engaged in the conquest of the land of Canaaan (Yehoshua 10,11) when hail stones fell on Yisrael's adversaries.

למען תדע, "so that you will realise, etc." Moshe told Paroh that he did not pray for Paroh in order that he should release Bnei Yisrael from bondage, he did not believe Paroh's assurances. The only reason he prayed was so that Paroh would acquire greater respect for the power of Hashem.

ואתה ועבדיך, "for both you as well as your servants, etc." Moshe mentioned the servants because he saw that they too had not paid heed to Hashem's warning and had left their livestock outdoors together with their shepherds. Should you query this by asking how did Moshe know this, seeing the servants had accepted Hashem's judgment when Paroh said: "Hashem is righteous whereas I and my people are the evildoers," remember that I have explained that Hashem had already revealed His intention to bring on the plague of killing the Mitzrim's firstborn. He had also warned in 7,4 that Paroh would not listen to Moshe and Aharon. As a result, Moshe was entitled to consider all the protestations of Paroh that he addmitted being a sinner, etc. as being merely a maneuver to gain time. If Paroh and his servants had truly repented it is hardly likely that Hashem would punish them by the plague of killing the firstborn. Moshe was therefore on safe ground when he said that he knew that Paroh and his advisers were not yet Hashem-fearing people.

ידעתי כי טרם חיראון, "I know you do not yet fear, etc." Moshe meant that Paroh's fear of Hashem lasted only as long as the latest plague had not yet been removed. As soon as they would experience relief they would continue in their rebellious ways against Hashem as previously. Moshe referred to previous examples of Paroh reneging on his promise to let Bnei Yisrael go as proof for his present lack of faith in Pharaohs protestations.

Moshe made it plain that he did not consider that Paroh was deliberately being deceitful in trying to convince Moshe that he should pray on his behalf; he was simply under psychological pressure at that time. This induced temporary fear of G'd in him and in his people. Moshe wanted Paroh to know that he himself could read Paroh's mind, as Paroh would be the first to acknowledge. He added that even if Paroh were to try and prove that Moshe was wrong in his prediction that he, Paroh, would renege after the hail had stopped, he would not be able to control his spirit sufficiently to keep his undertaking.

והפשתה והשעורה נכתה, both the flax and the barley were smitten, etc. Why did the Torah tell us of this detail before describing Moshe as concluding his prayer? According to normal practice the Torah should have reported that Moshe did as he had said, namely that he prayed to G'd for the plague to stop.

Perhaps the Torah wanted to provide us with a reason why the Mitzrim had not really become penitent. Whereas the hail had destroyed the flax crop and the barley crop, it had not caused more than minimal damage to the wheat and the spelt which ripened at a later date. According to Midrash Tanchuma the reason that the Torah uses the letter ו in front of the word הפשתה where it could not possibly be understood as a conjunctive is that a miracle within a miracle happened so that only these two crops were smitten. Had nature taken its course, both the wheat and the spelt should also have succumbed to the hail. Basing themselves on the strange phenomenon that the wheat and spelt had escaped unharmed, Paroh and his servants concluded that G'd's authority did not include the wheat and the spelt. This encouraged them to continue in their obstinate ways. This is why Moshe was able to say that he realised that Paroh had not yet come to fear G'd truly. He cited as the reason what happened to the wheat, or rather, what did not happen to the wheat. G'd had spared the wheat in order to encourage Paroh to remain obstinate.

וירא פרעה כי חדל המטר, Paroh saw that the rain had stopped, etc. The Torah mentions this to show that Paroh's repentance already evaporated; he continued to sin almost immediately. When the Torah reports him as ויוסף לחטא, "he continued to sin," this does not refer to his continuing on his previous path; it means that Paroh added additional sins to the ones he had committed already. He now made a commitment not to release Bnei Yisrael under any terms and conditions.

ויאמר ה׳ אל משה, Hashem said to Moshe, etc. The Torah mentions אמירה, the soft approach as well as Hashem's name as the Merciful One. This did not refer to the "sender," i.e. to Hashem, but to the messenger Moshe, as we see in verse 3. [Whereas as recently as 9,35 the Torah referred to Moshe as having spoken sternly, דבר, to Paroh, now there is a change of mood. Ed.] Moshe spoke in a kindly manner to Paroh even while delivering a warning of a devastating plague. Hashem warned him to do so as otherwise he might have lived up to the description of the righteous man in Tehillim 58,11 where the Holy Spirit describes the righteous as rejoicing when he observes Hashem taking revenge. Moshe is reminded that what truly makes the righteous happy is seeing Hashem's attribute of Mercy in action.

Furthermore, the Torah employs the attribute of Mercy to remind us that Hashem did not send the plague immediately after the warning but gave Paroh time to change his mind and to release Bnei Yisrael. If he did this then he and his country would be spared the suffering entailed by the plague of locusts. According to Shemot Rabbah 9,12 a week or even twenty-four days would elapse between the warning and the implementation of the plague. All this was part of the attribute of Mercy in action.

On the other hand, it is possible that our verse underlines that even the attribute of Mercy agreed joyfully that the time had arrived to take revenge on this enemy of G'd and the Jewish people (compare my comments on 7,2).

כי אני הכבדתי את לבו, "for I have hardened his heart, etc." G'd means that Moshe would realise as of now that He had indeed hardened Paroh's heart. Even the most obstinate person would have broken down by now if he had experienced what Paroh had endured during the last seven plagues. Only intervention by G'd could have accounted for his continued refusal to let Bnei Yisrael depart. G'd did not, of course, interfere outright with Paroh's free will; rather He performed a miracle such as the immunity of the wheat and spelt to the plague of hail, to give Paroh a chance to delude himself that G'd's power did not extend to those two categories of grain. When G'd said כי אני הכבדתי He referred to that phenomenon in the past tense.

It is also possible that G'd's words were directed primarily at Moshe who must have despaired of the purpose of going to Paroh time and again without accomplishing his mission. G'd told Moshe that Paroh's obstinacy was not that of an ordinary human being, but the reason he could not respond as he should was that G'd Himself had hardened his heart. The moment G'd decided not to interfere with whatever motivated Paroh's decisions he would relent and send Bnei Yisrael on their way.

ואת לב עבדיו, and the heart of his servants, etc. The reason Hashem also had to harden the heart of Paroh's advisers was so that they would not urge him to release Bnei Yisrael. Hashem had to do so in order to bring the plagues not only on Paroh but on the whole nation. If Paroh had been the only one punished, this would not have made an impact on the people. Although Hashem had not mentioned this detail to Moshe at the beginning of his mission, and He had spoken only of hardening Paroh's heart at that time, He had told Moshe the essential part of what would happen. Perhaps Hashem wanted to explain to Moshe at this stage that not only one man was obstinate, i.e. Paroh, but also his servants. He may have been prompted to do so now because of Moshe's gratuitous remark in 9,30 that both Paroh and his servants had not yet developed true fear of Hashem. Moshe's comment had indicated that he had not previously understood the word "Paroh" to include also Paroh's entourage. Therefore Hashem explained to him that the obstinacy of the servants could also be explained by the same phenomenon as that of their master, i.e. that Hashem had interfered with their normal decision-making process. Up until now, Moshe had assumed that the servants were naturally obstinate whereas Paroh had only remained obstinate because Hashem had interfered. Hashem was at pains to correct Moshe's error.

למען שתי אותותי אלה בקרבו, "so that I might display My signs in the midst of them." Why did the Torah have to write אותותי אלה, "these My signs?" This implies that the main reason Hashem hardened Paroh's heart was to have an opportunity to display miracles. Furthermore, why did the Torah have to add בקרבו, "in their midst?" Where else would Hashem perform these miracles? We may understand these expressions on the basis of Shemot Rabbah 12,5 that the plagues in Mitzrayim were to demonstrate that Hashem is Ruler and Master. He is Master inasmuch that He desires to bring Yisrael closer to become His servants and to cleave to Him. In order to do this He had to demonstrate that it was foolish to put one's trust in anyone but Him. He had not yet shown them that He creates the wind and employs the wind as His angels (messengers). He had also not yet demonstrated to Bnei Yisrael that He created light and darkness. Having told Moshe that He, Hashem had made Paroh unresponsive, Moshe would have been entitled to ask: "why bother?" Hashem therefore justified the plagues which were yet to occur as designed to demonstrate His creative power in the spheres we have just mentioned. Regarding the chance of Paroh's responding to them, it was true that these miracles were somewhat wasted, but their impact on Yisrael was vital. The seven plagues which had occurred so far did not offer an answer to people who wanted to worship such powers of nature as the sun and the moon. Anyone who claimed that the force which created earth was not the same force which created the wind could not find proof that he had been wrong by experiencing any of those plagues. The plague of locusts would demonstrate Hashem's power to employ the wind as His messenger, by the wind bringing the locusts and removing them. It would even carry away all the locusts which had died so that the Mitzrim would not benefit from the dead locusts as mentioned in Shemot Rabbah 13,7. The plague of darkness would demonstrate that Hashem had created the luminaries, and exercised control over them. The plague of the dying of the firstborn demonstrated that Hashem creates every creature and can distinguish between who was the issue of the first drop of semen (Baba Metzia 61). This plague also generated the commandment in 13,2 to sanctify every firstborn. One of the reasons for that commandment was that it serve as a reminder that it is Hashem who creates the firstborn out of the womb of his mother in order that he should be His servant. When Hashem encountered this evil Paroh, He made use of him by hardening his heart and performing miracles which would make him taste the cup of retribution. Had it not been for these various considerations Hashem would not have troubled Himself to orchestrate all these major changes in nature.

ולמען תספר, "and in order for you to tell, etc.," Why did Hashem have to provide this additional reason to justify the plague of locusts? Besides, what is the meaning of the words אשר התעללתי במצרים? Why did Hashem add: "and My miracles," as if this was something distinct from אשר התעללתי? Why did Hashem add: וידעתם כי אני השם?

I believe that first and foremost Elokim wanted to make it plain that it was not His purpose to bring on the plague as an act of revenge on Paroh. Rather, the miracle was designed to strengthen Yisrael's faith in Elokim so that they would remember these miracles forever. This could be achieved only if Elokim not only performed the miracle without hurting any Yisraeli by it but that Paroh himself would be so impressed by the miracle that it would also impress Elokim's power on the minds of Bnei Yisrael in an unforgettable manner. The psychology of the aforesaid is demonstrated in the halachah of the בן פקועה in Chulin 75. This concerns a fetus found alive [if the pregnancy was incomplete, or dead if the pregnancy was complete. Ed.] inside an animal after the mother-animal has been ritually slaughtered. The question is if the ritual slaughter of the mother-animal made the fetus fit for consumption by Yehudim without further ado. The Talmud discusses whether such an animal may be eaten without it being slaughtered seeing that the onlooker may suspect the person eating it of committing a sin; it concludes that when this animal has been different in at least two exceptional ways such as that it does not have a cloven hoof, everyone will remember what its origin has been and one will not suspect someone eating it without having performed ritual slaughter as having committed a sin. Although Elokim had demonstrated miracles which clearly proved His power, this would not have sufficed to make a lasting impression on Bnei Yisrael unless He had at the same time proven that He distinguished miraculously between the guilty and the innocent, i.e. between Bnei Yisrael and the Mitzrim and that the miracles had hurt only the guilty parties. When Elokim said: "in order that you will tell your children and your children's children, etc." He meant that this would be assured only if He performed the miracles in such a way that only the Mitzrim were seen to be hurt by them. The first impression would be created by אשר התעללתי במצרים, "How I wrought the plagues on Mitzrayim;" the second and more lasting impression would occur when Bnei Yisrael realised את אותותי אשר שמתי בם, that what occurred was an outstanding miracle even if the Mitzrim had not been a factor at all. These combined experiences would prompt Bnei Yisrael to tell their children about what they had seen. The purpose of telling their children was "so that you will know beyond doubt that I am Hashem Elokim."

ויפן ויצא מעם פרעה, He turned and left Paroh's presence. By not asking permission to leave Moshe demonstrated his lack of regard for this king who had once again reneged on his promise even after he had proclaimed: "Hashem is righteous and I and my people are sinners." Actually, the wicked Paroh repaid Moshe for this slight when he had him brought back to the palace unceremoniously in verse 8. After that Paroh expelled Moshe from the palace in verse 11. He was aware of his lack of deference when he begged Moshe to pray for him again in verse 16 adding: "I have sinned against Hashem your Hashem and against you." He had never previously apologised to Moshe, only to Hashem.

עד מתי יהיה זה לנו למוקש, "how long will this one continue to be a snare for us?" Paroh's servants were most certainly not prepared to let Bnei Yisrael depart for the prophecy G'd had told Moshe i.e. that He had hardened both the heart of Paroh and that of his servants would contradict such an assumption. All the servants had in mind was to ensure that Bnei Yisrael's departure would be such that they would be sure to return after having offered their sacrifices. This is why the servants did not pursue the matter once Moshe had made it plain that they would take both their children and their aged with them. Their very words proved that they considered Moshe's invoking G'd as the driving force behind Bnei Yisrael's demands merely as a snare. They could not believe that the great and powerful G'd whose existence Moshe had demonstrated would bother to punish the Mitzrim in order to let Bnei Yisrael go to the desert for three days. There is no greater denial of G'd than that.
הטרם תדע כי אבדה מצרים, "do you not know yet that Mitzrayim is about to be destroyed?" They meant "why wait till after Mitzrayim is destroyed before letting these people go? Let them go now!"

Why would the servants suddenly agree to take a chance of Mitzrayim being destroyed after Moshe had spelled out who was going to the desert? What made them keep their peace when they heard Moshe's latest demand? In order to understand this we must first explore what Paroh and his servants had thought initially. Is there anyone so foolish that he would risk all the discomforts, pains and even danger of submitting to these plagues? Not only that but these people had endured that their deities were smitten, their livestock killed, their crops ruined, and even they themselves came within an inch of destruction. Ordinarily it would be considered unbelievable that there are people who are so stupid! Nonetheless, these people must have had some plausible reason to act in such a foolish fashion. Their behaviour is all the more strange as Hashem had not demanded from Paroh that he free Bnei Yisrael but only that he should give them a three-day vacation! It is true that I have written (3,18) that Moshe had never mentioned the three-day limitation to Paroh, that he had only spoken about celebrating in the desert (5,1) not mentioning any time frame, and that the only ones who did mention three days were the people (5,3); this indicated that Hashem had not demanded a total release of Bnei Yisrael.

I believe that Paroh's error was based on these conflicting demands by Moshe on the one hand and Bnei Yisrael on the other. There could be no question that the word of Hashem was the truth. Paroh and his servants had to consider two possibilties. 1) Hashem did not desire a total departure of Bnei Yisrael but only an absence of three days' travel into the desert. 2) At the same time Paroh felt that Bnei Yisrael's demand for three days was a trick designed to cloak their true intentions never to return to Mitzrayim. If so, this was proof (in the mind of Paroh and his servants) that the Hashem of the Hebrews was unable to orchestrate an Exodus in the proper sense of the word. He had instructed His messengers to make a lesser demand, one that He was able to perform. Keeping in mind that Paroh and company were non believers, they preferred an interpretation which implied that Hashem's power was limited. As a result of this they remained obstinate, probing for weakness in Hashem's power. When the servants contemplated the fact that they had already endured seven plagues none of which had advanced Bnei Yisrael's cause substantially, i.e. they were still enslaved in Mitzrayim though they had not performed slave labour for a while, they had to adopt an attitude concerning the warning of the plague of locusts.
