The first three are the lamb, the unleavened bread, and the bitter herbs; then there is the Haggadah followed by the seven days of the festival and the benediction over wine on the night of the festival. The Torah has to phrase it as בעבור זה עשה because the seven days of the festival do not count as seven separate commandments in the list of 613 commandments.

והיה כי יביאך, "It will be when He will bring you, etc." The Torah underlines once more that it is Hashem who will bring you to the Holy Land so that you should not forget about His commandments in the belief that you yourself have achieved all this, especially after your border will gradually extend further and further. Although this commandment is not applicable until after conquest of the land, it remains in force even if the land is lost as it is a commandment that involves the body and not the earth. Kidushin 36 teaches that all commandments which are performed by one's body apply throughout the ages and wherever a Yehudi resides.

והיה כי ישאלך בנך, "It will be when your son enquires of you, etc." The Torah means that when your son observes you perform the ceremony of redeeming a firstborn he will ask you the reason for that commandment. In that event you are obligated to explain the meaning of the commandment. If the son does not ask you, you are not obligated to answer him except on the night of the Passover. This is the reason the Torah added the word מחר, "tomorrow;" This means that even if your son will ask you already tomorrow you are immediately obligated to tell him the reason for this commandment. The Torah adds the word לאמור to indicate that what is meant is a situation when your son expects an answer to his question. If the son, however, simply asks מה זאת, i.e. "what is this all about?" a derisive way of questioning, then you are under no obligation to answer him at that time.

The question need not necessarily be exactly "what is this all about?" Any question whose upshot appears to be that the questioner wants to be told what our tradition is all about is to be answered forthwith. It is clear therefore that the Torah does not speak of the night of the Passover but of the commandment to sanctify the firstborn of the womb. When our sages (Mechilta) comment that the four occasions when the Torah cites the sons as asking refer to four different types of children this is all homiletics.

והיה לאות על ידכה, "it will be as a sign on your hand, etc." Our sages in Menachot 37 explain that the unusual spelling of the word ידכה is to indicate that the phylacteries are to be worn on the weaker hand, i.e. the left hand. Why did Hashem not want us to wear the phylacteries on our right hand, i.e. on the stronger hand? Our sages answer that the phylacteries should be placed opposite the heart, and the heart is predominantly on the left side of the chest. The sages are not only correct, but I believe I can demonstrate that the verse itself supplies the reason why the phylacteries are to be worn on the left arm. The Torah refers to חזק יד, "the strength of the hand" employed by Hashem when He led us out of Mitzrayim. We must appreciate that the attribute described by Hashem as "hand," can be either one of two kinds. It can be יד הגדולה, the "great hand," or it can be יד החזקה, "the strong hand." The former is the aspect of the hand which practices kindness and goodness, the latter is used by Hashem when He exacts retribution, when He repays the wicked for their wickedness. When Hashem led Bnei Yisrael out of Mitzrayim, He inclined His יד החזקה, His "strong hand" and smote His enemies with ten plagues; as a memorial of this Hashem commanded us to put the phylacteries which contain the passage describing this event on our weak hand as our left hand is symbolic of the "strong hand" which led us out of Mitzrayim. This is why the Torah emphasises which aspect of His hand Hashem employed for the purpose, i.e. בחוזק יד. Although we find on some occasions that Hashem's "great hand" is used in a context which describes Hashem as exacting punishment, this only means that in those instances the attribute of Mercy concurred in the punishment Hashem's attribute of Justice handed out on that occasion. Under normal circumstances the יד החזקה is used to describe Hashem's punitive arm in action.

ויהי בשלח פרעה את העם, It happened when Paroh discharged the people, etc. Why does the Torah employ the word ויהי which always indicates some painful experience? The Torah should have described the Exodus in glowing terms! Besides, why does the Torah attribute the Exodus to Paroh rather than to G'd? After all, He took us out of Mitzrayim, something the Torah does not tire of mentioning on numerous occasions!

The word ויהי may be justified in view of the pursuit by Paroh and the resulting fear Bnei Yisrael were to experience shortly. The Torah hints that the reason such a pursuit occurred was because Paroh had a hand in the Exodus, i.e. Hashem had waited till Paroh himself had been willing to liberate the Yehudim. If it had all been Hashem's doing such a pursuit would not have occurred. As soon as the Yehudim departed Paroh schemed to find a justification to pursue them and to convince his people that the attempt to bring Bnei Yisrael back would be worthwhile. We will explain later Paroh's reasoning in greater detail. All Paroh's scheming constituted something negative for Bnei Yisrael. It was far from a foregone conclusion that Hashem would simply kill the Mitzrim. We know from Megillah 10 that Hashem is greatly concerned when the necessity arises to destroy His creatures. We do not recite the whole of Hallel on the seventh day of Passover when Hashem eliminated the last of our Mitzri enemies because "when Hashem's creatures drown in the sea it is no cause for rejoicing." Paroh had deluded himself that it was up to him to decide whether or not to allow Bnei Yisrael to depart. If so, he could just as easily renege as he had done during the course of his protracted encounters with Moshe and Aharon. Yisrael had ample reason to be concerned about such an eventuality. For all these reasons the introductory ויהי is more than justified. In fact the conjunctive letter ו at the beginning of the words ולא נחם, indicates that Yisrael had additional reasons to be concerned of negative developments on the horizon.

Another detail to watch in our verse is the word עם. The Zohar second part, page 45 states that whenever Yisrael is described as עם it is an allusion to the mixed multitude of converts that joined Bnei Yisrael at the Exodus. In our portion you will find Bnei Yisrael are variously described as בני ישראל and as העם. For instance, in the next verse already the departing Bnei Yisrael are referred to as בני ישראל. Apparently G'd wanted to make certain that we realised that the people described as העם were not natural born Yehudim. Our sages in Shemot Rabbah 42,6 consider Yisrael's corruption in the desert as inspired by these converts. They were the ones who wanted to appoint a new leader to take them back to Mitzrayim (Bamidbar 14,4). They were also the ones who said: "make a god for us who will walk before us, etc." (Shemot 32,1). All this is alluded to in the word ויהי at the beginning of our paragraph. מThe meaning of the words בשלח פרעה את העם is that whereas G'd liberated Bnei Yisrael, Paroh allowed the newly converted fellow travellers to depart. G'd had been interested only in acquiring for Himself a great nation as His inheritance. Paroh's reasoning in allowing these newly convertedd Yehudim to depart with the main body of the Jewish people was that they would somehow prevail on the natural born Bnei Yisrael to return to Mitzrayim. In view of this we can understand even better why G'd did not let Bnei Yisrael travel a route to Kenaan which would have taken them through territory owned by the Plishtim although it was the shortest route. We may understand the word קרוב as describing people who had only recently converted to Judaism and were not yet rooted firmly in sanctity. When people like that faced the Plishtim they might turn back and return to Mitzrayim as the lesser of two evils.

The word קרוב may also suggest that these people came close to becoming sinful and as a corollary to also corrupt the (natural born) Bnei Yisrael. They would indict themselves by their reaction when they would realise they were expected to battle the Plishtim. As a result they would regret their recent conversion and would return to Mitzrayim. The letter ו before ולא נחם would refer therefore to another potentially painful aspect of their departure courtesy of Paroh.

We also have a tradition mentioned in Shemot Rabbah 20,3 that Paroh accompanied Bnei Yisrael begging them to pray for him. The merit Paroh acquired by seeing Bnei Yisrael off enabled him to survive longer and pose a threat for Yisrael. We can deduce what negative effect Paroh's accompanying Yisrael had for the people by comparing this with the story related in Sanhedrin 96 according to which Nevuchadnetzar was greatly rewarded for recalling a messenger bearing a letter to Chizkiyah king of Yehudah congratulating him on his recovery from his sickness. In the original draft of that letter Nevuchadnetzar's scribe had extended greetings to Chizkiyah and to Hashem in that order. Upon reflection, Nevuchadnetzar realised he should have first extended greetings to Hashem. He personally ran after the messenger to recall him and change the order of greetings. The angel Gabriel interfered with Nevuchadnetzar after he had travelled only four steps. Rabbi Yochanan said that if the angel Gabriel had not stopped Nevuchadnetzar there would have been no remedy for Yisrael. Nevuchadnetzar's gesture of running four steps in order to accord due respect to Hashem resulted in his being allowed to destroy the Holy Temple and the Jewish state. Imagine what negative effects for the Jewish people Paroh's gesture in accompanying Bnei Yisrael must have had on their fate! Hashem apparently changed Bnei Yisrael's route to one that would discourage Paroh from continuing to accompany them. Had Bnei Yisrael travelled in the direction of the land of the Plishtim, Paroh might well have accompanied them all the way and acquired great merit in the eyes of Hashem. Put differently: The reason Hashem did not lead Bnei Yisrael through the land of the Plishtim was in order to deny Paroh sufficient merit to entitle him to succeed in his quest for Bnei Yisrael to return to Mitzrayim.

According to this approach, the extra letter ו in ולא נחם is a hint that even the short distance Paroh accompanied Bnei Yisrael caused Bnei Yisrael sufficient discomfort so that they viewed themselves in real danger when Paroh pursued them a few days later. Shemot Rabbah 21 refers to this by saying that the words ולא קרב זה אל זה כל הלילה indicate that Paroh's merit had not yet been neutralised by Bnei Yisrael's repentance until the latter cried out to G'd, i.e. מה תצעק אלי in verse 15.

When the Torah continues: כי אמר, "for G'd had said, etc." this is as if the Torah wrote "and because G'd said, etc." It refers to an additional reason that G'd did not let the people face the Plishtim, i.e. the lack of faith in G'd of the newly converted ערב רב.

וחמושים עלו בני ישראל, and Bnei Yisrael went up armed, etc. It is possible that if Bnei Yisrael had not been armed they would not have listened to Moshe's (Hashem's) order to make an about turn away from the land of the Plishtim so that they would not face an immediate battle. Bnei Yisrael therefore needed two reasons for not returning to Mitzrayim at the slightest danger, i.e. possession of arms and the unlikelihood of having to use these arms. Combining these two factors would result in לא ינחם, that they would not have second thoughts.

פקד יפקד אלוקים, "when Hashem will surely remember you, etc." The reason the Torah repeats the word פקד is in order to emphasise the manner in which Moshe kept faith with the promise made to Yosef by his brothers. The first time the word פקד simply means that Hashem will certainly keep His promise to redeem Bnei Yisrael. This included only removal of the negative aspects of the Yehudim's exile. There was, however, also a positive aspect to the bondage, the one described in Bereshit 15,14, namely that Bnei Yisrael would leave Mitzrayim as wealthy people. According to Bechorot 5 not a single Yisraeli took less than ninety donkeys' loads of silver and gold out of Mitzrayim. Yosef foresaw that Bnei Yisrael's preoccupation with loading the animals with all these valuables were a reason for their leaving his bones behind; this is why he made the brothers swear that even the preoccupation with their newly acquired wealth should not make them forget his bones at that time. In any event Moshe was the only one who instead of loading his animals with valuables went in search of Yosef's remains and eventually loaded Yosef's bier on his donkey (compare Shemot Rabbah 20,19). At a later date Hashem rewarded Moshe by letting him keep the splinters of the precious stones from which he carved the second set of tablets.

מזה אתכם, "with you from this place." The word מזה does not mean "from here," i.e. that Yosef thought the brothers would have to locate his remains exactly in the place where he made them swear this oath. Yosef used the expression as the reason he asked the brothers to swear such an oath. He considered it as a small repayment of all the favours he had done for the brothers during their stay in Mitzrayim. He went so far as to hint that taking his bones out of Mitzrayim for burial in the Holy Land would compensate for the time when they had separated themselves from their brotherhood with him; the angel had told Yosef in Bereshit 37,17 that the brothers נסעו מזה "had departed from זה" (the number 12, symbol for the 12 brothers, compare Bereshit Rabbah 84). Yosef used the words מזה אתכם to indicate that if the brothers would fulfil their oath he would consider them as having re-instated him in their midst. The sin they had committed against him at that time would then have been wiped out. In other words, Yosef would forgive the brothers posthumously, for simply swearing the oath.

וה׳ הולך לפניהם יומם, And Hashem would walk in front of them by day, etc." The Torah chooses the word לנחותם to indicate that Hashem made the journey comfortable. When it was hot Hashem made the cloud spread over them to protect them against the sun. The cloud performed this function only by day. The cloud described here has nothing to do with the column of cloud which preceded Bnei Yisrael which smoothed rough passages and showed them the way to go. We have some proof for this in Devarim 1,33 where the Torah is specific by stating that the cloud in front of them was "to seek you out a place where to pitch your tents. The column of fire by night was to show you the way you were to walk, and a cloud by day." The Torah speaks of three separate phenomena then, 1) to seek you out the way; this cloud was with them all the time. 2) The column of fire to enable them to see at night. 3) a cloud by day. The latter was the cloud which we described as providing shade against the heat of the sun. We do not agree with Rashi who understands the word לנחותם as להנחותם, and that the letter ה is missing. Rashi tries to prove his point by citing לראותכם (Devarim 1,33) as a parallel. According to our interpretation the letter ה is also not missing in the verse in Deuteronomy.

ולילה בעמוד אש להאיר, and at night in a pillar of fire to provide light." According to Shabbat 22 Bnei Yisrael "walked" during the entire forty years only by light provided by G'd which was so powerful that it enabled them to look even into the darkest spot. [The discussion in the Talmud centers around the question why Aharon had to light the candelabra in the Tabernacle when G'd had already illuminated all with His own light. Ed.] The Talmud cannot speak of the hours of darkness as this would not agree with the language employed there. If that were the meaning, what does the Talmud mean "they marched only by the light of the heavenly fire?" Surely the Talmud means that Bnei Yisrael did not march by sunlight during the days. Why then would the night not be as bright as the day so that they had no need for a special column of fire at all? If we want to understand what took place at that time we must pay attention to the words ללכת יומם ולילה, "to walk by day and by night." Why was the Torah not satisfied with writing: "in order to provide light for them," and had to add the words: "to walk by day and by night?"

We must conclude therefore that A) the light Hashem provided for Bnei Yisrael at that time never departed from the camp of Bnei Yisrael as our sages explained, but that B) it also never extended beyond the boundaries of that camp either. There was a good reason for this. In the terrible desert which normally is the domain of impurity, a region in which the forces of the קליפה are at home (Zohar section 1, page 126), Bnei Yisrael were the beneficiaries of the heavenly light within the boundaries of their camp; outside their camp it was night (dark) for them just as it was for everybody else. Normally, Bnei Yisrael did not travel at night. Whenever Hashem wanted them to travel at night, however, they did not require the light dispensed by the pillar of fire within their camp as Hashem's light illuminated every place within their camp. The pillar of fire was needed only to illuminate the way beyond the boundaries of their camp. This is what the Torah had in mind when it wrote להאיר להם, "to provide light for them." The reason Hashem had to provide this additional light was "so that they could travel by this light both by day and by night." Just as Bnei Yisrael were able to see into the distance by day without recourse to the pillar of fire, so at night the pillar of fire provided illumination for them equal to that of the sunlight by day. This then explains the wording of the Torah לראותכם בדרך אשר תלכו בה (Deut.1,33), "to enable you to see by it." This is not in agreement with Rashi's explanation.

דבר אל בוי ישראל וישובו, "speak to the children of Yisrael so that they will turn backwards, etc." Anyone who reads this verse cannot help wondering why Hashem would give an order designed to trick Paroh into pursuit of Bnei Yisrael, when He has many other means at His disposal to bring about the same result?

In view of our awareness that Hashem wants to try and put Yisrael in a favourable light so as to justify the favours He does for His people, it is even harder to understand how Hashem devised a scheme which resulted in Bnei Yisrael expressing their dismay at the developments which followed in the most sarcastic manner when they accused Moshe of leading them into the desert to die as if there were not enough burial grounds in Mitzrayim (14,11). Actually, the arguments Bnei Yisrael used against Moshe were not new ones as the Torah itself testifies. However, Hashem displayed extreme wisdom here by luring Paroh into the kind of sin (pursuit of Bnei Yisrael) which would give Him an opportunity to demonstrate to Yisrael that He would exact true vengeance on Paroh. Hashem did not want to spell out more detail than to say that Bnei Yisrael's action in turning backwards would encourage Paroh to pursue them, as a result of which Hashem would deal with him severely. Having thus informed Bnei Yisrael of what to expect they should have been able to face these developments with calm. Unfortunately, even though Bnei Yisrael had been warned what to expect, Hashem did not succeed completely as we observe from the reactions of various groups of Bnei Yisrael in the verses following. Having read of Bnei Yisrael's reaction after Hashem had given them advance notice of Paroh's pursuit you may imagine how much more violent their reaction would have been had this development taken them entirely by surprise.
ואמר פרעה…. נבוכים הם בארץ, "and Paroh will say 'they are entangled in the land, etc.'" This would be Paroh's reaction when his spies brought him up-to-date on Yisrael's travels.

ויגד למלך…כי ברח העם, ויהפך לבב פרעה, "when the king was told that the people had fled, Paroh had a change of heart, etc." Why does the Torah speak about Bnei Yisrael "fleeing" instead of their "going?" If the words ויהפך לבב פרעה mean that Paroh now developed remorse about what he had done this would be very peculiar seeing that he had never "done" what he did voluntarily! He had dismissed Bnei Yisrael only as the result of having suffered extremely serious plagues, so much so that Mitzrayim was in danger of total collapse. How could the Torah then ascribe Paroh's dismissal of Bnei Yisrael to something "he had done?" One can only change one's mind if one's mind had operated with balanced judgment, not if one acted under duress! Furthermore, what does the expression "what is this we have done" mean in this context? The people had no more acted voluntarily than had their king!

Perhaps we have to fall back on the Zohar's premise that every time the Torah speaks about העם what is meant is the new multitude of converts commonly known as ערב רב. Accordingly, the report Paroh received about "the people" having fled referred to the new converts whom Paroh sent along with Bnei Yisrael in order for them to bring about Bnei Yisrael's return to Mitzrayim. These people had now decided to throw in their lot with Bnei Yisrael permanently. Inasmuch as they had been Mitzri subjects, their defection could properly be described as the flight of Paroh's people.

ויהפך לבב פרעה, Paroh had a change of heart, etc. This means that Paroh was sorry now that he had sent these new converts along with Bnei Yisrael. He did not regret letting Bnei Yisrael go. When the Mitzrim exclaimed: "what did we do?" this refers to the Mitzrim's surprise at their own stupidity in having sent these converts along with Bnei Yisrael. They explained their stupidity as being the result of allowing Bnei Yisrael to depart as free men. (According to Yalkut Shimoni 208 Paroh had even executed a deed granting Bnei Yisrael the status as free men.) The words shilachnu me-ovdenu then are a reference to this document granting Bnei Yisrael their freedom. Even though it was conceivable that Bnei Yisrael would decide to return, they would do so as free and equal citizens, not as slaves. The Mitzri people's upset was very real for in the absence of Bnei Yisrael to perform slave labour all the work Bnei Yisrael had performed up to this point would now become something they had to do for themselves as well as for the government. The people who joined Paroh in the pursuit were concerned mostly with bringing back the new converts described as העם. Hashem did not need to influence Paroh to make a decision concerning this pursuit at all. However, Hashem influenced Paroh to also pursue Bnei Yisrael themselves by allowing him to think that the latter had become entangled in the land.

Paroh was also motivated by another consideration which I have already discussed in 10,7, namely that his whole obstinacy was based on the miscalculation that Hashem was not all-powerful and that is why He resorted to deceptive tactics. Paroh and his servants had reasoned that if Hashem were all powerful He would do things outright instead of achieving His aims by devious means. On the day Elokim killed the firstborn the Mitzrim finally admitted to themselves that Hashem could indeed do whatever He wanted including destruction of the universe itself if He so desired. In view of this, the Mitzrim concluded that the request of Hashem transmitted through Moshe to let Bnei Yisrael travel three days into the desert could be taken at face value and was not a scheme to leave and then not to return. They discounted Paroh's repeated concern that the fact that Bnei Yisrael were not prepared to leave anyone or anything behind was proof of their intent not to return, and they credited this to Bnei Yisrael's declared intent to celebrate a holiday, something that is best done in the midst of one's family and possessions. It was considerations such as these that prompted the Mitzrim to "lend" Bnei Yisrael their valuables. They did not suspect Hashem of having influenced their decision to lend these valuables to Bnei Yisrael as they reasoned that if Hashem had wanted to He could have forced them to hand over all of their possessions to the departing Yehudim. Their reasoning was reinforced by the knowledge that Bnei Yisrael had become thoroughly familiar with all their valuables during the plague of darkness without exploiting their opportunity to steal these goods at a time when they could have done without fear of being discovered.

When the informer told Paroh that "the people" had fled, he meant that the Yehudim had decided not to return at the end of three days as had been the commonly held belief at the time of their departure. Paroh and the Mitzrim were now convinced that Bnei Yisrael under Moshe's leadership had made this decision on their own, as their G'd would never have become a party to deception. Such considerations then all contributed to Paroh, his servants, and his people undergoing a change of heart in their attitude towards Bnei Yisrael. They never regretted having let them go at that time, as they had only let them go for a holiday. They regretted their stupidity in giving the people a letter releasing them from bondage. This had been an unpardonable stupidity because even their G'd had never demanded this. They reasoned that what they should have done in the first place was to send a military escort with Bnei Yisrael to assure their return at the end of the three days.

Another way of looking at what happened is this: When the news reached Paroh that the Bnei Yisrael had "fled," Paroh reconsidered his premise that the Yisraeli Elokim was all-knowing and all-powerful. This Elokim apparently had been forced to use deception because He was not omnipotent. This is why He kept His intention that Bnei Yisrael should depart permanently a secret up until now.

The Torah advisedly speaks of the לבב, "a dual heart" of Paroh undergoing a change. Paroh's considerations were due to conflicting feelings (i.e. "two hearts"). Originally, He had thought that G'd was unable to orchestrate Bnei Yisrael's exodus otherwise He would not have had to almost beg him to let Bnei Yisrael go. As a result, he, Paroh had refused to let them go. Next, Paroh had convinced himself that G'd's love for the Jewish people might only be temporary. In the meantime Paroh had come to realise that his estimate of G'd liking the Jewish people only temporarily had also been wrong and as a result of both these considerations of telling him to let Bnei Yisrael go, he had done so in the firm belief that there was nothing he could do to stop this process. Now, in retrospect, he realised that he had been wrong after all, that G'd had lacked the power to orchestrate the Exodus without help from Paroh himself. This is why he decided to mount the pursuit.

ואת עמו לקח עמו. "and he took his people with him. The Mitzri people had never been involved in the negotiations with Moshe and Aharon. Paroh had to convince the Mitzrim that what he was about to do had a chance to succeed as the people were greatly afraid The words לקח עמו in this context mean that "he convinced them."

ויחזק ה׳ את לב פרעה, Hashem hardened the heart of Paroh, etc. The Torah means that Hashem needed to harden the heart of Paroh otherwise he would not have had the courage to face a nation which had recently left Mitzrayim with their heads held high. The various considerations we described above were part of this process the Torah describes as "Hashem hardened the heart of Paroh."

ופרעה הקריב….והנה מצרים נוסע אחריהם, when Paroh drew close Bnei Yisrael raised their eyes and saw that Mitzrayim was marching after them, etc. Why was this whole line necessary? Would the words: "they caught up with them while they were encamped by the sea" not have sufficed to describe what took place? Why did the verse commence by telling us about what Paroh did and conclude by telling us what Mitzrayim was doing? The Torah should have continued that "Paroh was marching after them;" Why is the word נסע "was marching" in the singular when many Mitzrim are being described as marching?

In order to understand this whole verse we must first understand Bnei Yisrael's comments to Moshe: "did you take us out of Mitzrayim because there are not enough burial places in Mitzrayim? What did you do to us, etc.?" Looking at these words one gains the impression that Bnei Yisrael were surprised that the Mitzrim pursued them. How could this be seeing that Hashem had told them beforehand that their whole maneuver was designed to fool Paroh and cause him to pursue them? Why did they suddenly become afraid? Possibly they did not realise that Paroh had so much military capability left after all that happened. Even so, in view of the assurances Bnei Yisrael had from Hashem that He would deal harshly with Paroh why did they display this mortal fear?

We must fall back on what our sages have taught as described in Shemot Rabbah 21,5 that when Bnei Yisrael noticed Paroh pursuing them they naturally turned their eyes heavenwards expecting Hashem to manifest Himself and to smite the Mitzrim. Imagine Bnei Yisrael's surprise when what they saw was the guardian angel of Mitzrayim whose name is Mitzrayim flying through the air. It was then that they became afraid as they realised that this angel had now come out in order to help his protegees, the Mitzrim. It is an accepted theory that the fortunes of these guardian angels are bound up with their charges. When the protegees of such guardian angels suffer a defeat so does the guardian angel himself. [In fact according to the Kabbalists when Hashem wants to destroy a people, He first destroys their guardian angel. After that, even if the people appear still to be going strong, their fate has already been sealed. Ed.] We are told in Yuma 69 that Alexander the Great was in the habit of observing the guardian angel of Macedonia at work whenever he went into battle. It is customary for a minister to take up position on the right side of the king and not in front of the people. Normally, a king who travels into battle with his troops takes up his position behind the infantry. In this instance Bnei Yisrael had the impression that the guardian angel of Mitzrayim was still going strong, far from being the first one to be defeated by Hashem. The Torah also describes Paroh הקריב, as coming close, i.e. travelling ahead of his troops not behind them. The reason Bnei Yisrael were able to see the guardian angel of Mitzrayim at all was because the guardian angel was positioned next to the king who travelled ahead of his troops. This unusual spectacle frightened Bnei Yisrael. They believed that celestial forces were now arraigned against them. In view of all this, the fact that Hashem had told them that the Mitzrim would pursue them and He would deal harshly with Paroh was no longer enough for the people to keep their cool.

There were two reasons why G'd had not interfered with the guardian angel at that time. 1) G'd was looking for a legal excuse to kill that guardian angel. The Zohar, section two, page 52 interprets 14,30 "Yisrael saw Mitzrayim dead on the beaches of the sea," as a reference to the guardian angel of Mitzrayim. The second reason G'd allowed the guardian angel of Mitzrayim to adopt such a visibly threatening posture was for Yisrael's benefit. G'd wanted Yisrael to do תשובה, to repent. They needed to acquire the merit of repentance in order to justify that G'd should perform the great miracle of splitting the Sea of Reeds on their behalf. This was something G'd had not promised them previously. Shemot Rabbah 21,5 also points out that the unusual form (causative) ופרעה הקריב "and Paroh caused himself to come close," instead of the usual ופרעה קרב, "and Paroh approached," is a clear indication of G'd's purpose being to cause Bnei Yisrael to do תשובה. In the event, G'd's expectations were fulfilled as the Torah reports that "the children of Yisrael cried out to G'd" (14,10).

התיצבו וראו "stand still and see!" Perhaps Moshe suggested to Bnei Yisrael to stand still in prayer now just as they had stood and prayed in verse 10. We find the expression "standing still" also in connection with Hanna's prayer in Shmuel I 1,26.

אשר יעשה לכם היום, "which He will work for you to-day." Hashem emphasised the word "to-day" because He did not want the people to worry that Paroh's punishment would be as long delayed as it had been in Mitzrayim when it took 12 months from the time they first heard the news that Moshe would be the redeemer.

אשר ראיתם את מצרים, "the way you have seen Mitzrayim, etc." Hashem explained that the reason He had allowed the Mitzrim to assume such a threatening posture was only because they would never again assume a threatening posture such as this. The Mitzrim would soon collapse in spite of their fear-inspiring guardian angel.

ה׳ ילחם לכם, "Hashem will fight on your behalf, etc." Inasmuch as the reason Bnei Yisrael had been frightened had been that they saw themselves confronting celestial forces, Hashem tells them that the most powerful celestial force, He Himself, will fight on their behalf. When Hashem is involved personally, even a thousand celestial forces equal to the guardian angel of Mitzrayim are nothing to be afraid of.

By emphasising the attribute השם i.e. the attribute of Mercy, the Torah suggests that even the attribute of Mercy concurred with the retribution G'd was about to exact from the Mitzrim. The Torah writes ילחם לכם, "He will fight on your behalf," because from Yisrael's point of view this would be a manifestation of the attribute of Mercy. Moreover, the word ילחם implies much more than mere assistance. G'd was going to conduct the entire war single-handedly, hence ואתם תחרישו "you have to keep silent."

We find a comment in the introduction to Eychah Rabbati 30 according to which four different righteous people when in difficulties each asked something different from Hashem. The one who represented the highest level of righteousness refrained from asking at all. The model for this approach quoted is King Chizkiyah who said (when facing the onslaught of Sancheriv): "I neither possess the strength to kill, nor to pursue, nor even to recite hymns of praise; hence I will sleep on my bed and You Hashem will do what needs to be done." Hashem did indeed kill the army of Sancheriv without any involvement of King Chizkiyah or his forces (Kings II chapter 19). When Moshe told the people that all they had to contribute was their silence, he implied that their present state of righteousness was of the same calibre as that of King Chizkiyah. According to the interpretation we offered that the word התיצבו means to stand still in prayer, we have to understand the words: "but you shall remain silent," as addressed to the attribute of Justice. Bnei Yisrael were to offer prayers in order to silence the attribute of Justice which might otherwise appeal to Hashem claiming that they were not worthy of the miracle about to be performed on their behalf.

מה תצעק אלי, "why are you crying out to Me, etc.?" The word "to Me" is difficult. Who else was Moshe supposed to cry out to if not to G'd? We find both in Yonah 2,3 and in Tehillim 118,5 that in times of distress one is supposed to cry out to G'd as did both Yonah and David successfully. If G'd meant that Moshe indulged in too much prayer that would seem an unjustified criticism as long as Moshe's prayer had not yet been answered. Besides, we see from G'd's instructions in verse 16 that Moshe was to raise his staff that G'd did answer his prayer. If so, why did G'd ask Moshe: "why do you cry out to Me? What is G'd's answer "speak to the children of Yisrael so that they will move on" supposed to mean? Where were they supposed to move to? The Mitzrim were behind them and the sea was in front! If G'd meant that they should move after they would observe the sea split, G'd should first have told Moshe to raise his staff and afterwards have given the command that Bnei Yisrael were to move into the bed of the sea!

We have to refer to Shemot Rabbah 21,7 where Samael is described as opposing the impending miracle claiming that until very recently Bnei Yisrael had worshiped idols with the same fervor as the Mitzrim. In other words, Bnei Yisrael were subject to the attribute of Justice. Hashem (i.e. the attribute of Mercy) told Moshe that Bnei Yisrael (or he) were addressing themselves to the wrong attribute in their prayers for help. We have a tradition based on Devarim 32,18 צור ילדך תשי, "you have weakened the Rock which begot you," that Hashem's respective attributes are "strengthened" or "weakened" in accordance with the deeds we perform or do not perform here on earth. While it was true that the attribute of Mercy was anxious to perform a life-saving miracle on behalf of Bnei Yisrael, they had not yet qualified for such a miracle by their deeds. Hashem advised Moshe "speak to the children of Yisrael to perform an act of faith such as entering the sea so that I can activate My attribute of Mercy and perform the miracle that I have in mind." Following such a demonstration of faith Moshe was to raise his staff to enable Hashem to perform the splitting of the Sea of Reeds. When Hashem said to Moshe: "why do you cry out to Me?," He meant: "the matter is altogether not in My hands." If and when Moshe had spoken to the children of Yisrael and they had demonstrated the necessary mesasure of faith, only then: "raise your staff, etc., and divide the sea!" This is precisely what happened after Nachshon ben Aminadav of the tribe of Yehudah walked into the sea up to his neck before the sea had split. Sotah 69 reports concerning him that the waters of the sea were about to drown him. In view of the foregoing none of the verses present a problem, neither as to content nor as to their sequence. The principal reason Bnei Yisrael had been handed over to the attribute of Justice was that they had said they were better off serving Mitzrayim than dying in the desert. This is why Hashem (the attribute of Mercy) had declared that their appeal to Him at that stage was useless.

ואני הנני מחזק את לב מצרים, "And I, behold I will harden the heart of Mitzrayim, etc." Hashem's attribute of Mercy informed Bnei Yisrael from a sense of compassion that they should not be worried when they saw that the sea did not close after they had crossed, but remained open for the Mitzri cavalry to descend into in hot pursuit. He explained that this was only the preamble of Hashem dealing with the entire Mitzri army and wiping them out.

ויסע מלאך האלוקים, The angel of Hashem travelled, etc. This verse is in perfect agreement with what we explained on 13,21 that Bnei Yisrael enjoyed the presence of three distinct clouds which accompanied them and served their specific needs. 1) The cloud which travelled ahead of them to serve as a moving pathfinder indicating the direction Bnei Yisrael were to take. 2) The cloud which protected them from the heat of the sun. 3) the pillar of fire which lit up the way for them at night. In our verse Elokim informs us of what He did on that particular night (of the 21st of Nissan). The angel of Hashem referred to in our verse as "travelling" was the cloud which normally travelled ahead of Bnei Yisrael showing them the way and which is described in Devarim 1,33 as travelling in front of Bnei Yisrael. In this instance this cloud moved behind them. The Torah also informs us that the cloud whose daytime function it was to protect Bnei Yisrael from the sun's heat also now took up its position behind the camp of Bnei Yisrael. In other words the two clouds normally in front of Bnei Yisrael moved behind them. The reason the second cloud was needed in that position was in order to darken the atmosphere in front of the Mitzrim so that they could not know exactly where Bnei Yisrael were encamped.; this is why the Torah says: "the cloud remained (in its position) and (the other cloud) lit up the night. Seeing that the camp of Bnei Yisrael was brightly illuminated by the pillar of fire, the other cloud had to blot out that light from in front of the Mitzrim. [The term "angel of Hashem" is used to tell us that the angel assumed the form of a cloud, etc. Ed.]

ויבא בין מחנה מצרים, and it came between the camp of Mitzrayim, etc. It is possible that this cloud filled the entire space between the two camps and filled it with darkness. The Torah only had to write this verse to acquaint us with this detail seeing that the cloud which separated the two camps has already been mentioned in verse 19.

ויט משה את ידו, Moshe inclined his hand, etc. Although the Torah reports that Hashem made a strong east wind blow all night which dried out the sea, this referred only to the deep waters. Hashem did not want Bnei Yisrael to have to descend to the very depths and to have to get tired by walking too far. This is why He first "froze" the deep parts of the sea by means of the east wind. If not for this consideration, Hashem would have dispensed with the east wind altogether.

It is of interest to know whether Moshe inclined his hand as a signal for the sea to split at the beginning of the night or at the end of the night. From the wording of the verse we may almost prove that it was close to morning. This is difficult, however, because if it was so how could one discern that the splitting of the sea was brought about by Moshe's action? We therefore have to understand the verse thus: "Moshe inclined his hand after Hashem had already made an east wind blow during the whole night which dried out the (deeper) parts of the sea;" as soon as Moshe inclined his hand the waters split. This would then be in line with my commentary on verse 15 that all this occurred after Nachshon had waded into the sea in response to Hashem's challenge to demonstrate an act of faith. Moshe had held off with inclining his hand until after Nachshon was in the sea. Bnei Yisrael then followed when the sea split. This also conforms to the way Shemot Rabbah 21 describes what happened. Another way of explaining the sequence of events is this: when the Torah writes "He turned the sea into dry land," all the waters of the sea crystallised in such a way that Bnei Yisrael did not need to descend into the bed of the sea, whereas the east wind had dried out all the waters of the sea. I consider the first explanation as more likely to be correct.
כל הלילה, all night long. The wind blew all night and the sea split at the end of the night causing Bnei Yisrael to begin marching through it.

בתוך הים ביבשה, in the midst of the sea on dry land. The words "in the midst of the sea" mean in the inner part of (what had formerly been) the sea; the word ביבשה means that the sea bed was not muddy but completely dry.

והמים להם חומה, and the waters formed a wall for them, etc. This means that parts of the waters had not been blown aside by the wind. The words: "on their right and on their left" mean that those waters did not form an actual wall but merely that they surrounded Bnei Yisrael on either side.

וירדפו מצרים, Mitzrayim pursued, etc. Even though the Torah says: "the cloud remained in place" (verse 20), what is mentioned here occurred in daylight already at a time when the cloud was not as impenetrable so that the Mitzrim could begin to discern where Bnei Yisrael were positioned. This enabled them to start their pursuit.

ויהי באשמרת הבקר, It happened during the morning watch, etc. We need to know why Hashem chose to perform this act of retribution in the morning and not during the night which is traditionally the time for the attribute of Justice to be active. I have seen in Yalkut Shimoni item 235 that this is exactly what the angel Gabriel argued before Hashem. Hashem answered him that he should wait until the hour during which the patriarch Avraham started out on the way to offer his son Yitzchak as an offering to Hashem (we read in Bereshit 22,3 that this occurred early in the morning). In other words, although the morning is not the time to exact vengeance Hashem reversed His usual procedure for the sake of Avraham's descendants just as Avraham at the time had reversed his natural feelings of love and mercy towards his son in favour of obedience to Hashem's request. Yisrael benefited in that Hashem performed the miracle personally, to match the fact that Avraham had personally saddled his donkey at the time though he had hundreds of servants at his disposal to perform that task for him. The Torah writes: "Hashem looked down on the camp of Mitzrayim; this means that He Himself went into action. The fact that the Mitzrim drowned in daylight enabled Bnei Yisrael to witness the death of their enemies.

נטה את ידך..וישובו המים, "Incline your hand so that the waters may come back, etc." Why was it necessary for Moshe to incline his hand in order to make the waters come back? Surely, the division of the waters was only for the time it took for Bnei Yisrael to cross? G'd had not revised the laws of nature permanently! In fact Shemot Rabbah 22 states that when the last of Bnei Yisrael ascended from the sea, the last of the Mitzrim entered the sea, implying that the sea would come back by itself.

Perhaps the sea reasoned that the area where the Yehudim had crossed was meant to remain a crossing and that just as Bnei Yisrael could cross so could the Mitzrim. Actually, Hashem had decreed that the waters should not close immediately behind Bnei Yisrael in order to lure the Mitzrim into pursuit. This is something the sea was not aware of. The sea did not concern itself with this, having kept its original promise to Hashem at the creation to split when the time came. When Moshe inclined his hand this was a signal to the sea that it had completed its task.

We have a rule in Masechet Yom Tov 5 that if a collegium of judges has made a ruling of even a temporary nature, this decree remains in force until a collegium of at least an equal number of judges declares the original ruling as void. This is also what happened here.

Another reason why it was necessary for Moshe to incline his hand was simply that though the waters of the sea would indeed come back on their own, this would occur at such a slow speed that the Mitzrim would be able to escape. Indeed, we have an opinion that some of the Mitzrim who were close to shore were able to save themselves. As a result of Moshe inclining his hand the waters returned with a rush as indicated by the word לאיתנו. Alternatively, seeing Moshe had been the agent who struck the sea it was only fitting that it should be he who restored the sea to its original position. We find support for this view in Yeshayahu 63,12.

Still another reason why G'd asked Moshe to incline his hand prior to the waters returning was to give the sea a signal not to allow a single rider or chariot of the Mitzrim to escape. Not even those who were close to the shore should be given a chance to save themselves. We know that the waters complied as the Torah writes that "the waters covered them and that not a single Mitzri survived."

לאיתנו, to its original position. Shemot Rabbah 21,6 understands this expression as לתנאי הראשון, to its original condition or contract which was made between the waters and Hashem at the time Hashem said in Bereshit 1,9 that the waters should gather to one place. Why does the Midrash describe this as the "first condition," when the first condition of the waters was its state of being divided, not possessing molecular adhesion. The directive that the waters should congregate i.e. adhere to each other was the "second condition!" Perhaps what is meant by our verse is that after the waters had returned to their original state they realised that Moshe had not destroyed their cohesion but that he had now allowed them to again resume their previous cohesion. It is possible that although the waters knew about the agreement made at the time with Hashem, they had not imagined that when the time came to honour this agreement that the result would be so radical i.e. that they would literally form walls of stone (frozen water). When things went back to normal the waters realised that what had transpired was only part of the original agreement, and that Hashem had not added new conditions. We must try and understand this agreement in depth, seeing that according to the Midrash the waters first refused to part at Moshe's request, claiming that inasmuch as they had been created before man they did not have to take orders from a human being. Hashem had to incline His right hand together with the right hand of Moshe (Yeshayahu 63,12 "who made His glorious arm march at the right hand of Moshe, who divided the waters before them, etc."). Another problem with the verse is that we know that selected individuals did experience that the waters were split on their behalf; an example is the sainted Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair (Chulin 7). If Hashem's contract with the waters at the time had been restricted to the sea splitting for the Yehudim at the time of the Exodus, by what power did Rabbi Pinchas ben Yair accomplish such a miracle?

We must perceive the condition or contract implied in the word איתנו, as an overriding condition applying to the work of creation as a whole, namely that all creatures, be they inert or alive submit to the requirements of the Torah and the people who are its carriers. In fact the authority of the Torah scholars in this respect equals that of the Creator Himself. This is the reason that individuals such a Yehoshua could order the moon and the sun to suspend their motion in the sky, etc. The statement we just made is the mystical dimension of Yeshayahu 43,1: "Yaakov your creator, Yisrael who has formed you;" In commenting on this verse in Vayikra Rabbah 36,4 our sages claim that Hashem asked the universe a rhetorical question: "who has created you, who has fashioned you if not Yisrael, and all this by means of the power contained in Torah." I have dealt with this also in my commentary on the word בראשית at the beginning of the Torah.

At the time of the Exodus Bnei Yisrael had not yet received the Torah therefore the decree that Torah scholars could dictate to the forces of nature did not apply as yet. This is why the sea's consent was needed for it to split at the behest of Moshe, and the sea was able to argue that Moshe had no authority seeing he (man) had been created only on the sixth day of creation and was therefore junior to it which had been created on the third day. The sea simply hinted that Moshe could not claim to order it around by reason of his mastery of the Torah. If he had truly possessed mastery of Torah which had been created prior to the universe, he himself could have claimed to be senior to the sea. Hashem therefore had to resort to a stratagem by extending His own right hand alongside that of Moshe's right hand. This was a sophisticated way of telling the sea that Moshe did indeed possess mastery of the Torah and therefore was entitled to order the sea about. The significance of the right hand in this respect is anchored in the Torah itself in Devarim 33,2: "from His right hand He flashed lightning at them." As soon as the sea noticed Hashem's right hand, it split without further ado. Henceforth every צדיק who lived after Bnei Yisrael had received the Torah at Mount Sinai could present "a copy" of the agreement Hashem had made with His creation to submit to instructions issued by those who represented mastery of Torah. Such people possessed not only the power to effect changes in the laws of nature, but they could inflict penalties on nature if it chose to disobey them.

ומצרים נסים לקראתו, while the Mitzrim were fleeing towards it. Although the Mitzrim were fleeing from the onrushing waters, they found that the sea was coming towards its original place. As a result they found themselves fleeing towards the waters regardless of which direction they were headed for. We find something similar in Bamidbar Rabbah 18 and Sanhedrin 110 describing the descent of Korach and his supporters into the bowels of the earth. The "mouth" of the earth is described as following the direction where any one of Korach or his companions happened to be standing.

וינער ה׳ את מצרים בתוך הים, Hashem hurled Mitzrayim into the sea. This statement is necessary seeing there are expert swimmers who are often able to stay above the waves even during a storm. The Torah says that Hashem hurled such expert swimmers into the sea so that they too had no chance to survive. According to Shemot Rabbah 21 the reference to מצרים as distinct from מצריים, the Mitzrim, means that Hashem hurled the guardian angel of Mitzrayim into the sea by pouring strong rain upon him.

לכל חיל פרעה, Paroh's entire army, etc. This refers to the fact that the chariots and their riders who were unable to speed up slowed down the infantry which was marching behind the cavalry. The waters simply covered them wherever they were so that not a single one of them escaped.

ובני ישראל הלכו ביבשה בתוך הים, but Bnei Yisrael had walked through the sea on dry ground. The reason the Torah states this fact a second time is merely to tell us that the Mitzrim were aware of this fact and also of the fact that the sea had formed a wall for Bnei Yisrael, whereas they themselves went down deeper into the earth. This was fulfilment of the prophecy in verse 18 that the Mitzrim would become aware of the true nature of Hashem. It is worth reading Ibn Ezra's commentary on verse 27 where he lambasts the commentators who tried to explain away the miracle. He debunks the theory that Moshe was well informed about the times of low tide and high tide respectively, whereas Paroh was ignorant of this and this is why he drowned with his army. The fact that Bnei Yisrael marched on dry land as described and did not merely wade through mud which had recently been covered by the sea, plus the fact that the Mitzrim observed the waters forming a wall on either side of Bnei Yisrael made it clear that all of this had nothing at all to do with high tides and low tides.

ביום ההוא, on that day, etc. The Torah simply means that the salvation only occurred on that day, not previously; even though the Exodus had occurred, Bnei Yisrael had not yet acquired much confidence in themselves vis-a-vis the Mitzrim.

וירא ישראל את מצרים מת, Yisrael observed Mitzrayim dead, etc. Why did the Torah have to tell us that the Mitzrim were dead? How could they be alive after they had drowned? The Mechilta explains this verse by saying that Bnei Yisrael observed the death of the Mitzrim. Accordingly, the Mitzrim did not finally die until they were washed up on the beaches. G'd arranged this in such a way that either party should clearly observe what was happening to their adversaries. The Mitzrim's last emotion before they died should be one of shame vis-a-vis Bnei Yisrael. We have to read the words מת על שפת הים as belonging together.

וייראו העם את ה׳… ואת משה עבדו The people feared Hashem …and they believed in His servant Moshe. This was not fear of punishment but awe of the Majesty of Hashem. The fear of punishment they had possessed already prior to the Exodus. According to what we explained on 12,43 that Bnei Yisrael did not accept the commandment of the King (Hashem), they did not even fear to be punished by Hashem otherwise they would not have remained uncircumcised until that time. At any rate the fear described in this verse is that they stood in awe at Hashem's Majesty. When the Torah describes Bnei Yisrael as "believing," this was the reward for their fear of Hashem's Majesty.

אז ישיר משה, Then Moshe began to sing, etc. It would have sufficed for the Torah to write וישר משה, "Moshe sang," without the introduction אז, "then." However, the Torah wanted to tell us of the preparation which resulted in that song of jubilation. After Yisrael acquired the fear of G'd's Majesty, which in turn resulted in a profound measure of faith both in G'd and in Moshe, they were divinely inspired to sing this song of thanksgiving.

The reason the Torah writes ישיר "will sing," instead of שר, sang, something that would be so much more appropriate with the word אז is, that to this day we sing this song daily in our morning prayers. Had the Torah written אז שר משה, we would have assumed that the song was appropriate only for the people who had been present when the sea was split.

ויאמרו לאמור, אשירה, they said saying: "I will sing, etc." This means that Bnei Yisrael said this to one another. The idea was that they wanted to coordinate their song; they did not want each one to use his own formulation. The fact that they succeeded in this is reflected in the singular "I will sing!"

כי גאה גאה, for He has triumphed gloriously, etc. As a rule songs of praise should commence with mention of the collapse of Hashem's enemies similar to what Shlomo said in Mishlei 11,10: ובאבוד רשעים רנה "when the wicked perish there is jubilation." Accordingly, we understand the words גאה גאה as referring to Paroh who was so boastful that his very name was "the boastful one." Normally, boastful people consider themselves superior to their peers. Inasmuch as their peers do not amount to much, neither does their own pride. Paroh was more presumptious than the average braggart, however, as he thought himself superior even to Hashem. This is why Moshe wrote גאה גאה, the braggart of all braggarts.

We may also understand the expression as analogous to Tehillim 93,1 "Hashem is king, He is robed in splendour." As long as Hashem had not disposed of Paroh He was known simply as גאה, glorious; after Hashem disposed of the braggart Paroh He assumed an additional dimension of glory, hence גאה גאה. The repetition of the expression גאה may also reflect that Hashem is glorious both in the celestial and in the terrestrial spheres. This would explain why no additional subject is appended after the word ורכבו. We may also understand the verse as follows: "I will sing to Hashem because He has proven so glorious; the words כי גאה גאה may also be read together with the rest of the verse, i.e. "He has flung into the sea both the horse and its boastful rider."

עזי וזמרת כה, "Hashem is my strength and song." The normal procedure when one composes a song for Elokim, praises Him or prays to Him, is to mention first how Elokim relates to oneself before mentioning how Elokim related to one's ancestors. Thus we find that the men of the Great Assembly who edited our major prayers began the עמידה by first referring to Elokim as "our Elokim," i.e. the Elokim of the petitioner and only afterwards did they define Elokim as also the Elokim of the patriarchs. Bnei Yisrael were similarly motivated when they first referred to what Elokim meant to them (each individual Yehudi), how Elokim had proven a Saviour for them in their present situation acting as the merciful Elokim (tetragram). They concluded the statement referring to their personal relationship with Elokim by saying זה אלי ואנוהו, "this is my Elokim and I will glorify Him," and only afterwards did they describe the same Elokim in His capacity as the Elokim of their fathers. Our sages copied this pattern when they formulated our prayers where we say אלוקינו ואלוקי אבותינו, "our Elokim who was already the Elokim of our ancestors." I have already explained why Bnei Yisrael in this instance chose to describe Elokim in the singular as "my Elokim" instead of as "our Elokim."

ה׳ איש מלחמה, "Hashem is a man of war," etc. This means that even when Elokim operates with the attribute of Mercy He is still "a man of war." The fact that He conducts war does not imply that He abandons the attribute of Mercy. His name remains י־ה־ו־ה and all that this implies just as we find in Maleachi 3,6: כי אני ה׳ לא שניתי, "for I the merciful Elokim have not changed, etc." Elokim has made this plain also at the beginning of פרשת וארא where He told Moshe אני השם, I am the attribute of Mercy.

תהומות יכסיומו, the deeps covered them, etc. The reason the Torah speaks of תהום in the plural must be viewed in light of my comment on 14,21 that half the sea was frozen whereas the other half was split. Each part was originally part of what is called תהום. Read what I have written on 15,8: "the deeps were congealed, etc."

ירדו במצולות, they descended into the depths, etc. This is an allusion to all those champion swimmers who made strenuous efforts to escape from the depths as I have discussed in connection with 14,27.

ימינך ה׳ נאדרי בכח, "Your right hand O Hashem is glorious in power," Bnei Yisrael marvelled at the power displayed by Hashem even when operating as the attribute of Mercy. Even that attribute "dashed the enemy to pieces." Alternatively, one may read this verse "backwards." "When is Your right hand visibly powerful? When it dashes the enemy to pieces." Then the fear of You overcomes people as described in verse 16.

וברב גאונך תהרוס קמיך, "And in the greatness of Your glory You destroy those who rise up against You." The verse tells us that G'd performs miracles to underline that it is He who destroys His opponents. In order that we should not think that G'd has to extend Himself in order to accomplish this, Bnei Yisrael added: "even when You merely send forth Your wrath they already turn to straw."

נערמו מים, גצבו כמו נר, "the waters were piled up, stood upright like a wall." This verse describes three distinct activities performed by Hashem when He split the sea. 1) The waters split and remained in one place as a heap so as to make a path available for Bnei Yisrael to cross. 2) The waters which would normally replace the newly created vacuum in the centre of the sea did not spill into that vacuum but piled up along the sides forming a veritable wall. 3) As already mentioned in my comments on 14,21 it was not the entire depth of the sea which was split, but the deeper layers of water were frozen so as to enable Bnei Yisrael to march through relatively high ground and not to have to descend to what had been the bottom of the sea. The expression קפאו, "were frozen already," reflects what we have said earlier that the freeze of the lower waters in the sea preceded the splitting of the upper levels of the sea. The expression לב ים refers to the lower level of the sea which froze. The reason that Bnei Yisrael again used the word תהומות in the plural was that Hashem made them travel along twelve separate lanes, each tribe having a lane to itself as we know from Shemot Rabbah 24,1.

אמר אויב ארדף אשיג, The enemy had said to himself: "I will pursue, I will overtake, etc." The reason that Bnei Yisrael repeated what we knew already about the Mitzrim pursuing Bnei Yisrael was to extol the manner in which Hashem performed the miracle at the sea. Hashem had succeeded in lulling the Mitzrim into a sense of false security so that they did not consider the pursuit into the sea as hazardous.

אחלק שלל, "I will divide the spoils." The wicked Paroh intended to accomplish three things. 1) Something in which all would share equally, i.e. division of the spoils. 2) He wanted to take the Yehudim back as slaves as they had been before. He said: "my lust shall be satisfied upon them." He referred to the sense of accomplishment he would feel once he captured Bnei Yisrael to make them slaves again. He also hinted that he would treat them at will and oppress them more harshly than previously. 3) He planned to kill Moshe and Aharon as well as the elders and leaders of the people. This is what he referred to when he said (in the words of Bnei Yisrael) "I will draw my sword and my hand will destroy them." We have an example of the previous Paroh attempting to kill Moshe by the sword (Shemot 2,15) where Shemot Rabbah 1,31 describes Paroh as unsuccessfully attempting to kill Moshe by the sword.

נשפת ברוחך, "You blew with Your wind, etc." This verse enumerates three disasters corresponding to three of Paroh's intentions. The reason that Paroh (and the Mitzrim) were covered by the sea was because he had said: "I will divide the spoils." Even though under normal conditions the horses could have saved themselves by swimming, he was made to lose his own most treasured property, his horses. He and the Mitzrim died a slow death as retribution for their declared intention to oppress the Yehudim even more harshly and to kill their leaders. This is why Bnei Yisrael referred to צללו. The Mechilta describes the words כעופרת like lead, as describing how the individual Mitzrim were tossed up and down repeatedly by the waves. In their song Bnei Yisrael spoke about במים אדירים, powerful waters, to describe two features. A) the descent, i.e. צללו כעופרת; B) their inability to die at once; this is alluded to in the words במים אדירים, the powerful waves which kept tossing the Mitzrim up into the air. Yisrael praised the Lord in recognition of all these phenomena.

מי כמוך באלים השם, "Who is comparable to You amongst the deities O Hashem?" Yisrael describes that they had seen the guardian angel of Mitzrayim die; hence they could say that absolutely no celestial force compares to Hashem our Hashem.

Another dimension of this verse is based on an observation in Chagigah 16 where our sages draw a comparison between Elokim and terrestrial kings. The latter is unrecognisable when he chooses to hide amongst his people (soldiers). Elokim is never unrecognisable when He is surrounded by His armies. The word באלים means that even when Elokim is amongst celestial forces, He is immediately recognised as such.

According to the Mechilta there is still another meaning to this comparison between G'd and other powers; whereas a king of flesh and blood inspires greater fear amongst his distant subjects than amongst those near at home, the reverse is true of G'd as we know from Vayikra 10,3: בקרובי אקדש. The composer of this song bemoans the fact that in the "distance," i.e. in the celestial regions, G'd is revered at all times, whereas here on earth He is revered only when He displays such miracles as the splitting of the sea, i.e. when He is נאדר בקדש.

Still another meaning of the comparison drawn by the composer of this song is based on Daniel 7,10 where the waters of the mythical river Dinor are described as the product of the sweat of the Chayot [permanent kind of angels Ed.] which proclaim the holiness of Hashem and to whom this is an awe-inspiring experience, i.e. נאדר בקודש (compare Chagigah 13).

נורא תהלות עשה פלא, "fearful in praises doing wonders?" Everyone ought to be afraid to tell His praises seeing His deeds are so wonderful that no one is able to acknowledge them adequately. How dare one even express an appreciation of G'd's wonderful works knowing one's own inadequacy?

נטית ימינך תבלעימו ארץ, "when You inclined Your right hand the earth swallowed them." Mechilta describes the sea as tossing the Mitzrim onto the dry land and the earth as tossing them right back into the sea. The dry land argued with the sea saying: "considering that I was cursed by Hashem for having merely absorbed a single human being's blood, i.e. Hevel's, at the time, what will Hashem do to me if I will accept an entire population of human beings unless Hashem swears an oath to me not to demand an accounting from me? [this is based on the meaning of "right hand" often being equated with an oath. Ed.] Targum Yonathan also explains our verse in this sense. We learn from here that the sea did not want to accept the Mitzrim and tossed them out. This contradicts something we have learned in Pessachim 118. Hashem is quoted as saying to the guardian angel of the sea: "spit them out onto the dry land." The guardian angel of the sea retorted: "Hashem of the universe, is there then a servant who has been given a gift by his master (food for the fish according to Rashi) and the master subsequently demands the gift back?" To this argument Hashem replied: "I will give you a gift worth one and a half times the original gift if you give Me back the original gift." The sea replied: "can a servant take a master to court?" Hashem answered: "I will guarantee My promise by giving you the river Kishon as a pledge." Upon hearing this the sea immediately disgorged the bodies of the Mitzrim onto the dry land and Bnei Yisrael were able to see that they were dead. It is clear from that story in the Talmud that the sea was quite unwilling to toss the Mitzrim onto the dry land. Why then was the sea not overjoyed when the dry land refused the bodies of the Mitzrim and tossed them back into the sea? Besides, why did Hashem have to repay the sea from the camp of Siserah (900 chariots versus the Mitzrim's 600 chariots, compare Shoftim 4,13)? Why did He not repay the sea personally so that He did not have to give the sea the river Kishon as a pledge?

Another difficulty is the fact that generally speaking the sea does not retain either people or animals but tosses them on to the beaches either on the day they drown or a few days later. According to the view of our sages the sea would prefer to retain these bodies; Rashi and Rashbam suggest that the sea needs these bodies in order to provide food for the fish. If all this is true we must try and understand why, in the case of the Mitzrim, the sea made strenuous efforts to get rid of these bodies instead of retaining them as food for the fish? Perhaps the bodies which the earth tossed back had already begun to decompose and would not only have polluted the sea but had also become unfit as food for the fish. This does not seem a satisfactory answer seeing that Hashem would not have prevented the earth from providing a burial for the dead Mitzrim if only in order to satisfy the commandment in Devarim 21,23 not to allow a person who has been hanged to remain unburied overnight. The shame of the people Hashem had executed did not have to be perpetuated beyond the time of their death so that they should serve as a frightening example.

It is not generally our custom to explain aggadic sayings of our sages. In this instance, however, it is necessary to do so in order to understand the plain meaning of the verse, and in order not to allow the impression that different Midrashim are at odds with one another. We have already referred to a Mechilta on 14,30 where the Torah told us that Bnei Yisrael saw the Mitzrim dead on the beaches of the sea. They beheld the Mitzrim in their last gasps just before they died completely. This was in order for the Mitzrim to see that Bnei Yisrael had been saved from the onrushing waters of the returning sea. This comment by the Mechilta throws light on the two apparently contradictory Midrashim. When the sea asked Hashem not to have to disgorge the Mitzrim (to give back the gift) this was because Hashem had ordered the sea to toss the Mitzrim out while they were still alive. Hashem's reason was to cause joy to His friends Bnei Yisrael whereas the Mitzrim would feel ashamed when they noticed that Bnei Yisrael had been saved. Although there is no direct mention of the fact that the Mitzrim still had some life in them when they were tossed ashore, our sages relied on traditions handed down to them throughout the generations. In view of this, the argument of the sea that a master does not demand return of a gift bestowed on a servant makes good sense. The sea was anxious to be allowed to complete its task of killing those who had angered Hashem. All of Hashem's creatures, be they in the celestial or the terrestial spheres, share the desire to carry out Hashem's commandments seeing that compared to human beings they have so few opportunities to carry out Hashem's commandments. You will find on the same folio in Pessachim that the Talmud tells of how anxious the angel Gabriel was to be the instrument which saved Avraham from the fiery furnace of Nimrod, and that Hashem did not withhold his reward allowing Gabriel to save three other human beings (Chanayah, Mishael, and Azaryah) as a reward for his volunteering to save Avraham. This teaches us that it is considered a meritorious deed for angels to perform deeds of loving kindness for the righteous. The sea was similarly motivated and that is why it objected to being asked to disgorge the Mitzrim prematurely. When Hashem offered to compensate the sea by allowing it to acquire the merit of drowning Siserah's 900 chariots when the time would be ripe, this was certainly a fair compensation.

The sea had another reason for asking that the Mitzrim be deprived of all vestiges of life while they were in the sea. It is the nature of the souls of the Gentiles to remain wherever their bodies died as we know from Kohelet 3,19 where Shlomo tells us that the "souls" of the beasts descend into the bowels of the earth. Idol worshipers are compared to animals and when they happen to die while in the sea the guardian angel of the sea acquires their souls. The concern of the sea was therefore that it did not want the earth (dry land) to acquire these "souls" rather than its own guardian angel. The sea's feelings were reflected when it exclaimed: "is there such a thing as a master taking back a gift?" Hashem therefore replied that at a future date He would compensate the sea handsomely. Hashem meant that He would give the "sea" i.e. the river Kishon, live bodies who would drown therein. The sea had never been interested in the bodies, only in the so-called souls. Seeing this was so, it did not want the dead bodies the earth was tossing at it as the sea is not a natural habitat for dead bodies. On the other hand, earth generally is the habitat for dead bodies seeing that the bodies of human beings are composed of earth as the primary raw material. Hashem therefore forced Earth to receive the bodies of the dead Mitzrim, seeing it was no more than natural.

Do not ask that according to the Talmud in Pessachim the fish opened their mouths thanking Hashem when Hashem paid off the sea, proving that they were very interested in the bodies of the dead soldiers. It is possible that when the sea receives fully alive human bodies the fish derive some benefit therefrom. Once the bodies die the fish are no longer interested in them. The song of the fish was in appreciation of their food supply.

אז נבהלו אלופי אדום, Then the chiefs of Edom were frightened. The word אז refers does not refer to what happened at this time, but to what will happen when the final redemption of the Jewish people is at hand. The same is true of the prophecy of Bilam concerning Edom being laid waste (Bamidbar 24,18). The same applies to the feelings of Moav and Amon whose lands will be appropriated by Yisrael in that future. The reason that Amon is not mentioned separately in the song Bnei Yisrael sang after crossing the sea, although it too was the product of Lot's daughter sleeping with him is, that it will share the general fate of the land of the Kenaani which Yisrael had not captured up to that time. The Torah therefore speaks of the ישבי כנען, people living in Kenaan at the time though they might not have a legitimate claim on that land. The reason the Torah uses the past tense is to assure us that this future is as assured as if it had already happened.

הפול עליהם אימתה ופחד, "Terror and dread will fall upon them, etc." Both this verse and the one following it refer to two separate conquests of the Holy Land, one during the period of Moshe/Yehoshua and the other at the time when the Messiah will arrive. This is the reason the author of the song appears to repeat what he says.

ה׳ ימלך לעולם ועד, "Hashem will rule for ever and ever." The author implies that the reason he did not speak about Hashem having reigned in the past is because of the challenge to Hashem's rule described in verse 19. Inasmuch as Hashem has exacted retribution from only one nation which has not recognised His sovereignty in the world it would be inappropriate to extol Hashem as having ruled in the past. כי בא סוס פרעה, "For the horses of Paroh came, etc." The fact that Hashem disposed of the challenge represented by Paroh was not yet proof of the impotence of all the powers which compete with Hashem on earth and which different nations worship. Hashem's true sovereignty will be established only when He deals with all competing deities.

Another way of understanding the sequence of the words in these two verses plus the fact that Elokim is described as sovereign only in the future is this: "Hashem will rule only in the future because all of Paroh's horses and their riders perished as one man. As a result the only ones left to tell about Elokim's mighty deeds were Bnei Yisrael who were saved in the midst of the sea." Had there been a few Mitzrim who had saved themselves and those Mitzrim had told the rest of the world of their experiences this would have suitably impressed the world. As it was, only Bnei Yisrael who had already recognised Elokim's sovereignty were around to tell the tale. This was not enough to convince the pagans.
ויסע משה את ישראל, Moshe made Yisrael move on, etc. This was the only march which was initiated by Moshe. Every subsequent move occurred at Hashem's initiative.

ויבאו מרתה, They arrived at Marah, etc. Why is this place sometimes referred to as Marah and other times as Maratah? Apparently the original name of the oasis was Maratah and the spring it contained did not have a separate name.

The Torah added: "they could not drink the waters of Marah," meaning that the spring itself was now named Marah because its waters were bitter. The name Marah therefore also became the name of the oasis after Bnei Yisrael had camped there and G'd had shown Moshe how to make the waters of that spring palatable. The words כי מרים הם were an allusion to an experience Bnei Yisrael were going to have.

וילונו העם על משה, The people murmured against Moshe, etc. The Torah criticises the manner in which the people provoked a quarrel. The Torah does not deny the validity of a people asking for drinkable water, i.e. the question: "what are we to drink?" They should have asked for their needs in an appropriate manner.

אם שמוע תשמעו לקול ה׳ אלוקיך, "if you will carefully listen to the voice of Hashem your Elokim, etc." This means that if Bnei Yisrael would hearken to the statutes and social legislation Moshe introduced in the name of Elokim immediately after this experience and they would observe them, they would also merit to listen to His other commandments and hear these commandments directly from Elokim's mouth. [the reference is to the impending revelation at Mount Sinai. Ed.] In Devarim 4,33 Moshe reminded Bnei Yisrael of their experience when he asked rhetorically: "Has any nation ever heard the sound of Elokim's voice out of the fire and remained alive as you have done?" According to Sanhedrin 56 Elokim gave Bnei Yisrael some of the Sabbath legislation as well as the laws of דינים, jurisprudence, while they were at Marah. The words שם ניסהו, "there He tested them," must be understood as a trial preceding the revelation at Mount Sinai. If Bnei Yisrael would prove receptive to the laws revealed at Marah there was reason to believe they would accept the entire Torah at Sinai when the time came.

Actually, the Torah alludes to four distinct commandments here, ללמוד וללמד, לשמור ולעשות, to study the law, to teach it, to observe the prohibitions, and to carry out the aspects demanding action. The words: אם שמוע תשמע allude to the duty to study these laws. The repetition implies the demand that one should commit what one has learned to memory.
