It had become clear only after Bnei Yisrael participated in the sacrifices to the calf that their active participation must have started already at an earlier stage, namely when they were invited to pay obeisance to the calf as their redeemer. G'd therefore told Moshe that participation of Bnei Yisrael in the worshiping of the calf was the result of their agreeing with the people who had said: "these are your gods O Yisrael, etc."

ויאמר ה׳ אל משה, Hashem said to Moshe, etc. The reason this is reported as a separate address by Hashem to Moshe (seing there had been no interruption since Hashem commenced to speak in verse 7) is that the first address was only an explanation of why Moshe had to descend from his lofty spiritual niveau. Now Hashem speaks to Moshe concerning the repercussions Yisrael's conduct will have on their own standing. Had the Torah not inserted the words ויאמר ה׳ at this point, we would have thought that the previous sentence "they have quickly departed, etc." was meant as an introduction to why the people would be punished.

ועתה הניחה לי, "And now, let Me be, etc." The reason Hashem said: "and now," was because He had already tried to put Moshe in a good mood by offering to make an entire new Jewish nation with Moshe as its founding patriarch when He said to him: "and I shall make you a great nation." This promise was designed to silence Moshe into not protesting Hashem's intention to destroy the present Jewish people. Moshe thought to himself that Hashem's promise was hardly any reassurance seeing that what happened to Avraham's descendants was liable to happen to his own descendants with similarly terrible results. This is why Hashem said to Moshe that he should leave Him be only "for now;" Hashem implied that if Moshe would leave Him alone now He would promise Moshe that history would not repeat itself with any of Moshe's descendants if he were to become the founding father of a new Jewish nation. There could be either one of two reasons why history would not repeat itself. 1) Moshe's descendants would be more virtuous than the present generation of Yehudim and they would not succumb to the kind of provocation by Satan that the present Jewish people had succumbed to. 2) Even assuming that the "new" Jewish people would succumb to a situation similar to that facing the present one, Hashem would not again ask Moshe or their leader at that time not to intercede on their behalf. There would always be a chance to nullify any decree of Hashem to destroy the new Jewish people.

A moral-ethical approach to the words הניחה לי would be that it was G'd's way of hinting that if Moshe were to allow G'd a brief moment of anger, i.e. ועתה הניחה לי, there was a chance that his subsequent intercession would prove successful. As soon as the present moment had passed Moshe was invited, so to speak, to intercede on behalf of "his" people. This brief moment had passed while G'd uttered the word ועתה. This is why Moshe immediately began to intercede with prayer.

According to our sages in Bereshit Rabbah 21,6 who say that the word ועתה in Bereshit 3,22 as well as elsewhere always contains an allusion to the need to do תשובה, repentance, G'd hinted to Moshe that it was up to him to do תשובה. Seeing that the entire debacle was due to Moshe's having told the people he would return at the end of forty days he had misled them. He had failed to inform the people that he referred to a return on the forty-first day.

Alternatively, Moshe needed to do תשובה for having accepted the mixed multitude as proselytes at the time without having first consulted Hashem. This is why Hashem referred to the perpetrators of the golden calf as Moshe's people, i.e. שחת עמך. When Hashem said: ועתה, He meant that the time had come for Moshe to become a penitent seeing he had a considerable share in the circumstances which made the golden calf episode possible. Not only this, the episode was to teach the Jewish people not to accept proselytes at the time when the Messiah would come (Yevamot 24). At that time it would be reserved for Moshe to accept the proselytes and thus to make up for the time he had accepted them without authority from Hashem.

הניחה לי ויחר אפי, "leave Me alone so I can become angry, etc." Why did Elokim have to ask Moshe to "leave Him alone?" Had Moshe done anything to prevent Elokim from venting His anger? On the contrary! Moshe had not even commenced to pray on behalf of Bnei Yisrael until later! Besides, the future tense "so that I may vent My anger" suggests that up until that moment Elokim had not even become angry as yet and that He was looking for a pretext to become angry! Since when is it one of Elokim's characteristics to want to become angry? We know that it is Elokim's virtue to squash His anger whenever possible! We have it on the authority of Rabbi Yishmael the High Priest that Elokim was pleased with his prayer asking Him to suppress His anger! (Berachot 7). Perhaps this was precisely Moshe's argument when he remonstrated with Elokim saying: למה יחרה אפך, "why do you want to become angry?" Moshe uses the future tense in this question, suggesting that up until that point Elokim had not shown signs of being angry. At any rate we are faced here with a difficulty in understanding the ways of our Hashem!

The whole matter may become clearer when we recall that the source of anger is an insult felt by one's heart. The degree of insult one experiences is in direct relation to the prominence and high position of the one who is guilty of the insult and the nature of the insult itself. There are two possible remedies which help one overcome the feeling of having been insulted. 1) One may take revenge on the person or persons who have insulted him. 2) One may respond to words of conciliation which puts the insult into its proper perspective.

Inasmuch as the guilty party in this case was Yisrael, the insult could not have been greater seeing that Yisrael was Elokim's chosen people. Elokim Himself had indicated this by saying: "they have departed quickly from the path, etc." i.e. while Yisrael was still My most recently wed bride it has already abandoned Me, its groom, by whoring around. Initially, Elokim felt so strongly about this that He did not think that any of the conventional ways of putting the insult into perspective would be effective and He had to take punitive action to get the feeling out of His system, so to speak. According to our sages in Shemot Rabbah 2,1 it is one of Elokim's virtues that He cannot tolerate seeing His righteous people, His "friends," suffer pain. Accordingly, how could Elokim inflict the pain of destroying His people on Moshe? Had He not waited with the onset of the deluge so that Metushelach, a righteous man and others like him should not witness it (compare Bereshit Rabbah 32,7)? Moreover, according to the Zohar volume 1 page 206 the use of the term נשמה in Bereshit 7,22 indicates that all the few good people, those possessed not only of a נפש, but even of a נשמה (a superior kind of soul), had died prior to the onset of the deluge. We also find in Yeshayahu 57,2 that the righteous person dies on account of the evil (which is to come). The prophet means that Elokim spares the righteous the need to witness the disaster. Surely Elokim was perfectly aware of how Moshe would grieve over the destruction of his people! How could He even contemplate this type of revenge (retribution) for the insult He had suffered at the hands of the Jewish people? Had there ever been someone closer to Elokim than Moshe that he should have to witness such a disaster? When Elokim considered all this and concluded that it would be better for Him to suffer the insult than to allow Moshe to suffer the anguish of seeing his people destroyed, He begged Moshe to allow Him to at least become angry for a moment. He asked Moshe not to be upset at what He asked of him. If Moshe agreed, this would give Elokim an opportunity to first become angry and then regain His composure. He suggested that He would make out of Moshe (his offspring in the future) לגוי גדול; He did not say He would make Moshe himself into גוי גדול. This meant that though Moshe was not at that moment a "great nation," He, Elokim, would see to it that Moshe's soul would possess the additional qualities needed to ensure that his descendants would be greater than the present Jewish people. The word אעשה also implied that Elokim had to undertake a new process in order for future children of Moshe to have the potential implied here.

G'd also wanted to ward off Moshe's argument (not yet voiced) "where is Your promise to the patriarch Avraham, i.e. the גוי גדול, the great nation that You promised he would become?" He used the expression לגוי גדול to paraphrase His promise to Avraham in Bereshit 12,2 suggesting that this very promise would be fulfilled via the descendants of Moshe.

Moshe's answer indicated that he could not allow Hashem to do as He had suggested and that he could not conquer his own anguish even for a moment at what Hashem planned to let him witness. Moshe expressed all this succinctly in the words ויחל משה in verse 11. The Talmud Berachot 32 gives a variety of explanations of the word ויחל, the common denominator of all these explanations being that it is an expression of profound anguish. [The word ויחל is variously connected to חלה to be sick, as connected to חלל, to desecrate, i.e. to violate one's promise; another meaning is the aramaic אחילו, fever or trembling. There are still other interpretations. Ed.] In response to Hashem saying: ויחר אפי, "so that My anger will be hot against them," an argument used by Hashem to explain that He had no alternative if He wanted to get over the insult heaped upon Him, Moshe countered: למה יחרה אפך, "why should You become angry instead of looking for a different method of assuaging Your hurt feelings?" By referring to the Jewish people as בעמך, "against Your people," Moshe suggested that killing the Jewish people would "boomerang," that Hashem would hurt Himself more than He would hurt Bnei Yisrael. After all, You have taken them out of Mitzrayim and thereby made a great name for Yourself amongst mankind. Are You going to let all this go to waste? Why would You give the Mitzrim such satisfaction? Moreover, why do You not remember Your promises to the Patriarchs? When You think about the Patriarchs surely You have reason to be well pleased? Moshe succeeded in his plea as we know from the line וינחם ה׳ על הרעה, "Hashem reconsidered the evil, etc."

למה ה׳ יחרה אפך, "To what purpose, O Hashem, will Your anger burn?" If we go back for a moment to the statement in Shemot Rabbah 42 that only the mixed multitude were involved in the making and worshiping of the golden calf, we had to conclude that Hashem's anger was directed at Bnei Yisrael for not having protested what the mixed multitude were doing. In that case, Moshe's question "Why be mad at Your people?" simply meant that Hashem's anger should have been restricted to the mixed multitude. This suggests that Moshe had made peace with the idea that Hashem would destroy the mixed multitude. Perhaps we can find support for this even in Moshe's words: "whom You have taken out of Mitzrayim?" Seeing that Hashem had not taken the mixed multitude out of Mitzrayim but they had come of their own volition, Hashem's image would not be tarnished if this mixed multitude were to perish! According to the Midrash then we may assume that all the members of the mixed multitude died at that time seeing that even their patron did not speak up on their behalf. Inasmuch as the mixed multitude were seducers, Moshe would have been totally out of order if he had asked for mercy on their behalf especially seeing that he himself was being punished for having accepted them as converts to begin with.

According to the plain meaning of the verse i.e. that Bnei Yisrael themselves made the golden calf and worshiped it, Moshe's argument applied to the part of the people who did not have a direct share in that sin. After all, the Torah reports that all those who had actively participated died. There were three such groups. 1) Bnei Yisrael who did not desist from worshiping the golden calf in spite of witnesses and proper warnings of the consequences were executed by the Leviyim. 2) The people whose sin had been witnessed but who had not been warned died at the hands of Hashem, 3) those who had been warned but whose deed had not been witnessed. They too died at the hands of Hashem. When Hashem said to Moshe that He wanted to destroy the people, He referred to those who were not included in either of the three groups we just mentioned. Moshe's outcry: "Why will Your anger burn against Your people, etc.," was on behalf of the people who did not belong to any of the three groups who had been active participants in the sin. His argument was simply that the sin of omission of not protesting the involvement of the others surely did not warrant extinction! Should they cease to be called "Your people" though they had not rebelled against You?

אשר הוצאת "whom You have taken out of Mitzrayim! He used this argument to refute Hashem's suggestion to make out of his descendants a great nation. Moshe meant that any nation descended from him will not have the experience of the Exodus. If a nation which had this experience nonetheless succumbed to the temptation of the golden calf, surely a nation which lacked that experience cannot be expected to resist such a temptation! You will find that at the beginning of the Decalogue Hashem emphasised the experience of the Exodus as the basis of Bnei Yisrael accepting Him as their Hashem (Shemot 20,2). This shows clearly how pivotal that experience was for the faith in Hashem displayed by the Jewish people, and their willingness to obey His commands. This theme occurs again and again throughout the Torah in connection with Hashem's commandments. One gains the impression that the Torah keeps reminding us that the justification of Hashem demanding fulfilment of His commandments is due almost entirely to the experience of the Exodus. Please refer to what I have written on that verse. When Moshe mentioned Hashem as having taken Bnei Yisrael out of Mitzrayim בכח גדול, "by expending a great deal of energy," he implied that Hashem could not afford to let all of this energy go to waste by destroying the Jewish people.

Seeing that Hashem had refused to associate His name with the people and had referred to them as Moshe's people, i.e. שחת עמך, how could Moshe dare say to Hashem "why would You become angry at Your people?" We must therefore understand that when Moshe referred to the Exodus by saying אשר הוצאת, that at that time He had still called them His people, i.e. אשר.

למה יאמרו הגוים, "Why should the nations be able to say, etc.?" Moshe suggested that it would be a public desecration of Hashem's name to wipe out the Jewish people whom Hashem had referred to in Shemot 4,22 as "My first-born son Yisrael" less than six months previously? It would appear in retrospect that Hashem had orchestrated the Exodus only in order to kill this people in the desert? Once all the nations which served idols realised that serving the one and only Hashem led to disaster they would be confirmed in preferring the various deities which they were in the habit of worshiping. They would conclude that the fact that the Hashem of Bnei Yisrael had not killed them (the Gentiles) for worshiping idols proved that it was an extremely dangerous thing to convert to Judaism and to acknowledge the Hashem in Heaven.

The reason Moshe added the word לאמור was that the Gentiles might not phrase this in these exact words; nonetheless it was clear that they would draw inferences of that nature when they heard what had befallen the Jewish people in the desert. Alternatively, Moshe may have added the word לאמור to show that he knew that this would merely be talk and would not describe the truth; still it was an argument the Gentiles were going to use which it would be difficult to disprove. This misrepresentation of the truth would not be confined to Mitzrayim but would be echoed -לאמור- by all the other nations on earth. There could not be a greater desecration of Hashem's name.

זכור לאברהם, "Remember Avraham, etc." Here Moshe did not refer to Hashem's oath to Avraham to make him into a great nation, etc., a comment Hashem had already replied to earlier. Moshe referred to the sadness which would engulf people when they would hear about what happened. Moshe also argued the merit of the Patriarchs based on Hashem's promise in the Ten Commandments (20,6) that He considered such merits for thousands of generations to those who "loved Him and observed His commandments." Moshe added the words "Your servants, and "You have sworn," in order to give still greater meaning to what Hashem had stated in the Ten Commandments.

וכל הארץ הזאת, "and this whole land, etc." There are many ways of interpreting these words. Some say that they are part of Moshe's words who quotes what G'd had said to the Patriarchs. It is equally possible that they are words spoken by G'd. The meaning of אמרתי would then have to be understood in a sense similar to Yeshayahu 3,10: "declare that the צדיק is good!" Here G'd would be proclaiming the superiority of the land of Yisrael by saying: "I declare that I have elevated the patriarchs by swearing to give such a superior land to their descendants, etc." We can find a parallel to this in Devarim 11,11-12, where the land of Yisrael is described in terms of being a superior land.

וינחם ה׳ על הרעה, "Hashem reconsidered the evil He had said He would do, etc." The meaning of the verse is that there were two reasons why Hashem reconsidered. 1) The decree was evil objectively speaking. 2) It would have resulted in evil for His people.
We may understand this statement also as emphasising the דבר aspect, i.e. what G'd had merely said He would do. If He had sworn to do this, He would not have been able to reconsider an oath.

A further dimension of this statement is that G'd only reconsidered the evil He had said to do, i.e. to wipe out the Jewish people; there were other evil parts which He had not reconsidered, parts involving the sin of the golden calf.

Furthermore, Hashem may only have reconsidered the evil he had said He would do to the people not directly involved in worshiping the calf, those who still were considered His people; those who had worshiped the calf be it with or without witnesses but who believed in it in their hearts would be subject to Hashem's original decision and Hashem punished them by death. Moshe examined some of the people by making them drink of the waters containing the gold dust of the calf, others were executed by the Leviyim.

ויפן וירד משה מן ההר, "Moshe turned around and descended from the Mountain." What is the significance of the Torah reporting Moshe as "turning around," i.e. turning His back on G'd's presence? Is this not something which reflects a lack of respect? Perhaps the fact that the Torah added the superfluous words "from the Mountain" were added to prevent the misconception that Moshe "turned his back on G'd", as it were. He only turned his back on the Mountain. If that were the meaning of the words "from the Mountain," the Torah should have written "Moshe turned away from the Mountain" instead of writing "Moshe turned and descended from the Mountain." Furthermore, why did the Torah have to mention Moshe as "turning around" altogether?

Perhaps the expression "he turned around" signified Moshe's reduced spiritual niveau which made it impossible for him to confront the angels. He therefore moved sideways on the Mountain, much like someone who tries to hide.

We may also understand the word as similar to what we learned in Devarim Rabbah 1, where the Midrash contrasts Moshe's mode of speaking directly to Bnei Yisrael, i.e. "you have sinned," with his speaking to Hashem in the third person "למה יחרה?" The meaning of ויפן, he turned around, then may refer to Moshe's change in attitude as he prepared to face his people.

לוחות העדות, "the Tablets containing the testimony." The word ה־עדות, indicating a unique kind of testimony may be an allusion to the way Elokim Himself had inscribed the Tablets so that the writing could be read from either side, something impossible if they had been inscribed by human hands. Such writing would appear as if it had been written backwards had it been inscribed on one side by a human scribe. The letter ה before the word עדות may also hint at the miraculous way the final letters ס and ם appeared with their respective centers suspended in the air miraculously (Megillah 3). Perhaps these two letters were "proof" i.e. "testimony" that the Tablets had indeed been inscribed by Elokim Himself.

וישמע יהושע, "Yehoshua heard, etc." The expression ברעה needs clarification. What precisely was the "sound" that Yehoshua heard which he interpreted as the sound of war? In order to understand Moshe's response to Yehoshua one has to have prophetic insight.

All of this may be understood in light of a statement in the Talmud Yerushalmi Taanit 4,5 that the righteous are able to distinguish certain sounds as implying either something positive or something negative. This power of aural perception is something G'd has granted to outstanding individuals. When Yehoshua heard the sound which indicated something negative happening, ברעה, he interpreted it as the sound of fighting amongst the people. Alternatively, Yehoshua did not refer to a civil war when he mentioned that he identified the sound as the sound of battle; rather he referred to the struggle between the evil urge and the urge to be good which he perceived as being waged inside Bnei Yisrael at that time. Moshe answered him that this was not how he perceived what he heard. When Moshe said that he did not hear קול ענות גבורה, he meant that he did not perceive the good urge being victorious over the evil urge; when he added that he did not hear the קול ענות חלושה either, he meant that the reason was not merely an inherent weakness amongst Bnei Yisrael; what he heard was קול ענות, a sound of affliction, i.e. that he heard the breaking of the staff of glory which used to be theirs and which had now been broken. The meaning of this is that as opposed to violating one or another of the commandments, something that is apt to occur in the life of every Yehudi from time to time and which weakens a person spiritually, this time they had uprooted all the commandments by becoming guilty of idolatry. This is because according to Chulin 5 the sin of idolatry is equal to violating the entire Torah.

Perhaps the word אנכי which follows the word ענות here is an allusion to the שכינה; it is reminiscent of Devarim 32,18 צור ילדך תשי, that the commission of a sin such a idolatry "weakens" the שכינה. The word שומע refers back to Yehoshua who had said that he heard the sound of battle within the camp. Moshe told Yehoshua that what he heard was the mystical dimension of the breaking apart of the שכינה, so to speak. Shlomo alludes to something like this in Mishlei 10,1 ובן כסיל תוגת אמו, "a foolish son is his mother's sorrow." Having written this, I have found the following statement in the Zohar second volume page 195: "What is the meaning of the word 'ברעה'? It refers to a voice (sound) from the סיטרא אחרא, the "negative part of the emanations." [This is based on the spelling of ברע with the letter ה at the end. Yehoshua is perceived as like the "moon" compared to Moshe, the latter being like the "sun" in our aggadic literature. The "negative emanations" are similarly perceived by kabbalists as being like the "moon" when compared to the positive emanations which are like the "sun." These negative emanations are perceived as having "stolen" the light of the moon which was equal in strength to that of the sun prior to its having had to diminish itself. Yehoshua was therefore especially attuned to these negative emanations. This is why he "beheld" this "voice." Moshe had not heard this voice as he was attuned primarily to the positive emanations, the ones perceived as akin to the "sun." Ed.] Yehoshua reported to Moshe on what he heard immediately.

ויהי כאשר קרב אל המחנה, It was, when he came close to the camp, etc. Our sages have already told us in Megillah 10 that whenever the word ויהי introduces a paragraph this is an allusion to a painful experience. In this instance Shemot Rabbah 46,1 describes that Moshe noted the letters on the Tablets "flying away." This caused us all the subsequent grief our forefathers and we ourselves have experienced ever since, including the experience of death itself. Had the original Tablets survived, every sorrow and calamity would have disappeared from the earth, and the world would have experienced freedom from the angel of death (compare section 41 in that Midrash.) The word ויהי also refers to the anguish experienced by Moshe personally when he saw with his own eyes what was taking place. The word also alludes to the feelings of shame experienced by Bnei Yisrael who felt like a thief who is caught in the act of stealing when they saw Moshe approaching. The word even alludes to the קליפה, the spiritually negative radiations which now bombarded the camp of Bnei Yisrael and which presaged death and destruction. These negative emanations had been called forth by the words: "these are your gods O Yisrael, etc."

כאשר קרב אל המחנה, as he approached the camp. Perhaps the Torah wished to tell us that Moshe espied the calf even before he actually entered the camp. This had to be so in order for the sacred Tablets not to have to share the same domain with the epitome of impurity, the golden calf. When the Torah writes: "and it was as he approached the camp he saw the calf and the dances (or the musical instruments used during dances)," our attention is drawn to the immediacy of Moshe seeing the calf and the activities surrounding it.

וירא את העגל ומחלות, he saw the calf and the musical instruments, etc. Perhaps the Torah describes that with the approach of Moshe the spirit of impurity took fright and flew away so that the calf became inert and lost its ability to utter the words "these are your gods, etc." Even the spirit of impurity which had fashioned the calf unassisted by any artisan or goldsmith departed out of fear of Moshe. The words עגל ומחלות side by side conjure up an image of the calf becoming as inert as the מחלות, the musical instruments, once the spirit which had misled the Jewish people into believing that the calf possessed powers of its own had departed from it.

Alternatively, the Torah uses the wording וירא את העגל instead of וירא העגל, to draw our attention to the fact that Moshe did not only behold the calf but also the spirit of impurity it contained, i.e. את. The righteous have the ability to recognise evil; a person of the stature of Moshe was certainly able to recognise evil when he faced it. According to our rabbis in Tikkunim 142, Moshe asked the calf who had made it to which the calf responded that it had been made by the mixed multitude. Seeing that inert things cannot speak, the meaning of that statement is that Moshe realised that the calf contained the spirit of impurity. When the Torah describes Moshe as seeing the dances, the word את in front of the word מחלות is absent. This lends credence to the statement that Moshe perceived the spirit of impurity as being within the calf.

It is also possible that the Torah wished to inform us that at the time Moshe approached the camp he did not encounter a single person as they were all too ashamed to face him. All Moshe was able to see therefore were the calf and the musical instruments used to accompany the dances.

ויחר אף משה וישלך מידיו את הלוחות, Moshe became very angry and he threw the Tablets from his hands, etc. We need to understand why Moshe took it upon himself to smash the Tablets ignoring the immeasurable damage this would cause to the Jewish people. Clearly he would not have destroyed something unless he was convinced that by the destruction of whatever it was he would perform something infinitely more useful than that which he destroyed. We are told in Avot de Rabbi Natan chapter 2 that Moshe did not shatter the Tablets until told to do so by Hashem. This view is confirmed by Rabbi Meir who cites Devarim 10,5 as support for this view. He derives this from Moshe saying "they remained therein as Hashem had commanded me." If so, we must understand why Hashem withheld the good contained in the Tablets from His people. [the question is appropriate in view of the Torah having told us that Hashem decided not to carry out His plan to destroy the people. Ed.]

We must remember that at the time of the revelation at Mount Sinai any residual pollutant of the original serpent had been expunged from the people as we know from Shabbat 146. This is the reason Hashem prepared for them legislation engraved i.e. charut on the Tablets. The word חרות which we read in the Torah with the vowel kametz under the first letter may also be read with the vowel tzeyreh instead; as a result of this change it means "freedom." The alternate spelling is an allusion to the freedom from the angel of death which the Jewish people had attained as a result of their ready acceptance of Hashem's Torah. Mortality, after all, had only been due to the pollutants with which the original serpent had injected Chavah through her eating of the tree of knowledge. The golden calf episode reversed this process and Bnei Yisrael became infected with something like the original pollutant once more, though not to the same degree as previously. As a result of their idolatry they became mortal once more and a set of laws designed for immortal people was no longer appropriate for them. This is why those Tablets had to be smashed. All of this is based on the opinions that Moshe had not acted of his own accord when he smashed the Tablets.

ויקח את העגל אשר עשו, He took the calf which they had made, etc. The words "which they had made" appear quite superfluous; perhaps the Torah had to mention this according to the view that the golden calf looked like a calf from the front and like a donkey when viewed from the rear as we find in the Zohar volume 2 page 192. If the Torah had written only "he took the calf," I could have understood this as a reference only to the front section of the calf and that Moshe burned only that section of the image. By adding the words: "which they had made," the Torah makes it clear that Moshe burned the entire inert creature.

Perhaps the lesson in these words is similar to the message of the prophet Yirmiyahu in Yirmiyahu, 2,19: "your wickedness itself has become your affliction;" i.e. the sin itself becomes the bane of the person who perpetrated it. By embracing evil, the sin itself destroys those who love it and who hate sanctity. When the Torah speaks of אשר עשו, it refers to the consequences of the act of making the calf. וישק את בני ישראל, he made Bnei Yisrael drink of it. This was designed to open the eyes of the blind and to teach them to hate evil and to love sanctity which implies a love for the good for goodness' own sake.

Furthermore, the Torah may have wanted to inform us about the nature of the evil the two sorcerers had perpetrated. The first evil was that they formed the golden calf, the second that the calf invited the people to worship it when it said: "these are your gods O Yisrael, etc." The Torah tells us that Moshe "took" i.e. seized both these aspects of wickedness the sorcerers had created. The expression לקח as a description of sanctity gaining control over spiritually negative forces, קליפה, is used by the Talmud in Yuma 69 where the members of the Great Assembly are described as seizing the spirit which seduces men into worshiping idols and other sins, and their trying to eliminate it. Moshe did something similar here when he "seized" the spirit of impurity within the golden calf, and burned it. The words וישרוף באש, "he burned it in fire," are far more appropriate when applied to the spirit within the calf than to the calf itself seeing that one cannot "burn" gold. Perhaps this is the mystical dimension of Yeshayahu 11,4 where the prophet describes the Messiah as "killing the wicked with the breath of his lips."

מה עשה לך העם הזה? "What did this people do to you?" Moshe recognised that the making of a cast idol for others is not one of the commandments for which one has to sacrifice one's life rather than to do so under duress. Compare Maimonides' treatise on the laws of idolatry chapter three in which he rules that a person who commits such a sin is punishable only by 39 lashes. If a person performs such a deed under duress he is not punishable at all. If he had not been forced to do what he did under threat of death he is punishable by 39 lashes even if he had not been warned of the consequences of his deed by witnesses acceptable in Jewish law (Makkot 6). Moshe therefore wanted to know the circumstances which caused Aharon to make the calf.

Aharon replied: אתה ידעת את העם הזה כי בדע הוא, "you know from observing the people that they are bent on doing something corrupt." He added that as far as Moshe's assumption that he, Aharon, had made the calf with his own hands was concerned, this was not so. All he had done was to throw the gold into the crucible. The calf emerged totally unassisted. This follows the description in the Tanchuma which we quoted earlier according to which the Mitzri sorcerers Yanus and Yambrus made the calf. Aharon explained that if not for this factor which was beyond his control, there would not have been a sin at all as he had made neither a form nor an image.

Another meaning of Moshe asking: "what have the people done to you?" could be this: "Did they put you under sufficient pressure so that you could legally have agreed to comply?" Moshe asked whether Aharon had correctly contrasted the enormity, חטאה גדולה, of the sin involved before deciding that he did not have to make a martyr of himself by agreeing to do whatever he did. Aharon replied by outlining the circumstances of what had transpired.
כי פרוע הוא, for it was out of control, etc. The Torah means that the people had forfeited the protective cover of the שכינה which had hovered over them since the revelation at Mount Sinai.

כי פרעה אהרון, "for Aharon had let them loose." Perhaps the Torah means that having heard Aharon's answer Moshe was now certain that the fault was entirely the people's seeing that Aharon's part in the debacle had been quite incidental. The real fault lay with the people who had contributed their gold, and the sorcery which had subsequently been performed with that gold. The literal meaning of these words then would be that by his explanation Aharon had let loose an accusation at the people.

לשמצה בקמיהם for a derision among their enemies. Any small measure of an abomination is called שמץ. Our sages in Sanhedrin 102 state that ever since the episode of the golden calf any punishment Bnei Yisrael face for any sin committed since, contains some small part of the punishment which had not been administered at the time they committed that sin. It may also mean that whenever the nations display hostility against the Yehudim one of their arguments of our unworthiness includes a reminder of the sin of the golden calf this nation had become guilty of.

איש את אחיו…ואיש את קרובו. "every man his brother …or his relative." We need to explore why the Torah had to add the words "and each man his relative," seeing the Torah had already authorised the Leviyim to kill even brothers who are the closest relatives. We have to remember that there are different categories of "brothers" whose outlook on life and whose lifestyles may be drastically different from one another although they are the sons of the same parents. On the other hand, there are people who are not at all related to each other by blood-ties and yet share the same outlook on life and the same lifestyle. All of this is due to the origin of the respective souls of these people rather than to the origin of their bodies. There are souls whose roots are very close to each other and who become separated from one another by being assigned to bodies which are far apart from one another. The reverse is true also. This is why Moshe's instructions to the Leviyim had to include both such possibilities.

בני לוי, the members of the tribe of Levi, etc. The Torah did not say that all the Leviyim displayed this loyalty by rallying to Moshe's call. We need to understand why this part of the verse had to be written at all and the Torah was not content with reporting the Leviyim's response to Moshe's call in verse 26 when all of them are reported as rallying around their leader. Perhaps the Torah wanted to stress that no one except the Leviyim acted as executioners at the behest of Moshe. Verse 26 in which all the Leviyim are reported as rallying around Moshe would not have made it plain that Moshe had charged only the Leviyim with the task of being executioners. That verse only told us that all the Leviyim responded to Moshe's original call. We could have thought that some Bnei Yisrael responded in addition to all of the Leviyim. The Torah had to make clear that only Leviyim actually carried out Moshe's instructions. The emphasis in "the Leviyim did what Moshe said" is not so much on the Leviyim who did not do so but on the absence of any of the members of other tribes being prepared to kill idolators.

כדבר משה, in accordance with the word of Moshe. The Torah emphasises that Moshe's word alone sufficed to prompt those Leviyim to take such drastic action against the active idolators. It could also mean that they did so without delay as soon as Moshe had finished giving them their instructions.

מלאו ידכם היום, "consecrate yourselves this day, etc." It is not clear what the word "consecrate" is supposed to mean in this context. If it referred to the matter of killing one's relatives, this had already occurred. It should have been reported prior to the Leviyim carrying out Moshe's orders.

I believe we can explain this verse as being in its proper place. The Torah felt that inasmuch as these Leviyim had carried out executions with their own hands, something that certainly is not characteristic of righteous people, their image had to be restored. We have learned in Makkot 7 that any court which carries out a death sentence once in seven years (according to some even once in seventy years) is labelled as "a murderous court." In this instance the Leviyim killed about 3,000 people in a single day. There was a fear that their souls could have been tarnished by the experience seeing that though what they had done was perfectly legal it might leave a residue of mercilessness or a streak of cruelty in their character. In order to reassure both them and the people, Moshe the man of Elokim, told them to "consecrate their hands." This was not a commandment but a reassurance that by the very act of carrying out the task allocated to them they had consecrated themselves to the service of Hashem. Not only did their action not hint at a character deficiency in them, but, on the contrary, it reflected that they were spiritually very enlightened. The proof was that they did not protest having to sacrifice their own sons or close relatives which put them in a category similar to that of Avraham at the time he was willing to offer up Yitzchak. Elokim testified that Avraham had reached the pinnacle of perfection after he had demonstrated that he had not withheld Yitzchak (Bereshit 22,12). Elokim had given Avraham a double blessing at that time (Bereshit 22,17). Moshe assured the Leviyim that they too were recipients of a similar blessing by Elokim as a reward for what they had done, i.e. ולתת עליכם היום ברכה.

Moshe was very precise in describing this blessing as עליכם, which implied something additional, instead of saying לכם. He told the Leviyim that not only was Hashem's blessing not required to restore a character defect which had been revealed when they acted as mass executioners, but there had not been a character defect in the first place, and He now added a further positive dimension to their respective characters by granting them this blessing. We may view the whole episode as similar to an orchard in which the trees have to be pruned in order to assure that the remaining branches develop more successfully. The house of Yisrael has frequently been compared to a vineyard (Psalms, 80,9 et al). When Moshe spoke of the blessing that Hashem would bestow עליכם, "upon you," the meaning of עליכם is "thanks to you," thanks to what you have done, the entire Jewish people will experience such a blessing. It was not the Leviyim who had been deficient but the people. By removing the superfluous members of the Jewish people, the Leviyim had assured the successful development of the remaining branches of the trees in that orchard. When we had previously quoted the Talmud which characterised a court that carried out death-sentences as "murderous," the circumstances described in the Talmud do not match what happened here at all, for two reasons. 1) The Leviyim (read court) executed their beloved ones. This demonstrated that their love for Hashem was greater than their love for their errant family members. 2) Failure to carry out these sentences would have condemned the whole nation to destruction at the hands of Hashem. The executioners therefore were the life savers of the people, not "murderous." Hashem's anger abated only as a result of their action.

חטא העם הזה, "This nation has committed a very grave sin, etc." It is possible that with these words Moshe alluded to something we have learned in Sotah 3, that no one commits a sin unless his brain had first malfunctioned, i.e. that he was out of his mind. This represents a defect in his spiritual life-force, his נפש. By saying חטא, Moshe meant that the people's spiritual makeup had lacked an essential ingredient. This was the reason that they made a molten image for themselves. This is one of the arguments man will use after death when he faces His Maker and has to account for his sins in this life. He will claim that when he committed a sin he was not of sound mind. Although he will be punished, seeing he himself was the cause of being of unsound mind, his punishment will not be as severe as if he had been of perfectly sound mind at the time he comitted the sin.

Another thought Moshe may have had in mind when he formulated these words is connected to the tradition (Kidushin 40) that when man is punished for idolatry he is punished for his idolatrous thoughts alone. When Moshe spoke of the people having committed a grave sin without specifying the nature of that sin, he referred to the idolatrous thoughts the people had entertained. As far as their sin in deed was concerned, Moshe spelled this out by adding: "they have made golden deities for themselves."

ועתה אם תשא חטאתם "And now, if You are prepared to forgive their sin, etc." We have to understand this wording as corresponding to a statement in Bereshit Rabbah 21,6 according to which the word עתה is always used as related to repentance. Moshe argued that seeing Bnei Yisrael had already repented, they qualified for forgiveness.

אם תשא חטאתם "if You forgive their sin, etc." Why did Moshe leave the second half of the sentence unfinished? Perhaps we must understand Moshe as saying: "and now," seeing that Bnei Yisrael have already done תשובה, i.e. they have done their part, it is up to You Hashem to do Your part. Moshe did not know if Hashem would accept repentance seeing the sin was so grave. This is why he did not complete the verse, waiting for Hashem to complete the other half of the sentence.

ואם אין מתני נא מספרן אשר כתבת "and if not, please erase me from the book You have written." A broker is entitled to a commission for all the deals he is instrumental in concluding between two parties. Inasmuch as Moshe had "brokered" many deals between Hashem and Yisrael of which Bnei Yisrael's acceptance of Hashem's Torah was not the least, he was certain that his part in all this had been duly recorded in Hashem's Book of records. He argued that if Hashem were not to forgive the people He would have to erase all the merits Moshe had acquired thus far and which had been recorded in that Book. His own merits, after all, had only been achieved through his association with the Jewish people. Hashem answered him that his reasoning was faulty; He would erase only the previously recorded merits of the sinner from His Book. The merits which had been acquired through someone's association with someone else would certainly not be negatively affected through sins committed subsequently by that third party.

Moshe's argument can also be understood in light of the Zohar volume 3, page 273 that all the souls of the generation of Bnei Yisrael travelling through the desert were "branches" of Moshe's soul. If Hashem were not to forgive the sins of Bnei Yisrael, the effect on Moshe's own soul would be devastating. This is why he urged Hashem to "wipe me out from Your Book." Hashem answered him that only the branches of his soul would be damaged by the sins their bodies committed, not the "trunk (i.e. root) of their souls."

Another meaning of Moshe's words may be that he told G'd that he himself had been guilty of many errors such as recorded in Shemot 5,22 when he had accused G'd of dealing harshly with the Jewish people. Apparently, G'd had forgiven him his errors else He would have to erase him too from His Book as his sin too was unforgivable. G'd answered Moshe that it was the nature of the sin of Bnei Yisrael,- "they sinned against Me," -which made it impossible to accept repentance without decreeing punishment. Idolatry is a sin against G'd's Essence. It cannot go unpunished even when the guilty have been truly penitent.

The entire dialogue between Moshe and Hashem concerned only the timing of the forgiveness. Moshe wanted Hashem to display forgiveness at once so that the generation of Bnei Yisrael who had committed this sin could still remain inscribed in the Book of the Righteous. As far as Hashem eventually forgiving the Jewish people was concerned, he had no doubts about that. It would certainly occur not later than the Day of Atonement. Moshe chose his words very carefully when he spoke about מספרך אשר כתבת, "from the Book which You have written." Hashem in the Heavens has three Books. One contains the names of the righteous, another contains the names of the wicked people on earth; the third contains names of people who are considered "borderline" cases. The three Books are open in front of Hashem on New Year's Day. Hashem personally inscribes the names of the "righteous," the deserving people in the first Book. This is why Moshe referred to that Book as "Your Book." He had to add the words "which you have inscribed," as the suffix "your" Book would not make clear whether Hashem ever reviews anything written in that Book. After all, seeing the whole universe belongs to Hashem, each Book in Heaven would certainly also be described as "Your Book."

Rosh Hashanah 16 explains the words מספרך as referring to the Book in which the righteous are listed; the words אשר כתבת refer to the Book in which the borderline cases are recorded; according to the Talmud (Kidushin 40) one must always view oneself as being a borderline case, as if the next act one performs could tilt the scales of the world either towards "guilty" or towards "innocent." Berachot 61 tenders similar advice. In view of the foregoing, Moshe considered himself as a בינוני, "a borderline case" just like every other Yehudi. If G'd were not to forgive the Jewish people, which would result in a diminution of his own merits, Moshe himself would automatically lose his place in the Book of the בינונים and would become part of the Book in which the names of the wicked appear.

Still another way of understanding this verse is that Moshe argued that his own standing would become that of a righteous person if G'd were to find Bnei Yisrael as righteous, seeing most of his own merits derived from them. If G'd were to fail to forgive Bnei Yisrael, Moshe would himself carry the burden of the sins of Bnei Yisrael as any merits he had acquired due to his efforts on their behalf would be considered as null and void or even worse. He would have been better off if he had never accepted the task of leading the Jewish people.

Another aspect of Moshe's argument is that it is part of his response to Hashem's offer to make a new Jewish nation out of him after Hashem had destroyed the present generation of Yehudim. Moshe simply told Hashem that if He were not willing to forgive the Jewish people now, he for his part would prefer to be wiped out of Hashem's Book rather than become the founder of what would in effect be a substitute Jewish nation. The underlying thought here is that a) a threat by Hashem not accompanied by an oath remains reversible, whereas an oath announcing retribution is irreversible. b) By the same token a promise by Hashem that He will do something perceived as good, as desirable, is irreversible even if it was a conditional promise (compare Makkot 11). Accordingly, when Hashem had promised to make a new nation out of Moshe, this had been recorded in Hashem's "Book," a book known as the Sefer Hayashar. Moshe's prayer then was that Hashem should cancel the entry which contained the promise to make a new nation out of his offspring. Hashem told Moshe that He would indeed not abrogate the promise to the Patriarachs concerning the future of their offspring while at the same time He would not retract the promise He had made to Moshe. We find that He fulfilled His promise to make a nation out of Moshe in Chronicles I 23, 14-18 which concludes with the statement: "the descendants of Rechaviah kept multiplying." Berachot 7 claims this means that there were more than 600,000 of Moshe's descendants.

אשר עשה אהרן which Aharon had made. What was the Torah's purpose in making this statement at this point? Perhaps Hashem wanted us to know that Bnei Yisrael were punished for causing Aharon to become the innocent maker of the golden calf. Hashem deals severely with anyone who causes a great and holy man such as Aharon to become involved in the performance of a sin.

Alternatively, the Torah wanted to ward off any accusation anyone had levelled against Aharon who was only technically the maker of the golden calf, and to place the blame where it belonged. The fact that G'd smote the people for a calf which Aharon had made, is evidence that G'd considered the people as having made the calf.

לך עלה מזה, "go and ascend from this place, etc." The mention of an "ascent" is significant. Perhaps the Torah alludes to Shabbat 88 where we are told that Moshe appropriated for himself the jewelry Bnei Yisrael stripped off themselves. [That "jewelry" was always perceived as being spiritual, such as the phylacteries. Ed.] This is alluded to here by the use of the word עלה in addition to לך. The apparently superfluous word אתה, "you," further supports the idea that the Torah speaks about an ascent by Moshe which signified a spiritual dimension. The spiritual ascent was limited to Moshe, i.e. אתה, as distinct from the people. As far as the people were concerned, G'd's instruction was only: לך, "go on."

לאמור, "to say, etc." When the Torah reported communications from Hashem to the Patriarchs, such communications did not usually involve לאמור, i.e. that they were to be passed on to others. The Torah wishes to remind us that whenever Hashem had spoken to the Patriarchs promising to give the Holy Land to their descendants, such promises were לאמור, i.e. they were meant to be relayed by the Patriarchs to their children, etc.

ושלחתי לפניך מלאך, "and I will send an angel ahead of you, etc." It is clear from this verse that up until now G'd had meant for Moshe personally to lead the children of Yisrael into the Holy Land and to distribute it to them. We have a line in Shemot 6,1 where G'd told Moshe: עתה תראה "now you will see," and many commentators understood this to mean that Moshe would be a witness only to the Exodus from Mitzrayim but not to the conquest of the land of Kenaan. Perhaps G'd had cancelled that decree in consideration of how Moshe had interceded on behalf of the Jewish people, putting his own future on the line.

פן אכלך בדרך, "lest I consume you on the way." There is no comparison between someone who angers his teacher while in his teacher's presence to someone who takes advantage of the teacher's absence to anger him. בדרך, "on the way." This is a hint that the announcement that "only" an angel will accompany the Jewish people would not apply at all times and in all circumstances. When Yisrael would be in a city, i.e. in a relatively safe environment, G'd Himself would be near them (compare Yeshayahu 26,1).

According to the Kabbalists the desert is the home of Samael who succeeded on several occasions to overpower and kill Yehudim who lacked G'd's protection due to their share in the sin. The Zohar volume 2 page 157 expands on that theme when commenting on the words המדבר הגדול והנורא in Devarim 1,17. It uses that verse as proof of how dangerous it is to be בדרך, "on the way."

ודבר ה׳ אל משה פנים אל פנים, "and Hashem spoke with Moshe face to face." The message of this verse is that the intimacy between Moshe and Hashem was in direct proportion to the preparation Moshe made to welcome Hashem's presence. This teaches each of us that the attainment of sanctity is in direct proportion to the efforts we make to attain it.

כאשר ידבר איש אל רעהו, "as a man speaks to his friend." We understand this simile as emphasising the word רעהו, "his friend." We find a similar thought in Mishlei 27,19: "as face to face [is reflected] in water, so man's heart [will be reflected by his counterpart]." Shlomo speaks of a mental telepathy between the hearts of people who do not even see each other but perceive whether their counterpart loves them or hates them. The relationship between man and invisible Hashem is based on something deeper than the exterior sense of sight. The heart senses the attitude of its opposite number. If someone prepares to love his fellow man the heart of his fellow man responds to such invisible feelings. Alternatively, the meaning is that just as his "friend" will not love him unless he has reciprocated the feeling of love, so is Hashem's attitude to us. If one wishes to gauge one's standing in the eyes of Hashem one needs only to examine one's own attitude towards Hashem and His service. If one feels the urge to serve Hashem and delights in doing so, this is proof that Hashem relates to such a person with love.

ראה אתה אומר אלי, "See, You are saying to me, etc." Moshe refers to the fact that on the one hand he was the leader (messenger) who was charged with leading Bnei Yisrael towards the land of Kenaan, whereas on the other hand Hashem had just told him that He would send an additional supernatural messenger, an angel, to lead Bnei Yisrael. Moshe wanted to know more about the nature of this supernatural messenger that would accompany Bnei Yisrael. This is why he said: ואתה לא הודעתני את אשר תשלח עמי, "You have not told me whom You are going to send with me." Moshe made his consent to the new arrangement dependent on knowing more about the nature of that angel. In the event that Hashem would tell him that his consent was not needed, Moshe added: ואתה אמרת ידעתיך בשם, "You have said 'I know you by name,' meaning that you have elevated me beyond the level of the Patriarchs (compare Shemot 6,3). He implied that his status of being familiar with the attribute י־ה־ו־ה was such that he was entitled to be consulted. The word ידעתיך in this verse corresponds to the word נודעתי in Shemot 6,3.

Moshe quoted something Hashem had said to him: וגם מצאת חן בעיני "you have also found favour in My eyes," as additional proof that he expected Hashem to consult him about any new arrangements. We find in Yalkut Shimoni item 173 (on Parshat Shemot) that during the dialogue between Hashem and Moshe at the burning bush, Hashem showed Moshe part of the future including Rabbi Akiva expounding the Torah and its intricacies such as the meaning of the various "crowns" on top of some of the letters. Moshe was so impressed that he suggested to Hashem to send Rabbi Akiva as the redeemer of the Jewish people instead of himself. Hashem had answered him at that time that He specifically wanted Moshe to fulfil that role. The Midrash obviously understood this as proof that Moshe more than anyone else had found favour in His eyes. The upshot of the allegorical conversation is that Moshe realised that although Rabbi Akiva was superior to him intellectually, Hashem preferred him for other reasons. He was correct in interpreting this as proof that he had found favour in the eyes of Hashem. [I believe that the reason the author quotes the story in the Yalkut is because the Torah did not previously report Hashem telling Moshe that he had found favour in the eyes of Hashem. Ed.] As a result of all these considerations Moshe asked Hashem to reveal more to him about His attributes.

ואדעך למען אמצא חן, "in order that I will know You and continue to find favour in Your eyes." Seeing that it is not good manners for a servant to tell his master that he wants to get to know him better, Moshe added the word למען, "for the sake of, etc.;" he explained that his request was not for his own satisfaction but in order for him to be a more effective leader of his people. This is what he meant when he referred to "finding favour in Your eyes."

וראה כי עמך הגוי הזה, "and consider that this nation is Your people." Moshe carried on this conversation with Elokim in complete privacy. He therefore reminded Elokim that the souls of the Jewish people were part of Elokim Himself, as I have explained in Devarim 32,9 on the words: כי חלק ה׳ עמו, "for His people are a part of Elokim." Elokim Himself also alluded to this in Shemot 20,20 when He said: "I am Hashem your Elokim." I have explained this more thoroughly in that context. When Moshe said: וראה, he referred to this as a known fact, implying that inasmuch as there was something divine about the Jewish people, how could Elokim despise something that was itself divine?

ויאמר פני ילכו, "He said: 'My presence will go with you.'" Many commentators have addressed themselves to these verses. I believe the correct approach to these verses must be based on a comment in Tikkunim 18 that the Torah refers to the שכינה as פני ה׳, seeing this is the aspect of Hashem visible to the Celestial Beings. This is also the allusion contained in the words of Shemot 23,15 ולא יראו פני ריקם, "they shall not see My Face (while) empty-handed." In our verse Hashem is responding to Moshe's arguments and informs him that He Himself will go with him as His attribute פני השם, i.e. the שכינה. Concerning the matter of Moshe having reservations about such an arrangement, Hashem added: והניחותי לך, "I will give you rest."

Hashem also meant that He would allow an extra-terrestrial light to rest on Moshe, one that would not fade; at the same time whatever degree of spiritual light Moshe had enjoyed thus far would continue, although seen from Yisrael's vantage point the Divine Presence שכינה would be perceived as preceding the people on their journeys. This was an aspect of Hashem's attribute of דין, Justice, as is evident from the name with which Hashem identified Himself here. [I believe that having said that the expression פני השם referred to the way Hashem is manifest in Heaven, the author concludes that this is an aspect of דין, seeing there is no need for the attribute of Mercy in the Celestial Regions. Ed.] Moshe responded to this offer by saying: "If Your presence will not go with me," in verse 15.

ואם אין פניך הולכים, "Unless Your face will go, etc." Moshe was not satisfied with Hashem's previous offer and said that unless Hashem's face would go with them as of now the people would be lost, and there was no point in even beginning their ascent towards the Holy Land. His reasoning was that the only way he could be certain that he had indeed found favour in Hashem's eyes was the method employed by Hashem in accompanying the Jewish people. He referred to Yisrael's distinction of Hashem relating to them as the Attribute represented by His Ineffable Name. Moshe was dissatisfied that only he and not the entire people should be the beneficiaries of the "great light" which Hashem had promised to bestow on Moshe in verse 14. [The author appears to feel that the fact that Hashem did not tell Moshe in verse 14 that His Attribute would walk with the people instead of ahead of the people, made Moshe refuse the offer. Ed.] He prayed for Hashem to accompany the people as His attribute of the Ineffable Name, i.e. as the attribute of Mercy. Hashem agreed to this request also when He said: "I will also carry out this matter which you have spoken of for you have found favour in My eyes." Hashem was careful to let Moshe know that His consent was due to His fondness of Moshe, not because of His being fond of the people.

כי מצאת חן בעיני ואדעך בשם. "for you have found favour in My eyes and I have become intimate with you by My revealing to you My attribute י־ה־ו־ה." When Moshe had previously referred to his having found favour in Hashem's eyes he had reversed the relationship of his finding favour and his being granted an insight into the meaning of the Ineffable Name (verse 12). The Torah revealed here that the revelation of the meaning of the attribute of the name י־ה־ו־ה was the mark of the highest degree of finding favour in Hashem's eyes. After all, even Noach had found favour in Hashem's eyes (Bereshit 6,8) but Hashem's attribute י־ה־ו־ה had not been revealed to him.

The Torah also wanted to make it abundantly clear that the reason G'd had revealed this most elusive attribute of His to Moshe was because he had found favour in His eyes. There was a causal relationship between these two experiences. This relationship had not been recognisable when Moshe referred to this in verse 12. If not for the present verse, we would have assumed that one could become privy to the revelation of G'd's supreme attribute without first having found favour in His eyes.

הראני נא את כבודך. "Please show me Your glory." While it is true that our sages in the Mechilta on Shemot 15,2 have said that Bnei Yisrael became privy to visions not even granted to the prophet Yecheskel when they stood on the beaches of the sea of reeds. We have already heard that Hashem spoke with Moshe "face to face," and these visions were only of "Hashem being a consuming fire." When Hashem told Aharon and Miriam that He had revealed Himself to Moshe far more clearly than to them (Bamidbar 12,7), this referred to a level below that which Moshe aspired to now when he asked to see Hashem's glory in our verse. Moshe perceived that the time was opportune for him to ask to be granted still further insights and this is why he now chose to ask.

אני אעביר כל טובי על פניך, "I will make all My goodness pass before you, etc." G'd referred to all His "positive" attributes which he employs for the benefit of His creatures. When G'd added the words על פניך, this is the reason for G'd doing what He said He was about to allow Moshe to perceive. Moshe's פניך, is a reference to the manner in which Moshe had achieved the intimacy with G'd thus far, as we explained earlier.

וקראתי בשם השם לפניך, "and I will proclaim the name of G'd before you." G'd announced to Moshe that He would "parade" each of His attributes before him identifying them by name; it is possible, that G'd meant that He would explain to Moshe that all these attributes were in fact part of the INEFFABLE name. There is no greater revelation man can experience than to have all this explained to him by means of his sense of hearing.
When G'd added: וחנותי את אשר אחון, "I will be gracious to whom I choose to be gracious to," this was a hint that Moshe's timing to ask for such revelations was particularly appropriate.

ויאמר לא תוכל לראות, He said: "you are not able to see, etc." G'd meant that it was not He who withheld visual insights from Moshe, it was simply that being a mortal human being, a composite of flesh and spirit, made such a thing impossible. This is why G'd added the word וחי, "and remain alive," to explain to Moshe that because G'd wanted Moshe to remain alive He could not grant his wish at this time. This would correspond to the thoughts expressed by the Psalmist when he said: (Tehillim 84,11) "better a day in Your courtyard than a thousand (days in Your palace)."

Alternatively, we may understand this verse to mean that even if man were חי, i.e. a perfectly righteous individual, immortal, G'd cannot be "seen" by man. We would have to understand the word חי in the sense it is used in Shmuel II 23,20 where Benayahu son of Yehoyadah is described as בן איש חי, "a perfectly righteous individual." The letter ו at the beginning of the word וחי in our verse indicates that it adds something to what had already been stated, i.e. the inability to "see."

Still another way of understanding the words כי לא יראני האדם וחי, is that even after death it is impossible for man to "see" Hashem. Hashem asks: How can you expect to "see" Hashem while still alive? Whatever "light" the righteous will be able to "see" in the hereafter does not come close to what you Moshe are asking of Me at this time.

וראית את אחורי, "you will see My back, etc." The essence of G'd is, of course, not divisible into "front" and "back." G'd is aware of the desire of all His creatures to "see" how His light spells the continued existence of His universe. At the same time it is impossible by definition that any creature can behold this light as it would spell its doom. What did G'd do? He surrrounded His Essence with a kind of "curtain" or screen in order to diffuse the light which would otherwise have proved too blinding. The creation of such a screen created the impression in the beholder that there is something in "front" and something at the "back" of such a screen. When we look at man who is composed of spirit and body, we peceive his body as his "back," and his spirit as his "front", or "face." The "light" that G'd's Essence has made accessible to the spiritually most advanced human being is called "back," whereas the "light" He has screened out is called "front" as it is beyond the screen. This is what G'd meant when He said: "you will see "My Back" but you cannot see "My Face."

It is also possible that the very mention by Hashem of His "face" immediately after mention of His "back," i.e. אחורי ופני, indicated that even the part of Him that He described as "My Back" contained a "face;" however, Hashem had arranged that only the rear of that two sided spirit or "light" would be visible so as to provide the prophet with some idea of when he faced a Divine presence.

The word אחורי may have been employed to indicate that Moshe would be very close to perceiving Hashem's Essence, that He did not "hide" behind multiple screens. If there had remained several "screens" between Hashem's Essence and Moshe, Hashem would have spoken of Achorey Achoray, and not simply of Achoray. Any intelligent and sincere servant of Hashem will make only minimum eye contact with his Creator [in other words not look at Heaven beseechingly while engaged in prayer. Ed.] when bowing down during prayer.

ה׳ ה׳ קל רחום וחנון, "Hashem, Hashem, Hashem is merciful and gracious;" Our sages in Rosh Hashana 17 explain the repetition of this attribute of Mercy as the difference between invoking this attribute before man has sinned and invoking it after he has sinned. The Rosh, (Rabbi Asher ben Yechiel) questions why man should be in need of mercy prior to his having sinned. He answers that seeing Hashem is already aware that man will sin at some future date, man is already in need of Hashem's attribute of Mercy. He suggests an alternative meaning according to which the Torah speaks of someone who contemplates idolatry only with his mind without as yet committing an overt act of any kind. Hashem's attribute of Mercy would "call out" to such a person to desist before he performed a punishable idolatrous deed. I must confess that I cannot understand either of the Rosh's two explanations. If man is in need of the attribute of Mercy because of penalties for sins not yet committed, why did Hashem create him in the first place, seeing He was aware that he would sin? Was Hashem really prepared to judge man for sins he had not committed so that He had to invoke the attribute of Mercy on man's behalf? Concerning a person who contemplates the sin of idolatry, but who had not yet committed an overt act, why would he be considered as not yet having committed a sin seeing that when it comes to idolatry even the intent makes one liable to punishment?

I believe that a person is in need of Hashem's attribute of Mercy even before he has committed a sin unless he had acquired merits through the performance of Hashem's commandments. The merit acquired by performance of positive commandments entitles a person to have Hashem invoke the attribute of Mercy on his behalf. Examination of Devarim 11,13 will demonstrate my point. The Torah writes: "It will be as a result of your hearkening diligently to My commandments ….and perform them,…I will give the rain of your land in its season…and you will gather in your harvest, etc." This shows that as a result of performing a good deed one will become the recipient of Hashem's goodness. If, on the other hand, a person has been prevented from performing Hashem's commandments by circumstances beyond his control he will neither receive the reward promised by the Torah for the performance of the commandments nor will he be punished for non-performance. How then would Hashem's Mercy become evident? This is why the Torah refers to Hashem's Mercy as something that needs to be invoked even before a person commits a sin. This "Mercy" will assure such a person of a harvest, etc., even if he had been unable to establish a claim to Hashem's goodness. In addition, Hashem promised Moshe that He would invoke His attribute of Mercy even on behalf of people guilty of sinful conduct.

Hashem informed Moshe of another aspect of the attribute of Mercy by telling him [by means of the repetition Ed.] that a sinner would not forfeit any of Hashem's goodness which he had been in line for before he sinned, and before Hashem invoked His attribute of Mercy on his behalf. This thought has helped me make peace with the fact that we observe the wicked who have been spared through Hashem's attribute of Mercy continue to prosper to the same degree as they prospered before Hashem invoked the attribute of Mercy on their behalf.

ילך נא ה׳ בקרבנו, "let Hashem go in our midst, etc." How could Moshe say this seeing Hashem had told him in 33,3 that He would not go up in their midst precisely because they were a stiff-necked people? Here Moshe tries to use the stiff-necked nature of the people as a reason for asking Hashem to go up in their midst? In 33,3 Hashem had warned Moshe that if He were to go up in the midst of the people this would lead to their destruction. How could Moshe take such a chance? Another difficulty in our verse is why Moshe had to ask for something Hashem had already been prepared to do as we know from 33,17: "I will also do this thing for you?"

The matter will become clearer when we look at the names for G'd Moshe used in the various verses. In our verse here Moshe requests that G'd should go up in the midst of the people in His manifestation as א־ד־נ־י, whereas in 33,3 G'd had warned Moshe that He would not go in their midst in His manifestation as י־ה־ו־ה. At first glance this reinforces our problem seeing that I have written that Moshe wanted G'd to accompany Bnei Yisrael in His capacity as the attribute of Mercy, and here he seems to request a harsher attribute of G'd.

Perhaps the insights Moshe had gained after Hashem had revealed to Him His Thirteen Attributes had led to Moshe's appreciation that if Hashem were to apply only His attribute of Mercy to the people, ignoring the attribute of Justice completely, the people would never survive the long trip because they were so stiff-necked [and would commit too many sins for Hashem to overlook permanently. Ed.] Moshe therefore reconsidered and asked Hashem to provide the kind of presence which would not allow the sinners to count on His Mercy as if it were an inexhaustible attribute. He expressed this by saying ילך נא א־דני, i.e. a mixture of Mercy and Justice. He did so in order for the occasional sinners not to become confirmed sinners when they would perceive Hashem as waiving punishment for their sins. When Moshe added: וסלחת לעונינו, וג׳ he asked for the appropriate attribute of Hashem, i.e. the addition of the attribute of Mercy to the attribute of Justice he had mentioned first. We observe something similar in Shemot 23,21, where Hashem had explained that an angel represents only the attribute of Justice and cannot temper Justice with Mercy. Moshe now realised how important it was to be under the guidance of both attributes of Hashem simultaneously.
ונחלתנו, "and take us to be Your inheritance." Moshe asked that G'd never exchange the Jewish people for some other people but that they should remain His "inheritance" forever.

שמר לך, "Observe for yourself, etc.!" How does the term "observe" apply to the subject matter of this verse? If the Torah refers to the commandment Hashem is about to reveal as something Moshe is to "observe" as Rabbi Avraham ibn Ezra suggests, why would Hashem select this commandment of not concluding a covenant with the seven Kenaani nations rather than any other of the many commandments as something for Moshe to be very careful about? After all, Moshe had already been told that it was not he who would conquer these nations What point was there in warning him specifically not to conclude such a covenant?

Perhaps there is a lesson here about how true repentance works. Seeing Bnei Yisrael had become guilty of worshiping an idol, the תקון, rehabilitation, for such a sin required that they destroy everything even remotely connected with idolatry if they wanted to attain complete atonement for their sin. This required that they cultivate a strong abhorrence for all forms of idolatry starting already now, long before they would displace the idolatrous Kenaani and destroy any vestiges of idol worship the Kenaani had been guilty of. The verb שמר may perhaps be understood in the sense that Yaakov used it when he heard Yosef's dream with the sun, the moon, and the eleven stars bowing down to him. At that time (Bereshit 37,11), Yaakov had begun to look forward to the way this dream would become fulfilled. Bnei Yisrael (including Moshe) were now meant to look forward to the time when they could carry out the commandment Hashem was about to give them.

Alternatively, Hashem implied that as long as Bnei Yisrael had not become guilty of making a molten image He would not have bothered to command them to keep a physical and cultural distance from the Gentile nations and their abominations. Seeing they themselves had become victims of the impulse to worship an idol, Hashem now had to give the people this law in order to ensure that they would not again be tempted to succumb to idolatry. The words שמר לך, are a reminder that the law was due to something Bnei Yisrael themselves had done.

A moral-ethical approach sees in the word לך "for yourself" a reference to Moshe; Hashem hinted to Moshe that the words: "I am going to drive out before you the nations, etc." are not a reference to what would happpen in the immediate future, but refer to the distant future, to messianic times. It corresponds to the statement of our sages in Bamidbar Rabbah 19,13 which describes the Yehudim (the generation which perished in the desert) as saying that: "the same Moshe who has redeemed us from Mitzrayim will redeem us in the future." Hashem told Moshe to be looking forward to that time, i.e. שמר לך. You may find support for this interpretation when you consider that the promise contained in the line "I will drive out before you, etc.," has never been fulfilled during the time Bnei Yisrael travelled in the desert.

פן תכרות ברית, "lest you enter enter into a covenant, etc." The Torah stresses that although the Kenaani would be prepared to accept the seven Noachide laws as a pre-condition to such a covenant, Bnei Yisrael must not conclude such a covenant with them. The reason is that these nations would display an irresistible temptation to engage in idolatry with their former deities as they do not truly believe in G'd, a fact which is evident to every student of Kabbalah. וזבחו לאלוהיהם, "they will offer meat-offerings to their deities," and they will invite you to participate in such meals. We have been taught in Avodah Zarah 8 that a Yehudi is considered as having participated in such a meal from the moment he has accepted the invitation to participate based on the word מזבחו. In chapter four of his treatise Hilchot Shechitah, Maimonides prohibits Yehudim from eating meat slaughtered by a Gentile even if he does not worship idols and the slaughter was performed under the supervision of a Yehudi. G'd detests the fact that a Gentile slaughters a beast. [Maybe in order to qualify for the right to kill animals for food, man must have demonstrated his superiority to the beast by observing at least the seven Noachide commandments. Ed.]

את חג המצות תשמור, "you are to observe the festival of unleavened bread." The reason that the Torah chose to mention this commandment at this point is the need for Bnei Yisrael to rehabilitate themselves from the sin of idolatry. The Zohar volume 4 page 40 states that the spiritual equivalent of leavened matter is an alien deity. This is the reason G'd has so insistently and repeatedly warned us about keeping or eating leavened matter on the festival of Passover. In this instance, G'd instructed us concerning the observance of all the festivals. The reason may be that all the major festivals are rooted in the Exodus experience of the Jewish people. Inasmuch as the sin of the golden calf elevated that idol to the redeemer which took Bnei Yisrael out of Mitzrayim, all festivals are a reminder of the Exodus. G'd repeated the legislation because it contained elements which demonstrated that he who observed these commandments expressed his opposition to idolatry by doing so. He also mentioned Sabbath observance since the observance of the Sabbath counteracts the previously performed idolatry. Just as idolatry cancels all merits one ever accumulated by performing G'd's commandments, so the observance of the Sabbath is considered as observance of all the commandments and a form of rehabilitation for the idolatry one was guilty of previously. Compare my comments at the beginning of Parshat Vayakel.

כי אוריש גוים מפניך, "For I will dispossess nations from your presence, etc." In the event that you would feel empathy with the nations whom you displace, Hashem assures us that we would not even see the remnants of these nations, i.e. מפניך, "out of the sight of your face."

והרחבתי את גבולך, "and I will expand your borders, etc." This may be understood in accordance with Gittin 57 which claims that the boundaries of the land of Yisrael will expand in direct proportion to the Jewish population in the country.
